title: Inside the Vercel intern experience
description:
The best way to learn is by shipping product to users in production, and that's why we don’t treat our interns as temporary guests. Every intern at Vercel is expected to operate like a core part of our engineering team from day one.

This past winter, we welcomed a small cohort of those interns to our headquarters in San Francisco. Over an intense four months, they contributed to some of our most important products: the CDN, v0, financial infrastructure, AI Gateway, and more. They shipped features used by millions, helped close the gap for enterprise deals, and in more than a few cases, left a mark that will outlast their time here.

Meet the Winter '26 intern cohort

Yash Kothari, CDN Team

University of Waterloo

What Yash shipped:

Yash's internship spanned the full CDN stack, from infrastructure to CLI to UI in the dashboard.

His first major project was Project-level routing, which is part of the new CDN tab in the Vercel dashboard. This feature lets customers update routing rules, including redirects, rewrites, and header transforms, from the dashboard, API, CLI, or SDK, without needing to redeploy their project or touch a single line of code. Yash built the underlying API endpoints (including a staging/publish workflow), the vercel routes CLI commands, and contributed AI-powered route generation. Right after launch, hundreds of teams immediately adopted it and created thousands of rules.

"One of my favorite things about my internship was that at Vercel you get a lot of autonomy and ownership," Yash said. "I hopped on calls with enterprise customers, saw my work featured on Vercel's changelog, and demoed my work in a live YouTube community session."

In the second half of his internship, Yash worked on Vercel's Firewall and Security products. He shipped the vercel firewall CLI command, enabling users and AI agents to configure custom rules, IP blocks, and firewall controls directly from the terminal. He also built an AI-powered Firewall Rule Builder that lets users describe a desired rule in natural language and generates a WAF custom rule automatically.

Kavin Valli, v0 Team

University of Waterloo

What Kavin shipped:

Kavin worked across the full v0 platform over four months, taking on projects that ranged from user-facing features to cost efficiency for the system’s backend infrastructure.

He started by building Folders and v0 Projects end-to-end: core CRUD operations, a library page redesign, favoriting, visibility controls (private/team/public), and folder sharing. He also closed a critical gap in v0's version history by shipping the manual commit button, which ensured that manual edits in the VM editor properly created commits and blocks, which closed the loop between manual edits and v0's iteration model.

His highest-leverage work came later in the term, when he focused on VM and sandbox infrastructure. By splitting VMs into tiered pools and routing smaller projects to a cost-efficient default pool, Kavin significantly reduced memory usage and infrastructure cost for roughly 80% of sandboxes.

"I worked on v0 and got thrown into the deep end pretty quickly, especially around the v1 launch," remembered Kavin. "It was a bit chaotic at times, but that's something I actually enjoyed."

His final and most involved project was taking ownership of the v0 Slack agent. He shipped Slack preview deployments for safe testing, rebuilt the router agent with improved thread history and SAML re-auth resume, redesigned project context tracking, and built out the full PR flow including v0 labels, Slack thread links, and merged/closed state tracking. The result was an agent that went from rough around the edges to something teams can genuinely rely on.

Mingchung Xia, Financial Infrastructure Team

University of Waterloo

What Mingchung shipped:

Mingchung pushed over 250 PRs in four months and became one of the top contributors on Vercel's central control systems monorepo.

His most externally visible project was the v1/billing/charges API endpoint and the vercel usage CLI command, which let users view their usage and costs in the standardized FOCUS v1.3 FinOps format. Originally scoped as a full-internship project, Mingchung completed it early and expanded its scope into a joint launch with Vantage. The work was subsequently adopted by Meta, Notion, Porsche, and other prominent companies to analyze their Vercel spend in a modern, compliant format.

His most technically complex project was designing and building Vercel's core entitlements system, which is the infrastructure that enables granting, revoking, and provisioning entitlements across project-based monetization, add-ons, enterprise, and marketplace work streams. The system architecture incorporated strong and eventual consistency guarantees, async and synchronous derivations, transactional outboxing, write-ahead logs, plan change manifests, stale-validation sentinels, and materializations. It was rolled out to production and backfilled across all active subscriptions.

"Most companies don't give interns or even existing engineers the opportunity to touch payment systems or billing infrastructure, let alone own it end to end," explained Mingchung. "Correctness is imperative when you're working with money, and I got to experience that firsthand at Vercel."

He finished his internship by shipping Vercel Buy, a new billing service supporting frictionless purchasing for agent credits, gateway credits, v0 credits, and pro subscriptions, complete with a CLI surface.

Mingchung will be joining Vercel full-time on the Financial Infrastructure team after completing his degree.

Kevin Thomas, v0 Team

University of Waterloo

What Kevin shipped:

Kevin's work spanned ML infrastructure, enterprise features, reliability engineering, and incident response, often simultaneously.

His most ambitious self-directed project was v0's auto model routing system: a full pipeline that automatically routes user prompts to the right model tier based on complexity. Kevin proposed the system, built the labeling pipeline, experimented with multiple classifier architectures (embedding-based MLP classifiers, TF-IDF baselines, fine-tuned TinyBERT), and integrated everything into TypeScript-only functions for production deployment. By launch, the system had processed over 1.4 million v0 messages and became the default for all non-enterprise users, reducing decision fatigue and latency for a very large share of v0's user base.

"From working on on-call incidents and vulnerabilities in month one to working directly with enterprise customers in April, I've gotten to work on an unusually wide range of meaningful problems," Kevin said at the end of his internship.

In the latter half of his internship, Kevin focused on enterprise work, most notably the v0 × Snowflake integration. He built enterprise admin controls for model access, RBAC for team skill management, resolved issues in SAML and isolated tenant environments, and shipped the integration itself. This work directly unblocked enterprise customers, supported renewals, and addressed live customer issues.

Kevin also served as a primary investigator for several incidents around signup, billing, auth, and account access, staying at the center of v0's reliability work throughout his term.

Sylvie Zhang, AI Gateway Team

University of Pennsylvania

What Sylvie shipped:

Sylvie worked across the AI Gateway service, contributing to everything from database and backend logic to observability, the frontend, and documentation.

Her first project was Price Strikethrough, surfacing provider MSRP as a strikethrough price alongside Gateway pricing, making provider discounts visible to end users. It touched the full stack and gave her a complete view of the AI Gateway product from the start.

"All that sounded daunting to a student like me with little experience," Sylvie said, "but it was the best learning experience I could have asked for."

Her most impactful and technically demanding project was the AI SDK v5 → v6 endpoint migration for AI Gateway's OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic-compatible endpoints. As the AI provider landscape had grown significantly more complex since v5 was designed, maintaining the legacy version had become a bottleneck, especially for handling token usage granularity differences across providers. Sylvie led the migration with a disciplined approach: deep cross-provider knowledge to catch incorrect AI-generated assumptions, systematic multi-turn and cross-provider testing scripts, concurrency testing to surface race conditions, proactive customer communication, and a deliberate fallback strategy that left legacy code in place until the migration proved stable.

The result was a cleaner, more maintainable Gateway service better equipped to handle the continued evolution of AI providers and models.

Advice for future interns

We asked these interns to share their top advice for future cohorts.

Take ownership from day one

Vercel gives interns real autonomy, but that means it's on you to use it well. Don't wait to be assigned work. Take initiative, identify what needs to be done, and start shipping.

Ask questions

Every intern said the same thing: no one at Vercel makes you feel like a burden for asking. The team genuinely wants you to succeed, so use that to your advantage and ask.

Work in public

Share your PRs in team channels. Post updates. Present at Demo Days. The feedback loop is fast, and the visibility helps you iterate and build trust faster.

Talk to people outside your team

Some of the best conversations happen across team lines with engineers, designers, finance, and people in roles you've never considered. Go to the office. Grab lunch with someone new.

Give yourself time to ramp up

The codebase, the culture, and the pace can be a lot at once. Don't rush. The first few weeks are for absorbing, not sprinting. Take time to ramp well, and you will be able to run fast.

Apply to become a Vercel intern

There are additional internship opportunities coming soon. If you want to join our next cohort, check our career site in September to apply.

title: Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) is now supported on Vercel CDN
description:
Vercel CDN now supports Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) for domains managed by Vercel DNS. ECH encrypts the Server Name Indication (SNI) in the TLS handshake, the last part of an HTTPS connection that revealed which hostname a client was connecting to. With ECH, network observers see a connection to Vercel's shared ECH hostname, vercel-ech.com.

ECH is managed at the platform level and automatically enabled selectively where supported, starting in the US for a limited number of TLDs, and expanding to more TLDs and regions over time.

Recent versions of Chrome, Edge, and Firefox support Encrypted Client Hello.

Learn more about ECH and how Vercel CDN protects your application in the CDN encryption documentation.

title: Sign JWTs from your Functions without managing private keys
description:
Vercel KMS lets you sign JWTs and arbitrary messages from your Vercel Functions using managed asymmetric signing keys, so private keys never live in your code or environment variables. Your function authenticates with its Vercel OIDC token, and the private key stays inside Vercel's key management service while verifiers use only the public key.

With Vercel KMS you can:

  • Create and rotate issuers and signing keys (RSA and ECDSA) from the CLI and dashboard.

  • Sign JWTs with custom claims and a configurable TTL, or sign raw bytes, using the @vercel/kms package.

  • Grant a project signing access per environment, including production, preview, development, and custom environments.

  • Constrain the claims a project can request per grant, and validate token claims against a JSON Schema.

  • Verify signed tokens anywhere. Each issuer publishes a public OpenID Connect Discovery document at https://kms.vercel.com/<issuerId>/.well-known/openid-configuration and a JWK set at https://kms.vercel.com/<issuerId>/jwks.json, so any standard OIDC or JOSE library can validate tokens without Vercel-specific code.

Sign a token inside a function:

Verify a token anywhere with a standard JOSE library, using the issuer's public JWKS:

Set up an issuer and grant a project access from the CLI:

As a best practice, create a separate issuer per project and environment. Isolating issuers keeps each token audience distinct, scopes signing access to exactly one project and environment, and lets you rotate or revoke keys for one without affecting the others.

To get started, read the docs or open Key Management in your team's dashboard.

title: The Vercel Sandbox CLI is now more agent-friendly
description:
The Sandbox CLI version 4.0.1 ships four output and error improvements:

  • New sandboxes point users towards how to connect into them.

  • A sandbox not found error shows where to look for existing sandboxes.

  • Common mistakes, like typing a command after sh, redirect to the command that was intended.

  • Outdated installs show an update notice when they create a new sandbox.

Each of these messages now carries the action to take next instead of leaving you to work it out.

New sandboxes tell you how to connect

create and fork output now ends with a connect hint, so a fresh sandbox never leaves you wondering what to type next.

Not found errors point you to your sandboxes

When a command references a sandbox that does not exist, the error is quiet and actionable instead of a raw API dump. Setting DEBUG=sandbox:errors restores the request detail for debugging.

A misused command explains the right one

sh opens a plain interactive shell, so it takes no command of its own. The CLI can now return precise answers that rewrite the attempt into the command that does what you meant, whatever the command is.

Outdated installs warn you at creation time

create, sh, and run check for a newer published CLI and print an update notice when the install is behind. The check is cached to a file and refreshed at most once per hour; when a lookup does run it happens concurrently with the creation request, so it adds no latency. Creation defaults, such as the base image, are chosen client side, so an outdated global install silently keeps old defaults. Prerelease versions skip the check, and SANDBOX_SKIP_VERSION_CHECK=1 disables it.

Learn more in the Sandbox CLI documentation.

title: $1 million hacker challenge for Vercel Sandbox
description:
Agents need to run untrusted code, and the microVM has become the standard way to do it: a dedicated guest kernel per workload, isolated from the host and from every other workload on the same machine.

But recent security research and real-world incidents have revealed that agents running untrusted code do not need to cross a VM boundary to escape containment; they only need one network path the security model failed to account for, which we explained in our post A sandbox without a network boundary is only half a sandbox.

Isolation only holds if both sides of it hold: the Firecracker microVM and the host-side network controls. Recently our CTO pointed an open-weight model with no safeguards at Vercel Sandbox. It did not escape, but it mapped the guest kernel, built a VM to reproduce its ideas, and wrote a fuzzer.

Defenders have first-mover advantage, but it won't last forever, and the choice is when to test the boundaries (we strongly encourage building a scanning program, which you can do on any budget with an open-source tool like deepsec and AI Gateway).

We are proactively choosing to test Vercel Sandbox on our own schedule, not an attacker's, and we are doing it in the open, with the best researchers in the world.

So for two weeks, we are paying up to $1,000,000 USD to the researchers who can escape a Vercel Sandbox.

The challenge

Starting today, Vercel is running a two-week public HackerOne program focused on Vercel Sandbox isolation.

  • Program: Public HackerOne program, open to all eligible researchers

  • Window: Tuesday, August 18 to Tuesday, September 1, 2026, or earlier if the reward pool is exhausted

  • Max per report: $50,000 USD, for a vulnerability that lets a threat actor read or modify another Vercel tenant's data

  • Total pool: Up to $1,000,000 USD in total payouts

Bounties are paid per report, scoped to a single root cause, and assigned by Vercel triage based on the maximum demonstrable impact. The full bounty table, detailed scope, and the list of known-duplicate classes are on the HackerOne program page.

How Vercel Sandbox is built

Vercel Sandbox runs on bare-metal EC2 hosts. Each sandbox gets its own Firecracker microVM with a dedicated guest kernel, and inside that microVM a Linux container runs the operator's code. The microVM, not the container, is the security boundary, so operator-supplied code runs two layers removed from the host. We assume that code is fully hostile: root inside the container, full kernel access inside the microVM, and motivated to reach the host or another tenant.

The network side of the boundary is enforced on the host, outside the microVM, where code inside the sandbox cannot modify or disable it. The sandbox firewall intercepts outbound TCP and DNS, checks each connection against the operator's domain and CIDR policies, and can inject credentials at the boundary so they never enter the microVM.

What we're looking for

In short: anything that breaks the sandbox boundary.

  • Compute boundary: Escaping the Firecracker microVM to the EC2 host, or reaching another tenant's sandbox through the compute layer (reading, modifying, or executing code in it), or crashing another tenant's sandbox from within another sandbox

  • Network boundary: Defeating the sandbox firewall without crossing the microVM: reaching destinations the operator did not authorize, exfiltrating data, or retrieving brokered credentials

Container namespace escapes that only reach the Firecracker guest OS are not in scope. Namespaces are a developer-experience feature, not the security boundary.

Bounties

Severity

Bounty

Critical

$25,000 – $50,000

High

$10,000 – $25,000

Medium

$5,000 – $10,000

Low

$1,000 – $5,000

The full bounty table, with example vulnerability classes for each tier, is on the HackerOne program page.

How to participate

The program is open now and closes on Tuesday, September 1, 2026, or earlier if the $1,000,000 USD reward pool is exhausted. Reports go through the HackerOne program page.

To reproduce a finding, boot a sandbox with the @vercel/sandbox SDK and demonstrate the impact with a live proof of concept. The default sandbox OS is enough for most reports; bring a custom image from the Vercel Container Registry only if your PoC needs extra tooling. We will not reward static-analysis-only findings; to issue a payout, we need to see the boundary break.

Full rules, eligibility, the complete scope and bounty table, and the submission process are on the HackerOne program page.

Results and payouts

We will triage reports from the day the program opens through one month after it closes. As findings are confirmed, we will pay bounties, ship fixes, and credit every researcher whose report holds up. The techniques discovered during this program will become permanent additions to the sandbox boundary, protecting every workload on Vercel long after the challenge ends. After the program closes, we will publish a follow-up writeup of the techniques and the fixes we shipped.

Thanks to HackerOne for standing up the program, and to the researchers who will spend the next two weeks trying to break what we built.

For example, use it to:

  • Investigate incidents: Ask why a deployment failed or what’s causing a runtime error. It investigates and explains what it found.

  • Write and review code: Work with your team and Agent to fix build and CI failures, review pull requests with production context, or turn a decision from the thread into a tested PR.

title: Updates to Hobby and Pro Terms of Service
description:
We are updating the Terms of Service for Hobby and Pro customers, effective October 19, 2026. The updates clarify some existing Vercel practices, expand terms on topics such as managed accounts and credits, and reflect applicable legal requirements, including certain cancellation and service-change rights for eligible consumers in the UK and EU.

Credits and billing

A new section sets out how credits work: plan-included credits expire at the end of the subscription term and purchased credits expire one year after purchase unless stated otherwise in the relevant credit purchase terms. Credits can only be used to pay Vercel fees, have no cash value, and are nontransferable. Credits are generally nonrefundable, but unused purchased credits are refunded if Vercel terminates your account without cause.

The Terms also clarify that credit purchases are billed in advance, subscriptions auto-renew unless you turn off renewal, and third-party pass-through rates may change when provider rates change. ⁠⁠

Managed accounts

Renewal and cancellation

You can turn off auto-renewal and cancel or downgrade through account settings or Support. Cancellation or downgrade generally takes effect at the start of the next renewal period. The Terms also explain statutory withdrawal and refund rights for eligible consumers.

Service changes

Eligible consumers in the UK and EU may cancel the affected subscription free of charge if a change has more than a minor negative impact on their access to or use of the Services. They have 30 days from notice or the change, whichever is later, and may receive a prorated refund of prepaid amounts for the remaining period.

Other updates

The service-specific provisions have been moved to a dedicated Service Terms page. The Terms also clarify sanctions-related obligations, including that use of the Services must not be in connection with or for the benefit of a sanctioned person under applicable laws.

title: Death to long-lived static credentials
description:
Fifteen years ago, TLS was something you'd use to protect the most sensitive areas of your app. Then Google, Let's Encrypt, the EFF, and others led the push for HTTPS everywhere, making encryption the default for every request. Without it, anyone between the browser and server can read and tamper with the traffic.

OAuth, OIDC, DBSC, and related standards already provide building blocks for secure authentication, but standards alone do not make secure methods the norm. HTTPS needed tooling that made encryption easy and a sustained push that made it expected. Machine-to-machine authentication still resembles HTTPS in 2010, with some vendors and enterprises leading the way while long-lived static credentials remain the default for many SaaS vendors and infrastructure providers.

At Vercel, we want to make fast and secure the default across the web, including in our own services and the integrations in our Marketplace. We’ve built OIDC UI, a shadcn/ui registry that gives providers trust-policy forms and token verification code. We’re expanding OIDC support across Vercel and setting new authentication requirements for Marketplace providers.

Long-lived static credentials are insecure

Long-lived static credentials are secrets such as API keys and database passwords that applications keep reusing, often with no expiration. As agents take on more useful work, we give them access to our systems, tools, and data through credentials that can grant permissions far beyond the task at hand.

Those credentials can leak into a code repository or chat, be stolen when a service or dependency is compromised, or be exposed when prompt injection leads an agent to reveal them. However it happens, an attacker can use the credential with the permissions it grants until it expires or is revoked. Recent credential-theft and supply-chain incidents across the industry show why encryption at rest isn’t enough when malicious code can read an application’s credentials in production.

Rotating exposed credentials takes time and coordination across the systems that use them, and mistakes can disrupt production. At Vercel, we’ve previously spent thousands of engineering hours on multiple, very painful key rotations out of an abundance of caution, and we never want to have to do this again.

Better solutions already exist

With OIDC, your application can authenticate without storing a long-lived provider key. A trusted issuer provides a signed, short-lived token identifying the application, and the receiving service verifies that token before deciding what access to grant.

A stolen token stops working when it expires, limiting how long that copy can be used even if the leak goes unnoticed. Your application can obtain fresh credentials programmatically, removing the need to distribute and manually rotate a persistent provider key across the systems that use it.

We’ve been prioritizing OIDC across Vercel so applications can access Blob, AI Gateway, and Sandbox without storing long-lived keys for those services. Our OIDC federation has been generally available since 2024, letting applications running on Vercel exchange Vercel-issued identity tokens for temporary AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure credentials under configured project and environment trust policies. But for developers to stop managing long-lived keys, that support has to extend to all the services their applications depend on.

The rest of the web hasn’t followed

We surveyed more than 1,000 SaaS vendors and found that only 8.4% supported secure authentication methods.

But getting vendors to support secure authentication is only part of the problem. Even when a service offers a secure method, developers often choose a static key because it can be simpler to use. We see three main barriers to broader adoption:

  • Tooling and setup that make secure authentication more complicated than using a static key.

  • Added latency from fetching or exchanging tokens on the request path.

  • Weak incentives for vendors to offer and prioritize secure authentication.

Our goal is to make secure authentication the default on Vercel, while also using our Marketplace to help push more vendors to support it.

Our commitment to a more secure web

We have a responsibility to make this change practical across the services we run, the tools developers use, and the integrations we build with partners.

Make secure authentication easier to use

Using a secure token has to be easier than pasting a key, or developers will keep pasting keys. On Vercel, code retrieves an OIDC token with a function call, and a custom audience specifies the service intended to receive it.

With Vercel Connect, applications and agents use their deployment identity to request provider tokens at runtime, without having to store long-lived provider secrets in environment variables. Once the connector is configured and linked to the project and the user’s account is connected, code can request a token for that user with scopes the provider supports.

We’re also extending OIDC support across the Vercel API and CLI to remove the need for long-lived Vercel tokens in deployment workflows.

OIDC UI for API providers

OIDC UI is a shadcn/ui component registry with a trust-policy configurator and a server-side token verifier. It includes provider forms for Vercel, GitHub, GitLab, Google, Bitbucket, AWS, Azure, and custom OIDC issuers. A provider can let customers configure trust for a particular Vercel project’s production environment, then verify incoming tokens against that policy without building the configuration interface and verification code from scratch.

Reduce the performance cost of secure authentication

A static key in an environment variable is already available when a function runs, so reading it requires no network request. Fetching a token or exchanging it for provider credentials can add network latency, so reducing those calls is part of making secure authentication practical.

Vercel Functions receive a platform-issued token in the request header, which the SDK reads without fetching another. The platform reuses unexpired tokens, while Vercel Connect caches provider tokens in process and refreshes them near expiry. Custom-audience and provider exchanges require network calls.

For example, an application can use the Azure SDK to access Cosmos DB with temporary credentials instead of a database key. With Azure configured to trust the Vercel project and its default token audience, the callback supplies a Vercel OIDC token to ClientAssertionCredential, which exchanges it for the Azure access token used by CosmosClient.

Give providers an incentive to support secure authentication

The Vercel Marketplace offers access to third-party databases, content management systems, observability tools, and more. Our goal is for all of these vendors to support short-lived, identity-based authentication, whether they accept OIDC tokens directly or exchange them for temporary credentials. We’re working to make integrations configure that authentication automatically when developers connect a service, so it does not require a separate setup step.

HTTPS everywhere did not win on ergonomics alone. Chrome put a “Not secure” label on plain HTTP, and then it set deadlines. Now we are setting ours. By November 30, 2026, vendors who do not support OIDC auth from Vercel to their services and use long-lived secrets for authentication will have a similar “Not secure” message on their listing. By January 2027, vendors who do not offer secure auth will be delisted. We are holding the Vercel API and our own native integrations to the same bar.

From static to dynamic

Fifteen years ago, encrypting every request felt like overkill. Today, the padlock is so normal that we only notice when it's missing. Secure authentication between services should become just as routine, so developers can connect the systems they need without storing another long-lived secret. Going from static to dynamic has always been the Vercel mission. It started with pages, and now it’s credentials.

Additional resources

  • OIDC federation covers how deployments get short-lived identity tokens, with guides for AWS, GCP, Azure, and your own API.

  • Custom OIDC token audiences scopes each token to the one service meant to receive it.

  • Vercel Connect requests short-lived, scoped provider tokens at runtime, so code and agents never store credentials.

  • Vercel Connect guides walk through building agents this way, from Slack bots to GitHub agents.

title: Snooze Desk: a local Gemma reads my GitHub notifications while I sleep
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

I have a confession. Most mornings I open GitHub, see the notification count, and close the tab. Then I feel guilty about it all day. Somewhere in that pile is a person waiting on my review, sitting right next to three dependency bumps and someone offering me free stars.

So I built Snooze Desk, a lazy developer's overnight desk.

While I sleep, it does the boring part:

  • A durable Temporal workflow pulls my GitHub notifications.
  • A local Gemma model running in Ollama sorts each one into needs-you, can-wait or ignore.
  • For the ones that need me, it drafts a reply that quotes real details from the notification, like the line number in a stack trace or the number of changed components in a PR.
  • It writes a short morning digest, so the first thing I read is three lines, not forty tabs.

In the morning I open one dark screen. Red means something needs my attention. Green means it is handled. For each draft I can approve, edit, reject or snooze. Snoozing starts a Temporal durable timer with a live countdown, and the item comes back when the timer fires. The timer lives in Temporal, not in a browser tab.

Who gets to be lazier: anyone with a noisy GitHub inbox. During Hacktoberfest, that is probably you.

Demo

Code

RockingThor / snooze-desk

Lazy developer's overnight desk: local Gemma, Temporal and Sentry triage your GitHub notifications while you sleep. DEV Hacktoberfest 2026 entry.

Snooze Desk 🌙

The lazy developer's overnight desk — Process GitHub notifications with local AI while you sleep.

A Hacktoberfest 2026 Open-Source AI Challenge project (Week 3: "Slow and Steady").

What It Does

Snooze Desk runs a durable Temporal workflow that processes your GitHub notifications overnight using a local Gemma model. Wake up to:

  • A 3-line morning digest summarizing what needs your attention
  • Smart classification: needs-you (red), can-wait (gray), or ignore
  • AI-drafted replies for issues and PRs that need a response
  • One-click actions: approve, edit, snooze, or reject each draft
  • Durable snoozing: workflow sleeps for hours or days, survives restarts

Everything runs locally. Your notifications never leave your machine. Zero API costs.

Why Open-Source AI?

  1. Privacy: All processing happens on your laptop. No data leaves your machine.
  2. Zero cost: No API keys, no usage fees. Run it forever for free.
  3. Offline-capable: Works without internet…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

The stack is Next.js for the desk, the Temporal TypeScript SDK for the overnight job, Ollama running Gemma for the thinking, Octokit for GitHub, and Sentry for tracing every model call.

Temporal does the waiting

The whole night is one Temporal workflow. Fetching notifications, classifying each one, writing the digest and posting an approved reply are all activities. That matters because a local model is a flaky dependency. With Temporal, a failed step gets retried, and the workflow picks up where it left off instead of starting over.

Snooze is a Temporal timer too. When I say "not now", the workflow just sleeps. It is the most relatable code I have ever written.

Gemma does the sorting

The classifier sends each notification to Gemma and asks for strict JSON back. My first prompt was simple. It turned out to be too simple, and Sentry is how I found out.

Sentry shows me what actually happened

Every model call is a Sentry span with op ai.inference, named classify_notification or generate_digest_summary. Each span carries the model name, the prompt version, input and output token counts, Ollama's load and eval durations, and the Temporal workflow id and attempt number. The Ollama HTTP call shows up as a child span.

On October 22 I did 7 live runs on a Linux box with 8 CPU cores and no GPU. I used six sample notifications that I know the right answers for: three that need me, a dependency bump and a friendly praise thread that can wait, and one spam message. Sentry accepted every envelope, 54 out of 54.

Here is what the traces told me:

Model Prompt Classify mean ms, min to max Input tokens, mean Output tokens, mean Tokens per second Digest ms Correct
gemma3:1b v1 1734, 1502 to 2081 215 71 44.3 1390 3 of 6
gemma3:1b v2 2926, 2417 to 3276 351 88 45.9 1991 3 of 6
gemma4:e4b v1 58123, 41556 to 71342 222 428 7.8 56679 5 of 6
gemma4:e4b v2 49195, 37485 to 65936 358 414 8.8 53766 6 of 6

[SCREENSHOT: Sentry Explore, Traces, filtered to the hacktoberfest-live environment, showing trace cc23c06aaa094eaea9dac4f2b95b6571 where Gemma 4 sorts all six correctly]

Finding one: the small model says yes to everything. gemma3:1b is fast, under 3 seconds per notification on CPU. It also labelled all six notifications needs-you. That includes one titled "FREE GITHUB STARS! Click here now!!!". So it scored 3 of 6, and only because three of them really did need me.

I assumed my prompt was bad, so I wrote a v2:

  • clear rules for each label, including "spam stays ignore even when it mentions you"
  • five few shot examples
  • the reason first, then the label
  • a JSON schema that only allows the three labels
  • temperature 0

On gemma3:1b this changed nothing. Still 3 of 6, still excited about free stars. At that point it is not a prompt problem, it is a model size problem.

Finding two: Gemma 4 gets it, and the better prompt makes it faster. gemma4:e4b got 5 of 6 with my original prompt. The one miss was the praise thread, which it thought needed me. With v2 it got 6 of 6, and the mean classify time dropped from 58.1 seconds to 49.2 seconds.

Finding three: Gemma 4 thinks more than it says. It produced around 400 output tokens for a JSON answer that is only a few lines long. That suggests hidden reasoning tokens. On a CPU at about 8 tokens per second, those extra tokens are where the time goes. A full run of six notifications plus the digest used 5205 tokens.

So the final setup is gemma4:e4b with prompt v2 for sorting, where being right matters, and gemma3:1b for the digest, where a quick friendly summary is all I need. About 50 seconds per notification sounds slow, but this runs while I am asleep. I am not in a hurry. That is the whole point.

As for cost: the model runs on my own machine, so there is no API bill at all. Sentry was on the free plan.

The night I unplugged the model on purpose

I wanted to see what happens when things break, so I killed Ollama in the middle of a run, right inside the first classify call.

[SCREENSHOT: Sentry Issues page showing the ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:11434 error and the SocketError other side closed error]

Sentry caught it right away: SocketError: other side closed, then connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:11434. The first attempt ended with an error status. Temporal waited and retried. I started Ollama again, and attempt 2 succeeded, cold model load included. The workflow went on and finished all six notifications. I did nothing except restart Ollama, which is exactly the amount of effort I like.

[SCREENSHOT: Trace 7c93349423c940d88d49e00f027c6900 with attempt 1 in error and attempt 2 ok]

The bug Sentry found before it bit me

This test also exposed a real bug. Before the fix, the classifier caught connection errors and quietly returned can-wait. So if Ollama was down all night, I would wake up to a calm digest saying nothing needed me. That is the worst kind of bug: it looks like good news.

Now a connection error makes the activity throw, so Temporal retries it properly. In the trace, it shows up as an error you cannot miss.

One honest gap: there is no single parent span per workflow yet, so one trace can hold several workflow runs from the same worker. Linking traces to the Temporal workflow id is next on my list.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

My GitHub notifications include private repos, security reports and the occasional grumpy comment. I do not want to send all of that to a server I do not control just to find out it can wait.

With Snooze Desk, the model runs on my own machine through Ollama. The notification content goes from GitHub to my laptop and nowhere else. The only content that leaves is a reply I approve, and it goes back to GitHub. Sentry is optional, and the spans carry timings, token counts and labels, not the notification text.

Open weights also made the debugging story possible. Because I could run two Gemma sizes side by side, change the prompt, and read every token count and timing, I could prove that the small model was the problem and not my prompt. With a closed API, I would have been guessing behind a paywall.

It also costs nothing to run. A tool that works while you sleep should not send you a bill in the morning.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Gemma: Gemma 4 E4B sorts the notifications and Gemma 3 1B writes the digest, all running locally in Ollama.
  • Best Use of Temporal: the whole night is a durable workflow with activity retries that survived a real model outage, plus durable timers for snooze.
  • Best Use of Sentry Agent Tracing: every model call is traced with tokens, latency, prompt version and retry attempt, and the traces found both a model quality problem and a silent failure bug.

Thanks for reading. I am going back to bed now. Snooze Desk has it covered.

title: GPT-4o and GPT-4.1 API Retirement: The January 14 Migration Checklist
description:
OpenAI published a deprecation notice on October 14 with a date that is
already uncomfortably close: on January 14, 2027, GPT-4o, GPT-4o mini,
GPT-4.1 and GPT-4.1 mini leave the API. Not the chat app. The API that
your code, your cron jobs and your agents call. That is 92 days of
warning, against OpenAI's own policy of six months. I read the notice,
the pricing pages and four independent migration writeups, then wrote
down the 10 checks I would run on any production system before touching
a single model name.

The short answer

On January 14, 2027, five OpenAI snapshots stop answering: gpt-4o-2024-08-06, gpt-4o-2024-11-20, gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18, gpt-4.1-2025-04-14 and gpt-4.1-mini-2025-04-14. The listed replacement is gpt-6-luna, which is dramatically cheaper on paper but is a reasoning model with different tool-calling behavior. Audit every model reference this week, test Luna on your own traffic, and finish the switch by mid-December so January is a monitoring month, not a firefight.

What is actually retiring

OpenAI's deprecations page is short and worth reproducing exactly, because paraphrasing model IDs is how migrations break:

Retiring snapshot Shutdown date Recommended replacement
gpt-4o-2024-08-06, gpt-4o-2024-11-20 January 14, 2027 gpt-6-luna
gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18 January 14, 2027 gpt-6-luna
gpt-4.1-2025-04-14 January 14, 2027 gpt-6-luna
gpt-4.1-mini-2025-04-14 January 14, 2027 gpt-6-luna

Two lines from that page carry most of the weight. First: "Fine-tuned versions of these models follow the same shutdown schedule as their underlying base models." Your ft-gpt-4o custom model dies the same day. Second: the notice itself is the anomaly. OpenAI's own page sets a minimum notice of six months for generally available models, and this one gives 92 days. The policy carries an exception for safety or compliance retirements, but I found no statement from OpenAI tying this notice to that clause. Read it as it is: an unusually short window.

Check 1: one of the retiring snapshots dies today

Before touching the January deadline, check the one that is already here. A separate notice from April 22, 2026 retires an older wave of models on October 23, 2026. Today. That wave includes gpt-4o-2024-05-13 (the very first GPT-4o snapshot), gpt-4-turbo, gpt-3.5-turbo, gpt-4.1-nano, o1, o3-mini and o4-mini.

If your codebase pins any of these, something may already be failing while you read this. The recommended replacements for this wave are the GPT-5.6 family (gpt-5.6-terra, gpt-5.6-sol, gpt-5.6-luna), not Luna, so do not blend the two migration lists. And keep December 11 on your radar too: the o3-2025-04-16 snapshot retires then, separate from both waves.


The main app gets attention. The silent failures live in the auxiliary tooling: the code review bot configured a year ago, the changelog summarizer in CI, the script that labels support tickets. They keep working until the day they don't. Grep everything, not just the repo you are proud of.

Check 2: find every pinned reference

This is the boring check that catches the expensive bugs. Search your code, your infrastructure and your vendor configs for the retiring model IDs:

grep -rn "gpt-4o-2024-08-06\|gpt-4o-2024-11-20\|gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18\|gpt-4\.1-2025-04-14\|gpt-4\.1-mini-2025-04-14" \
  --include="*.py" --include="*.ts" --include="*.js" --include="*.json" \
  --include="*.yaml" --include="*.yml" --include="*.env*" .

Do not stop at the app code. Check CI workflows, prompt files, agent definitions, Docker build args, Terraform, and any .env or secrets manager that stores a model name. Then check the tools you did not write: plugins, no-code automations and third-party integrations often hardcode a model ID at install time, and their vendors may or may not have migrated you. If your stack stores the model name in an environment variable, a single config change flips the whole system. If it does not, this migration is also the moment to start.

Check 3: do not forget the fine-tunes

I keep repeating this because teams keep missing it: fine-tuned versions follow the base model's shutdown schedule. A fine-tune on GPT-4o is not a separate asset with its own lifecycle; it is a lease that expires with the base model.

The uncomfortable part is the replacement story. The reported model pages list fine-tuning as "Not supported" on gpt-6-luna, which means a model swap is not a plan for fine-tune teams at all. You need a retraining target: either a model that supports fine-tuning, or a rewrite of the workload as a prompted pipeline on Luna with enough evals to prove the quality holds. Either way, start the eval work now, because retraining on a new base model needs its own data and its own timeline, and January is closer than it feels.

Check 4: Azure buyers get three extra months

If you call OpenAI models through Azure, the dates differ. Microsoft's retirement schedule (last updated September 23, 2026) lists April 14, 2027 for the gpt-4o and GPT-4.1 snapshots that OpenAI itself removes on January 14. The very first GPT-4o snapshot, gpt-4o-2024-05-13, retires on Azure on December 9, 2026.

Treat the April date as planning buffer, not an exemption. Being pinned to Azure buys you time to migrate carefully; it does not buy you immunity from the migration. If your deployment spans both direct OpenAI API calls and Azure endpoints, migrate to the direct-API date. The system is only as durable as its earliest deadline.

Check 5: understand the 92-day notice

OpenAI's normal minimum is six months for generally available models. The October 14 notice gives 92 days. That is a third shorter runway than its own policy, with no reason stated.

There is exactly one official escape hatch I could verify: OpenAI says that in some cases developers may be able to provision dedicated capacity for continued access after a model's shutdown date, arranged through the sales team. That is an enterprise conversation with enterprise pricing, not a migration plan. If you need it, start that conversation now, because sales cycles do not respect deprecation calendars.

The honest read of the short notice is that model retirements are becoming routine. OpenAI, Anthropic and Google all deprecate older generations on a couple of years' cycle. Any pipeline that hardcodes a single model ID has a built-in expiry date, and the professional response is not outrage. It is a model layer you can swap, which is what Check 9 is about.

Check 6: GPT-6 Luna is a reasoning model, not a drop-in swap

This is the trap the headline writers skip. Luna is dramatically cheaper per token, but it does not behave like GPT-4o or GPT-4.1, and the differences are exactly the kind that pass a smoke test and fail in production:

  • It reasons by default. Luna's reasoning.effort defaults to medium, and reasoning tokens are billed as output tokens. The same request can produce far more output tokens on Luna than on GPT-4o, so per-token prices do not translate directly to per-request costs.
  • Tool calls need the right API. Function calling through the Chat Completions API needs reasoning_effort set to none. Combining reasoning with tools requires the Responses API. If your agents call tools through Chat Completions, this is a code change, not a config flip.
  • Parameters change. Enabling reasoning drops temperature, top_p and logprobs that GPT-4.1 supported. If your prompts rely on temperature tuning for variety or consistency, expect different behavior and retest.

Set reasoning_effort to none if you want the closest thing to 4o-style behavior and cost. My recommendation: only enable reasoning for workloads where you have measured that it improves the output. Reasoning is a cost you choose, not a default you accept.

Check 7: run the bill math before believing the headline

The headline number is real and it is misleading at the same time. Standard list prices per million tokens:

Model Input Output Fine-tuning
GPT-4o $2.50 $10.00 Supported
GPT-4o mini $0.15 $0.60 Supported
GPT-4.1 $2.00 $8.00 Supported
GPT-4.1 mini $0.40 $1.60 Supported
gpt-6-luna $0.10 $0.50 Not supported

Against GPT-4o that is 25x cheaper on input and 20x on output. But a worked example from the cost analysis tells the fuller story: on a month of 200M input and 20M output tokens with reasoning off, Luna costs $30 against $42 for GPT-4o mini. The saving is real. But at the default medium reasoning effort, the saving evaporates once Luna's reasoning tokens pass about 24M a month, roughly 1.2x the visible output. One reported catch: once a prompt exceeds 272,000 input tokens, the input rate doubles and the output rate rises 50 percent for the whole request.

So do the math on your own traffic, with your own reasoning effort setting, not on the headline ratio. I ran through this exercise myself on my own API bills in my real cost of running an AI SaaS work, and the pattern holds every time: the headline price is the least important number in your bill.

Check 8: test the replacement on your own data

Every careful writeup agrees on this step, and they are right. A newer model formats answers differently, follows the same instructions differently and costs differently. Move a copy of real traffic, not a curated sample, and compare three things: output quality against your existing evals, output format stability (parsers downstream of the model are the first casualty of a swap), and cost at your actual volume.

If you have no evals, write a small one before the migration. Ten to twenty representative prompts with recorded expected outputs is enough to catch the big regressions. Shadow-run Luna beside the retiring model for a week and diff the outputs. The teams that get hurt by model retirements are never the ones that tested; they are the ones who treated the swap as a config change.

Check 9: pin the replacement so this does not happen again

The deeper lesson from this retirement is architectural. Pinning a dated snapshot does not avoid migration; it trades "whenever the alias is retargeted" for "the retirement date on the provider's schedule," which at least you can plan around. That is strictly better, and it is what made this checklist possible at all.

For the next cycle, build the swap point once:

  1. Read the model name from an environment variable or config service, never hardcode it in application code.
  2. Pin to dated snapshots in production so a provider-side alias change cannot surprise you mid-week.
  3. Keep a per-workload mapping of model to API surface (Chat Completions vs Responses), so the next forced move is a table update, not an archaeology dig.

Model lifecycles in the API era are a couple of years at best. The teams that survive them calmly are the ones whose model choice is a row in a config file, not a string buried in twelve repos.

Check 10: the timeline I would follow

Deadlines work when they are earlier than the real one. Mine:

  • This week: run Check 2 across every repo, config and vendor integration. Inventory fine-tunes (Check 3) and note which workloads call tools (Check 6).
  • By mid-December: finish evals and shadow runs (Check 8), complete the bill math (Check 7), and switch production traffic. December is for migration; January is for monitoring.
  • January: watch error rates and costs on the new model for two weeks. Keep the old code path behind a feature flag until you are confident, then delete it. Dead code referencing dead models is how the next retirement surprises you.

What I would actually do

If I were handed this on Monday morning, I would not start with Luna. I would start with the grep, because in my experience the inventory is always worse than the team believes: at least one model reference will be hiding in a place nobody remembers. Then I would split workloads by tool use. Anything that calls tools through Chat Completions either gets reasoning_effort: none on Luna or moves to the Responses API, and that decision is per workload, not per company. Fine-tune owners get the uncomfortable conversation early, because retraining has its own timeline and January does not negotiate. The price drop is genuinely good news, but I would treat it as a bonus discovered after the migration is proven, not as the reason for it.

Frequently asked questions

Which OpenAI models retire on January 14, 2027?

Five snapshots across four models: gpt-4o-2024-08-06, gpt-4o-2024-11-20, gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18, gpt-4.1-2025-04-14 and gpt-4.1-mini-2025-04-14. The notice was posted on October 14, 2026, which is only 92 days of warning. Fine-tuned versions of these models follow the same shutdown date as their base model.

What should I migrate to instead of GPT-4o or GPT-4.1?

OpenAI's deprecations page lists gpt-6-luna as the recommended replacement for all five retiring snapshots. It costs $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens against $2.50 and $10 for GPT-4o, but it is a reasoning model with different tool-calling behavior, so it is not a drop-in swap.

Does my fine-tuned GPT-4o model keep working after January 14?

No. OpenAI states plainly that fine-tuned versions of these models follow the same shutdown schedule as their underlying base models. A fine-tune on GPT-4o dies the same day as GPT-4o, and gpt-6-luna does not support fine-tuning, so fine-tune teams need a retraining plan on a different model, not just a model swap.

Why is GPT-6 Luna not a simple drop-in replacement?

Luna is a reasoning model that defaults to medium reasoning effort, and reasoning tokens are billed as output tokens. Function calling through Chat Completions needs reasoning_effort set to none; combining tools with reasoning requires the Responses API; and turning reasoning on drops temperature, top_p and logprobs that GPT-4.1 supported.

Does Azure OpenAI retire GPT-4o on the same date?

No. Microsoft's retirement schedule, last updated September 23, 2026, lists April 14, 2027 for the gpt-4o and GPT-4.1 snapshots that OpenAI removes on January 14. Azure buys you three extra months of buffer, not an exemption. Plan to be migrated by January anyway.

What happens if I miss the January 14 deadline?

API requests to the retired model IDs start failing after that date, which means whatever still names them goes silent: chatbots, triage scripts, code review bots, summarizers. In some cases OpenAI says developers can provision dedicated capacity for continued access after shutdown through its sales team, but that is an enterprise escape hatch, not a plan.

The money angle

Retirement deadlines are consulting gold. Every team pinned to GPT-4o or GPT-4.1 needs the same three things between now and mid-December: an audit, an eval-driven migration, and a bill review. If you offer OpenAI migration work to clients, this is your outreach angle for the next six weeks, and it expires on January 14. The same playbook applies to every future retirement, so the first engagement builds you a reusable offer.


If your production system calls GPT-4o or GPT-4.1 and you want the audit and migration handled by someone who has done it before, reach out through the contact section on my homepage. I take on a small number of API migration and cost-optimization engagements each month.

Sources
