title: Chrome DevTools: The Complete Guide for Developers and Testers
description:
Chrome DevTools is a set of tools built into the Chrome browser that lets you look inside any web page. You can see its HTML, change its styles, run JavaScript, watch network requests and measure how fast it loads, all without installing anything.

Developers use it to build and debug pages. Testers use it to find out why a page misbehaves, reproduce bugs and check what the browser is really sending and receiving. Anyone who works on the web ends up opening it sooner or later.

The tool also keeps changing. Google ships DevTools updates with every Chrome release, and recent versions added AI help, better performance tracing and an official server for AI coding agents. This guide covers the basics, the panels, the newer features, mobile debugging, practical testing workflows, advanced techniques, the Chrome DevTools Protocol and a shortcut cheat sheet. It ends with how HeadSpin lets you use DevTools on remote real devices.

What Are Chrome DevTools (Chrome Web Developer Tools)?

Chrome DevTools, also called Chrome Web Developer Tools, is a group of debugging and analysis tools that ship inside Google Chrome. They run in the browser itself, so they see exactly what Chrome sees. That includes the live DOM, the CSS that was actually applied, every network call and the JavaScript running on the page.
Anything you change in DevTools only affects your current session. Refresh the page and it goes back to normal, which makes it a safe place to experiment.
DevTools helps with three kinds of work.

  • Building. Try CSS and layout changes live before touching source code.
  • Debugging. Pause JavaScript, inspect variables, and trace errors to their source.
  • Testing and analysis. Check network traffic, storage, accessibility and performance, and reproduce issues on different screen sizes and connection speeds.

How to Open Dev Tools in Chrome

There are several ways to open DevTools in Chrome, and the right one depends on what you want to look at first.

  • Press F12, or Ctrl+Shift+I on Windows and Linux, or Cmd+Option+I on Mac
  • Right-click any element on the page and choose Inspect, which opens the Elements panel on that element
  • Press Ctrl+Shift+J (Cmd+Option+J on Mac) to jump straight to the Console
  • Press Ctrl+Shift+C (Cmd+Shift+C on Mac) to turn on the element picker, then click anything on the page
  • Open the Chrome menu, then More tools, then Developer tools

Once DevTools is open, you can dock it to the right, bottom or left of the page, or pop it out into its own window. Press Ctrl+Shift+D (Cmd+Shift+D on Mac) to cycle through dock positions. Press Escape to show or hide the drawer, which holds extra tools like the Console, Rendering and Network conditions.
The Command Menu is worth learning on day one. Press Ctrl+Shift+P (Cmd+Shift+P on Mac), start typing what you want, such as "screenshot" or "disable JavaScript", and pick it from the list.

Chrome DevTools Panels Explained

Each panel answers a different question. Here are the ones you'll use most.
1. Elements
The Elements panel shows the live DOM and the CSS applied to each element. You can edit text, add or remove attributes, toggle styles and see the box model for any element.

  • Edit HTML and CSS and see the result immediately
  • Force states like :hover, :focus and :active
  • Debug Flexbox and Grid layouts with visual overlays
  • Check computed styles, accessibility properties and event listeners

2. Console
The Console shows errors, warnings and messages logged by the page, and lets you run JavaScript against it directly.

  • Read JavaScript errors with stack traces
  • Run code snippets against the current page
  • Use helpers like $0 (the selected element), $$('selector') and copy()
  • Filter messages by level, source or text

3. Sources
The Sources panel is where you debug JavaScript. You can open files, set breakpoints, step through code and watch variables change.

  • Add line, conditional and logpoint breakpoints
  • Step over, into and out of functions
  • Read original code through source maps
  • Save changes locally with Workspaces and Overrides

4. Network
The Network panel records every request the page makes, with timing, headers, payloads and responses.

  • Filter by type, such as Fetch/XHR, JS, CSS and images
  • Inspect request and response headers and bodies
  • Throttle the connection to simulate slow networks
  • Export a HAR file or copy a request as cURL or fetch

5. Performance
The Performance panel records what the browser does while a page loads or runs, and shows it as a timeline.

  • Find long tasks that block the main thread
  • See layout, paint and scripting costs
  • Throttle the CPU to simulate slower devices
  • Review Core Web Vitals and built-in insights

6. Memory
The Memory panel helps track down leaks and heavy memory use.

  • Take heap snapshots and compare them over time
  • Record allocation timelines
  • Find detached DOM nodes that never get cleaned up

7. Application
The Application panel shows what the page stores in the browser.

  • Inspect cookies, localStorage, sessionStorage and IndexedDB
  • Check service workers, caches and web app manifests
  • Clear site data with one click
  • Simulate offline mode and storage limits

8. Lighthouse
Lighthouse runs automated audits and gives a score with specific fixes.

  • Audit performance, accessibility, best practices and SEO
  • Run in mobile or desktop mode
  • Get a list of issues ranked by impact

9. Recorder
The Recorder captures a user flow, such as logging in or checking out, and lets you replay it.

  • Record clicks, typing and navigation
  • Replay flows and measure their performance
  • Export them as Puppeteer or other test scripts

10. Privacy and Security
This panel flags problems with certificates, mixed content, cookies and other security-related behavior that can break a page or put users at risk.

  • Spot mixed content and certificate errors
  • Review third-party cookie behavior
  • Check how the page handles privacy-related features

New Chrome DevTools Features Worth Knowing

DevTools moves quickly. These recent additions, announced across releases from Chrome 134 to the September 2026 release, are the ones most useful to developers and testers. Feature availability can vary by Chrome version and region.
1. AI Assistance
Chrome now has built-in AI help in DevTools. You can ask questions about styles, network requests and performance traces, and get explanations of Console errors. Since Chrome 147, it can pick the right context automatically, so you can ask open questions like "What are the slowest network requests?" without selecting anything first.
2. Chrome DevTools for Agents (MCP Server)
The Chrome DevTools MCP server lets AI coding agents drive a real Chrome browser. They can inspect the DOM, read network requests and console messages, run Lighthouse audits and record performance traces. It's useful for teams trying AI-assisted debugging and testing.
3. Better Performance Tooling
The Performance panel keeps getting smarter. It now includes calibrated CPU throttling, performance insights that explain issues in plain terms, support for soft navigations and the ability to export traces with source maps and resource content so teammates can open the same data.
4. Updated Device Mode
Device Mode now groups presets by form factor, including mobile, foldables, tablets and desktops, and adds newer devices like recent iPhone, Pixel, Galaxy Z Fold and iPad Pro models. The toolbar was also refreshed.
5. Faster Network Debugging
Recent Network updates include editing and resending a request as fetch from the Console, automatic decoding of gzip and deflate response bodies, and a safer curl copy for Windows command prompts.
6. Stronger Memory Analysis
The Memory panel can now filter and sort heap snapshot data by retained size, query objects by property name and give clearer errors when a snapshot can't be parsed.
7. Smarter CSS Debugging
The Elements panel shows inactive styles that no longer match, supports regex filters in the Styles and Computed panes, and has editors and badges for newer CSS features. Keyboard accessibility has also improved across the panel.
8. Application Panel Additions
The Application panel gained an Ads section showing ad density, CPU and network use by ads, plus easier cookie flag editing.
Testing Responsive and Mobile Layouts with Device Mode
Device Mode lets you see how a page looks and behaves on different screen sizes without leaving your desktop. Open it with Ctrl+Shift+M (Cmd+Shift+M on Mac), or click the device icon at the top left of DevTools.

What You Can Do in Device Mode

  • Choose a device preset like an iPhone, Pixel or iPad, or drag the edges to set any size
  • Rotate between portrait and landscape
  • Change the device pixel ratio to test sharp or blurry images
  • Throttle the network and CPU to mimic slower phones and connections
  • Simulate touch input, geolocation, device orientation and sensors
  • Capture screenshots, including full-page ones

A Simple Responsive Test Pass

  • Start at the smallest width your site supports, around 320 pixels.
  • Slowly widen the viewport and watch where the layout breaks.
  • Add a breakpoint check at each major width, such as tablet and desktop.
  • Switch to landscape and check navigation, forms and images.
  • Turn on network throttling and reload to see how the page loads on a slow connection.

Where Device Mode Falls Short
Device Mode is an emulation, not a real phone. It doesn't reproduce a device's actual GPU, memory limits, touch behavior, browser quirks or battery behavior. Mobile Safari on iOS also uses a different engine from Chrome. Treat Device Mode as a fast first check, then confirm on real devices before you call a layout done.

Remote Debugging Mobile Devices with Chrome DevTools

Remote debugging lets you inspect a page running on a real Android phone from DevTools on your computer. You can see the DOM, console, network traffic and performance of the actual device.

How to Set Up Remote Debugging on Android

  • On the phone, turn on Developer options, then enable USB debugging.
  • Connect the phone to your computer with a USB cable.
  • In Chrome on your computer, open chrome://inspect#devices and make sure "Discover USB devices" is checked.
  • Accept the debugging prompt on the phone.
  • Open a page in Chrome on the phone. It appears under your device in the list.
  • Click Inspect to open a DevTools window for that page.

You can also turn on screencast to see the phone's screen inside DevTools and interact with it from your computer.

What About iPhones and iPads?
Chrome DevTools can't attach to pages on iOS. For iPhones and iPads, testers use Safari Web Inspector from a Mac, or a remote device platform that exposes the right debugging tools.

Common Limits

  • You need a cable, a driver setup on some systems and a device in your hands
  • Each person can only debug devices that are physically connected to their machine
  • Distributed teams can't easily share a single device lab

Those limits are the main reason teams look at remote real device platforms, which is covered later in this guide.

Chrome DevTools for Testers: 10 Practical Workflows

Testers get the most out of DevTools when they use it as a way to ask the browser what's really going on. These ten workflows come up again and again.
1. Check API Calls in the Network Panel
Open the Network panel, filter by Fetch/XHR and perform the action you're testing. Confirm the endpoint, method, status code, payload and response match what the spec says. Many "UI bugs" turn out to be a failed or malformed request.
2. Copy Requests to Postman or cURL
Right-click any request and choose Copy as cURL. Paste it into a terminal or import it into an API tool to replay the call, change values and check how the backend handles them.
3. Simulate Slow and Offline Connections
Use the throttling menu in the Network panel, or the Network conditions tab in the drawer. Try Fast 4G, Slow 4G and Offline, and watch for spinners that never stop, missing fallbacks and broken error messages.
4. Force Errors with Overrides and Blocking
You can block a specific request or override a response with Local Overrides. This lets you see how the page behaves when an API returns a 500, an empty list or unexpected data, without waiting for the backend team to break something.
5. Watch the Console for Hidden Errors
Keep the Console open while you test. Uncaught exceptions, failed resource loads, CORS errors and deprecation warnings often show up there before a user sees anything wrong.
6. Reproduce Bugs on Different Devices and Locations
Use Device Mode and the Sensors tab to change screen size, user agent, locale and geolocation. It's a quick way to reproduce bugs that only show up for certain users.
7. Run Accessibility Checks
Run a Lighthouse accessibility audit, check color contrast in the Styles pane, inspect the accessibility tree and use the Rendering tab to emulate vision deficiencies. Axe and similar extensions work inside DevTools too.
8. Inspect Cookies and Local Storage
In the Application panel, check what the site stores. Confirm that login tokens expire, consent choices are saved and sensitive data isn't sitting in localStorage. You can edit or delete values to test how the app reacts.
9. Record and Replay User Flows
Use the Recorder to capture a flow like sign-up or checkout. Replay it after each change to catch regressions, or export it as a Puppeteer script to seed an automated test.
10. Measure Page Performance
Run Lighthouse for a quick score, then use the Performance panel to find what's slowing a page down. Look at Largest Contentful Paint, Interaction to Next Paint and layout shifts, and check results with CPU and network throttling turned on.

Advanced Debugging Techniques

Once the basics feel comfortable, these techniques help with harder problems.
1. Use Smarter Breakpoints
A plain line breakpoint stops every time. Conditional breakpoints stop only when an expression is true, and logpoints print a message without pausing at all. You can also pause on DOM changes, XHR or fetch calls and specific event listeners, which is handy when you don't know which code changed something.
2. Ignore Third-Party Code
Add libraries and framework files to the ignore list so stepping and call stacks skip them. You see your own code instead of wading through bundled code.
3. Debug with Source Maps
When code is minified or compiled, source maps let DevTools show your original files. Make sure they're available in the environment you're debugging, and you can step through TypeScript or JSX as written.
4. Edit Files with Workspaces and Overrides
Connect a local folder as a Workspace to save CSS and JavaScript changes straight to your source files. Use Local Overrides to keep edits to a live site's files between reloads, which is useful for testing a fix on production before shipping it.
5. Hunt Memory Leaks
Take a heap snapshot, perform the action you suspect, take another and compare. Growth that never gets cleaned up, such as detached DOM nodes, points to a leak. Repeat the action several times so real leaks stand out from normal caching.
6. Read Performance Traces
Record a trace during the slow action. Look for long tasks on the main thread, forced reflows, and heavy scripting. Throttle the CPU so problems that hide on a fast laptop become visible.
7. Find Unused Code
The Coverage tool shows how much of each JavaScript and CSS file actually ran on the page. Large unused portions are good candidates for code splitting or removal.
8. Debug Rendering Problems
The Rendering tab can highlight paint areas, layout shift regions and scrolling issues, and emulate print media, dark mode and reduced motion. It's often the fastest way to find out why a page flickers or jumps.

What Is the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP)?

The Chrome DevTools Protocol is the interface DevTools itself uses to talk to the browser. It's a set of commands and events, sent as JSON over a WebSocket connection, that lets outside programs inspect and control a Chromium-based browser.
The protocol is split into domains, such as Page, DOM, Network, Runtime, Emulation, Input and Performance. Each domain has commands you can call and events you can listen to.

How CDP Works

  1. Start Chrome with remote debugging turned on, for example chrome - remote-debugging-port=9222 - user-data-dir=/tmp/profile.
  2. Open http://localhost:9222/json/version to find the WebSocket address.
  3. Connect to it and send JSON commands such as Network.enable or Page.navigate.
  4. Receive events like Network.responseReceived as things happen on the page.

Recent versions of Chrome require a separate user data directory when you use the remote debugging port, so include - user-data-dir as shown.

When to Use CDP
CDP is a good fit when you need fine control over a Chromium browser, like capturing network traffic, emulating devices, collecting performance data or intercepting requests. It only works with Chromium-based browsers, so cross-browser tests still need other approaches.

Chrome DevTools Keyboard Shortcuts Cheat Sheet

Using Chrome DevTools with HeadSpin

Local DevTools is great for what's on your desk. It gets harder when the bug only appears on a certain device, network or country. HeadSpin lets you use the Chrome DevTools you already know on browsers running on remote real devices.

How HeadSpin Connects DevTools to Remote Devices
Integrating Chrome DevTools with HeadSpin brings the power of real-world testing into your debugging workflow, allowing you to test mobile browsers on real devices from any remote location. Here's how you can achieve this:

  1. Open an Android device in HeadSpin.
  2. Under 'Remote Debug' in the Tools section, copy the command. A prerequisite for Remote Debugging is the HeadSpin CLI. Here's how you can install it.
  3. Paste the command in your terminal. This will bridge the remote device to your local system.
  4. Open the webpage you want to inspect, on the remote device
  5. On Chrome Browser, open chrome://inspect to see the connected device and inspect it.
  6. Select your remote device and click inspect.
  7. This opens DevTools on your device.

HeadSpin allows users to remotely leverage Chrome DevTools on real mobile browsers from any location. By providing access to real devices through its global infrastructure, HeadSpin enables testers to use Chrome DevTools for debugging, performance monitoring, and network testing directly on actual mobile devices, no matter where they are located.

What You Can Do

  • Debug real mobile and desktop browsers on devices in global locations without owning them
  • Use the same Elements, Console, Network and Performance panels you use locally
  • Connect Puppeteer, Playwright or WebdriverIO to the same remote browser through the proxy
  • Run Lighthouse audits from the Lighthouse CLI against remote browsers
  • Share devices across a distributed team instead of passing phones around

title: Rewriting a JSON File in Place Let My Reader See It Half-Written: Temp File, fsync, os.replace and Three Traps
description:
Now and then my page-building script died with JSONDecodeError: Expecting value: line 1 column 1 (char 0), reading a JSON index of video clips that looked perfectly fine when I opened it a second later. Another script rewrote that index every time a new clip landed, and most of the time the two got along.

Nothing was corrupting the file. The reader was opening it during the short window when the writer had emptied it and not yet finished filling it back in.

Disclosure: I make an Android camera app. Nothing below uses its code or describes how it stores anything. Every script here ran on one Linux machine with Python 3.10.12, in a throwaway folder, and the outputs are pasted unedited.

What the tests showed:

  • open(path, 'w') empties the file before you write a byte. A reader polling the file while it was rewritten failed far more often than it succeeded.
  • A crash in the middle of that write loses the old version too. Killing the writer left a fragment on disk and nothing to fall back to.
  • Write a temporary file next to the real one, then os.replace it into place. With that change the same reader did not see a single broken file.
  • The pattern has three traps around it: a temp folder on another filesystem, file permissions, and symlinks. Each one showed up in a few lines of test code.

Test one: a reader polling a file that is rewritten in place

The writer dumps a list of clip names into index.json with the usual with open(PATH, 'w'). A thread reads and parses the same file in a loop for as long as the writer is busy.

import json, os, sys, threading, time

PATH = "index.json"
clips = [{"name": "clip_%05d.mp4" % i, "bytes": 1000 + i} for i in range(20000)]

def write_in_place(n):
    for _ in range(n):
        with open(PATH, "w") as f:
            json.dump({"clips": clips}, f)

def read_loop(stop, seen):
    while not stop.is_set():
        try:
            with open(PATH) as f:
                json.load(f)
            seen["ok"] += 1
        except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
            seen["bad"] += 1
            seen.setdefault("first", str(e))

write_in_place(1)
stop, seen = threading.Event(), {"ok": 0, "bad": 0}
t = threading.Thread(target=read_loop, args=(stop, seen))
t.start()
write_in_place(200)
stop.set(); t.join()
print("good reads:", seen["ok"], "| failed reads:", seen["bad"])
print("first error:", seen.get("first"))

good reads: 162 | failed reads: 904
first error: Expecting value: line 1 column 1 (char 0)

Two different failures show up across runs. char 0 means the reader opened the file after open(..., 'w') had truncated it and before any data arrived, so it parsed an empty file. On another run the first error was Unterminated string, which means the reader caught the file partly written. Either way, the reader got a file that was not any valid version of the index.

The exact counts change from run to run, because they depend on how the two threads happen to interleave. What stayed the same across every run I did is that failures were common, not rare. A bigger file means more time between the truncation and the last byte, which gives a reader more chances to land in between.

Test two: the writer dies halfway

A separate process opens the index for writing, writes the first half of a new version, flushes it, and then sits there. The parent kills it with SIGKILL, which stands in for a crash or an out-of-memory kill.

import json, os, signal, subprocess, sys, time

PATH = "index.json"
json.dump({"clips": ["clip_00001.mp4"]}, open(PATH, "w"))
print("before:", os.path.getsize(PATH), "bytes, valid JSON")

child = r'''
import json, time
f = open("index.json", "w")
f.write('{"clips": ["clip_00001.mp4", "clip_00002.mp4"')
f.flush()
time.sleep(30)
f.write("]}")
'''
p = subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, "-c", child])
time.sleep(1)
p.send_signal(signal.SIGKILL)
p.wait()
print("writer exit status:", p.returncode)
print("after:", repr(open(PATH).read()))
try:
    json.load(open(PATH))
except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
    print("JSONDecodeError:", e)

before: 29 bytes, valid JSON
writer exit status: -9
after: '{"clips": ["clip_00001.mp4", "clip_00002.mp4"'
JSONDecodeError: Expecting ',' delimiter: line 1 column 46 (char 45)

The old index was valid before the child started. Once the child opened the file in 'w' mode, the old version was gone, and the new one did not finish. Any program that reads this file after the crash gets the fragment.

This is the case that hurts more than the torn read, because retrying does not help. The reader in test one could try again a moment later and succeed. Here the file stays broken until something rewrites it.

The fix: build the new version beside the old one, then swap

The idea is that the real path should not point at a half-built file at any moment. Write the complete new version to a temporary file in the same folder, make sure it is on disk, and then rename it over the real name in one step.

Python's documentation for os.replace describes the step that makes this work: "If successful, the renaming will be an atomic operation (this is a POSIX requirement)." A reader that opens the path gets the old file or the new file, not a mixture.

import json, os, tempfile

def atomic_write_json(path, obj):
    path = os.path.realpath(path)
    folder = os.path.dirname(path)
    fd, tmp = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=folder, prefix=".tmp-", suffix=".json")
    try:
        with os.fdopen(fd, "w") as f:
            json.dump(obj, f)
            f.flush()
            os.fsync(f.fileno())
        try:
            os.chmod(tmp, os.stat(path).st_mode & 0o7777)
        except FileNotFoundError:
            os.chmod(tmp, 0o644)
        os.replace(tmp, path)
    except BaseException:
        try:
            os.unlink(tmp)
        except FileNotFoundError:
            pass
        raise
    dfd = os.open(folder, os.O_RDONLY)
    try:
        os.fsync(dfd)
    finally:
        os.close(dfd)

Line by line, the choices that matter:

  • os.path.realpath(path) resolves symlinks first. Trap three below shows why.
  • tempfile.mkstemp(dir=folder, ...) creates the temp file in the same folder as the target, not in the system temp folder. Trap one shows why.
  • f.flush() then os.fsync(...) pushes the new bytes to the disk before the rename, so the swap does not publish a name that points at data still sitting in a buffer.
  • The os.chmod copies the old file's permission bits onto the temp file. Trap two shows why.
  • On any exception the temp file is deleted, so a failed write does not leave clutter behind. A process killed outright skips that handler, so a fixed prefix like .tmp- also makes leftovers easy to find and sweep later.
  • After the rename, the folder itself is opened and fsynced. A rename is a change to the folder, not to the file, and this asks the operating system to write that change out as well.

Here is the reader from test one again, pointed at the new writer:

import json, threading
from atomic_write import atomic_write_json

PATH = "index.json"
clips = [{"name": "clip_%05d.mp4" % i, "bytes": 1000 + i} for i in range(20000)]

def read_loop(stop, seen):
    while not stop.is_set():
        try:
            with open(PATH) as f:
                json.load(f)
            seen["ok"] += 1
        except json.JSONDecodeError:
            seen["bad"] += 1

atomic_write_json(PATH, {"clips": clips})
stop, seen = threading.Event(), {"ok": 0, "bad": 0}
t = threading.Thread(target=read_loop, args=(stop, seen))
t.start()
for _ in range(200):
    atomic_write_json(PATH, {"clips": clips})
stop.set(); t.join()
print("good reads:", seen["ok"], "| failed reads:", seen["bad"])

good reads: 3034 | failed reads: 0

Every read parsed.

Trap one: the temp file lives on a different filesystem

It is tempting to call tempfile.mkstemp() with no folder and let it pick the system temp directory. The Python documentation for os.replace warns that "The operation may fail if src and dst are on different filesystems." On this machine /tmp and the project folder are on different disks, so that is easy to show:

import os, tempfile

fd, tmp = tempfile.mkstemp(dir="/tmp", suffix=".json")
os.write(fd, b'{"clips": []}')
os.close(fd)
print("temp file:", tmp)
print("same filesystem?", os.stat("/tmp").st_dev == os.stat(".").st_dev)
try:
    os.replace(tmp, "index.json")
except OSError as e:
    print(type(e).__name__, e.errno, e.strerror)
finally:
    if os.path.exists(tmp):
        os.unlink(tmp)

temp file: /tmp/tmp1c9a6qvr.json
same filesystem? False
OSError 18 Invalid cross-device link

Error 18 is EXDEV. A rename cannot move data between filesystems; it only relinks a name inside one. shutil.move, for example, falls back to copying when a rename fails across filesystems, and a copy is exactly the non-atomic write you were trying to avoid.

Whether /tmp shares a disk with your data depends on the machine, which is what makes this trap nasty: the same code can pass on a laptop and fail on a server, or the other way around. Creating the temp file in the target's own folder removes the question.

Trap two: the new file quietly gets different permissions

mkstemp creates its file so that only the owner can read and write it. That is a sensible default for a temp file, and a surprise once the temp file becomes your real one.

import json, os, stat, tempfile

PATH = "index.json"
json.dump({"clips": []}, open(PATH, "w"))
os.chmod(PATH, 0o644)
print("before:", stat.filemode(os.stat(PATH).st_mode))

fd, tmp = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=".")
with os.fdopen(fd, "w") as f:
    json.dump({"clips": ["clip_00001.mp4"]}, f)
os.replace(tmp, PATH)
print("after naive replace:", stat.filemode(os.stat(PATH).st_mode))

before: -rw-r--r--
after naive replace: -rw-------

The index went from readable by everyone to readable only by its owner. If a web server or a second user account reads that file, the first atomic write is the moment it starts getting PermissionError. Nothing in the writer fails, so the cause is easy to miss.

The os.chmod line in atomic_write_json copies the old mode across before the swap. Ownership is a separate matter: a rename keeps the temp file's owner, so if the old file belonged to a different user, the new one will not, and copying it back needs privileges a normal script does not have.

Trap three: a symlink gets replaced instead of followed

Suppose index.json is a symlink into a shared folder, and other programs read the shared copy.

import json, os
from atomic_write import atomic_write_json

os.makedirs("shared", exist_ok=True)
json.dump({"clips": []}, open("shared/index.json", "w"))
if os.path.lexists("index.json"):
    os.unlink("index.json")
os.symlink("shared/index.json", "index.json")

import tempfile
fd, tmp = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=".")
with os.fdopen(fd, "w") as f:
    json.dump({"clips": ["clip_00001.mp4"]}, f)
os.replace(tmp, "index.json")
print("naive: index.json is a symlink?", os.path.islink("index.json"))
print("naive: shared/index.json =", open("shared/index.json").read())

os.unlink("index.json")
os.symlink("shared/index.json", "index.json")
atomic_write_json("index.json", {"clips": ["clip_00001.mp4"]})
print("realpath: index.json is a symlink?", os.path.islink("index.json"))
print("realpath: shared/index.json =", open("shared/index.json").read())

naive: index.json is a symlink? False
naive: shared/index.json = {"clips": []}
realpath: index.json is a symlink? True
realpath: shared/index.json = {"clips": ["clip_00001.mp4"]}

The naive version replaced the link with a regular file. The shared copy kept its old content, and the program that wrote the update had no idea it had stopped updating the file everyone else reads. Resolving the path with os.path.realpath first, and creating the temp file in the real file's folder, writes through to the shared copy and leaves the link alone.

Hard links are a related case I did not script: a rename gives the name a brand-new file, so any other hard link to the old file keeps pointing at the old content.

Things I did not test

  • A real power cut. The fsync calls are there so that a successful return means the data and the rename have been handed to the disk. Whether a given disk honors that is a property of the hardware and filesystem, and a script cannot pull its own power cable.
  • Windows. os.replace exists there and overwrites an existing file, but how it behaves while another process holds the target open may differ from Linux, and none of these runs touched it.
  • Network filesystems and sync folders. Everything above ran on a local disk. A synced or network folder may not give a rename the same atomic behavior.
  • Several writers at once. Atomic replace keeps readers from seeing a broken file. It does not stop two writers from each building a version from stale data and the second one silently winning. That needs a lock, which is a different problem.

Sources. Quotes are from the os.replace entry in the Python os module documentation. Test results come from the scripts above, with the output pasted unedited. Test one was run several times, since its counts vary; the other scripts gave the same results when re-run.

If you want an old phone to record clips in the background so there is a folder worth indexing, the app I make is Background Camera RemoteStream on Google Play. Nothing above depends on it.

A file that other programs read should change by being replaced, not by being rewritten.

title: How to auto-trade the calls from a Discord trading server (without a bot token)
description:
How to auto-trade the calls from a Discord trading server (without a bot token)

Most people who trade from a Discord server do the same thing: a call lands, the phone buzzes, they open the broker app, type the ticket, and get filled somewhere between thirty seconds and never. The server is the signal. The human is the bottleneck.

I spent a while trying to close that gap with my own code, and I build Nyria now, which does it as a product. This post covers what I learned the hard way with a self-written bot, and then the setup I use today, which takes no bot token, no server and no code. Disclosure up front so you can weigh the rest.

The do-it-yourself route, and where it leaks

The obvious plan: create a Discord application, get a bot token, invite the bot to the server, listen for on_message, parse the text, hit the broker API.

@client.event
async def on_message(message):
    if message.channel.id != CALLS_CHANNEL:
        return
    text = message.content or embed_text(message)
    side, ticker = parse(text)
    broker.place_order(ticker, side, qty)

It works for an afternoon. Then the problems arrive in this order:

  1. Permissions. You can only invite a bot to a server where you have Manage Server. A paid room you merely belong to will not let you add one, and reading it through your own user account is against Discord's terms and gets accounts banned.
  2. Formats. Callers post plain text, embeds, screenshots, quoted tweets. Your parse() grows a case for each and still misses the one written at 9:31 in a hurry.
  3. Noise. The same channel carries "nice fill", questions and someone's lunch. Every false positive is a real order.
  4. Hosting. The listener has to be awake at 3 AM when the crypto call hits. Laptops sleep. Free tiers restart.
  5. Exits. An entry is one message; the exit is another, hours later, in different words. Matching them against what the account is actually holding is the part most home-grown bots never finish.

None of these are hard individually. Together they are a part-time job that pays nothing until the trading does.

The setup I use now

Nyria has its own Discord bot. You invite it to a server you run and it asks for one permission, View Channels. There is no token to manage, nothing to host, and it never reads messages on your personal account. The steps, in the order the app walks you through them:

1. Connect Discord. Integrations, Discord card, Connect Discord. Discord asks for two scopes: identify, to map your Discord user to your Nyria account, and guilds, to list the servers you belong to. That is all.

2. Create a strategy with Discord as the source. On the channel step, select Invite bot to server. You need Manage Server in that server, which is the same rule as any Discord bot. If the caller you follow runs the room and you don't, the fix is at the end of this post.

3. Pick the channel and narrow it. One channel per strategy. Add an Author filter when several people post in the same channel, and a Keyword filter such as ALERT when calls share the channel with chatter. The preview shows the last 25 messages so you can see exactly what the bot will read.

4. Teach it the format from real messages. On the strategy's Alert format card, assign one past message to each trade type you enable: long entry, long exit, shorts if you trade them. Nyria shows what each message would have traded. If it reads one wrong, assign a different message or change the strategy before any bot runs. Nobody in the channel changes how they write.

5. Deploy on paper first. Deploy bot, choose Nyria Paper, set a budget per entry. Paper is free and needs no card. Let a few calls fire and read each fill on the bot's Logs tab, next to the message that caused it.

6. Then the broker. When the paper fills track the posts, deploy a second bot on your Alpaca, Tradier, tastytrade or Charles Schwab account with the same sizing. The next message that passes the filters places a trade.

What a call needs to contain

A ticker, a direction and an action. The wording is the caller's own. These all read:

Entering BTC long at support
BTO AAPL 345c 11/20 @ 12.50
long SPY
STC SPY 772c
sold half, trimming the rest at 780

Embeds are read first, then a quoted tweet, then the plain text. A message with no size, no price and no venue, like long SPY, is still a complete alert: the strategy and the bot supply the size (budget per entry), the order type (market, or limit at the alert's price if it names one) and the account.

How exits work

Nothing waits at the broker between messages. An exit is an exit alert: STC SPY 772c, or a plain "sold" with no contract, closes what the entry opened in the same instrument, matched against what the bot is holding. The next move is always the next message.

This is the design choice that made my own bot hard: it forces you to think of the channel as the whole state machine, which is also why it holds up.

What to watch on the Logs tab

Every order sits beside the alert that caused it, with the receive time and the fill time to the millisecond. Every refusal does too, written in plain words: the budget per entry is lower than one unit costs, the message passed the filters but named no ticker, the market is closed for that asset. Nothing is ordered on a refusal. Read the log for a week on paper and you will know exactly which messages in that channel are trades and which are talk.

If you don't run the server

The bot can't join a paid Discord you only belong to, and nothing legitimate can. Two honest options:

  • Ask the caller to publish their calls as a strategy on Nyria. Members subscribe and deploy a bot in their own broker account; the caller gets paid per tier, through Nyria, Stripe or Whop. Many callers want this once they see their members are retyping every entry.
  • Run your own server for your own alerts: TradingView webhooks, a script, your own posts. Same setup, no permission problem.

Where to start

Make a free account at nyria.io, create a strategy with Discord as the source, point it at a channel you run and deploy a paper bot. No card, no token, no server to keep awake. When the paper fills match what the channel posts, you'll know whether it is worth pointing at a real account.

title: Node.js Message Queue Setup: Create, Publish, and Run Background Tasks
description:
The least complex Node.js setup to create a message queue and publish a background task is a durable queue with a worker that owns the deadline, an idempotency key, and a visibility timeout longer than normal processing time. For a B2B SaaS renewal reminder, a timer in the web process is a poor fit: deploys, crashes, and multiple instances turn a timer into an unreliable promise.

TL;DR: put a reminder job on a durable queue with its due time, have a worker claim it, and make the send operation idempotent. Start with an SLO such as 99.9% of reminders delivered within 60 seconds of their business deadline. Then size worker concurrency and retention from the deadline volume and retry policy, rather than from the queue's marketing description.

The page fires before the reminder does

The on-call page usually arrives as a queue-age alert: renewal reminders are sitting longer than the allowed delay, and the dashboard shows a growing count of due jobs. The visible symptom is late mail. The earlier signal was quieter: the worker's successful completions per minute had fallen below the rate at which reminders became eligible.

That distinction matters. A queue can be empty while the system is still wrong if the producer has stopped publishing, and it can be full while delivery remains inside the SLO if jobs are scheduled for tomorrow. Alerting on raw depth alone confuses planned waiting with operational backlog.

For a renewal workflow, I would trace the job through four timestamps: created_at, eligible_at, claimed_at, and completed_at. The alert should evaluate completed_at - eligible_at for eligible work, with a separate alert for a missing producer signal. The instrumentation change is small but consequential: publish a metric for eligible jobs, record queue delay and processing duration separately, and include the tenant and job id in structured logs without putting customer content there.

The threshold has a cost in both directions. Set it too low and a brief traffic burst wakes the on-call team for a queue that will drain before the deadline. Set it too high and the first page arrives after the renewal message has missed its business purpose. False positives consume the same finite on-call budget needed for database and payment incidents.

What should a Node.js background task actually own?

The application should publish a durable description of intent, not hold an open request until a calendar date. A renewal job might contain a tenant identifier, a renewal identifier, an eligible_at timestamp, a schema version, and an idempotency key. The worker resolves the current account state before sending; it does not trust a stale copy of the entire customer record embedded in the message.

The queue's job is delivery and temporary exclusion. The worker's job is business correctness. Those boundaries prevent a retry from accidentally sending a second reminder after a timeout, and they let the application change its worker pool without changing the API request path. A queue does not solve an ambiguous business deadline, an unbounded downstream dependency, or a missing idempotency record; those limits stay in the application design.

The main limitation is the extra operational boundary: someone must own retention, redelivery, dead letters, and capacity alarms. The trade-off is reasonable only when losing the job or holding a request open is more expensive than operating that boundary. For a low-volume internal reminder, a transactional database row and a periodic poller may be the better choice.

That is the whole trick.

Here is the smallest useful shape for a worker-side decision. The queue adapter is deliberately generic; a production adapter must implement the acknowledgement and visibility semantics of its chosen transport.

package reminder

import (
    "context"
    "time"
)

type Job struct {
    ID           string
    RenewalID    string
    EligibleAt   time.Time
    Idempotency  string
}

type Queue interface {
    Receive(context.Context) (Job, string, error)
    Ack(context.Context, string) error
    Retry(context.Context, string, time.Duration) error
}

type Sender interface {
    SendIfNew(context.Context, string, string) error
}

func Handle(ctx context.Context, q Queue, s Sender, now func() time.Time) error {
    job, receipt, err := q.Receive(ctx)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if wait := time.Until(job.EligibleAt); wait > 0 {
        return q.Retry(ctx, receipt, wait)
    }
    if err := s.SendIfNew(ctx, job.Idempotency, job.RenewalID); err != nil {
        return q.Retry(ctx, receipt, 30*time.Second)
    }
    return q.Ack(ctx, receipt)
}

The SendIfNew operation needs a durable uniqueness constraint, usually keyed by the business event and reminder type. An acknowledgement is not a transaction with the email provider or notification service. The worker can send successfully and crash before acknowledging, so at-least-once delivery requires deduplication. Exactly-once processing is not a property I would put in an SLO unless the complete side-effect path supports it.

EligibleAt also deserves a precise definition. If the business deadline is 09:00 in an account's local timezone, resolve that timezone when the reminder is created, store the resulting instant, and test daylight-saving transitions explicitly. A queue delay is measured from eligibility, not from the moment a customer first configured a renewal date.

Which queue boundary fits the failure mode?

The important comparison is operational, not fashionable. A managed queue generally reduces broker patching and quorum work, while a self-hosted broker can offer richer routing and local control at the cost of storage, upgrades, and a larger on-call surface. A Redis-backed library inside Node.js can be pleasant for application teams, but its durability and failure behavior depend on how Redis is operated.

Option Useful boundary Cost or risk to plan for Fit for renewal reminders
Amazon SQS Managed durable queue with visibility timeout and redelivery Less control over broker internals and routing semantics Good when the team values lower broker operations and can model work with simple queues
RabbitMQ Self-managed broker with acknowledgements and routing patterns Cluster storage, upgrades, partition behavior, and paging become team responsibilities Useful when routing topology is a real requirement, not just a preference
BullMQ Node.js job library backed by Redis, with delayed jobs and worker APIs Redis persistence, failover, and queue semantics remain part of the platform design Practical when the team already operates Redis and accepts that boundary
Build a database scheduler Familiar storage and transactional writes Polling, locking, index growth, and retry recovery become application code Reasonable at modest volume when a queue would add more machinery than it removes

This is a buy-vs-build decision with a capacity consequence. Suppose 120,000 reminders become eligible in a busy hour and the worker's measured end-to-end service time is 250 ms. A single worker slot can process about four jobs per second before overhead; 120,000 jobs in 3,600 seconds needs an average of 33.3 jobs per second. The design therefore needs more than nine continuously healthy slots, plus headroom for retries, downstream throttling, and deploys. I would provision and test closer to the peak concurrency implied by the SLO, not the average arrival rate. If the downstream provider permits only a much smaller rate, adding queue consumers makes the failure worse by increasing rejected work, so the worker pool needs a limiter as well as more capacity. That is a real boundary of queue-based scaling: storage absorbs bursts, but it cannot manufacture notification throughput.

The exact number is not a promise about any queue product. It is a capacity-planning example showing why queue depth is an output of worker capacity and deadline distribution. Measure the service time at the notification boundary, then include retry traffic in the arrival rate.

More workers are not always better.

Why does visibility timeout change the retry story?

Visibility timeout is the interval during which a received message is hidden from other consumers. It is not a processing lease that makes the work safe forever. If the worker runs longer than the interval without extending it, another worker can receive the same job while the first worker is still sending. If the timeout is enormous, a crashed worker can delay redelivery and push the reminder past its SLO.

Choose an initial timeout above the high percentile of normal processing time, then extend it while a long-running operation is genuinely making progress. Cap total attempts and route exhausted jobs to a dead-letter destination with enough metadata to diagnose them. The retry delay should respect downstream rate limits; immediate retries can turn one provider failure into a synchronized storm.

A useful test sequence is deliberately boring: claim a job, stop the worker, wait for the timeout, confirm redelivery, make the first attempt appear successful but skip acknowledgement, and confirm that the second delivery does not create a second reminder. Repeat it with a worker deployment and with a slow notification dependency. These are the cases that expose a design that looked correct in a unit test.

The queue API should also distinguish a transient failure from a permanent one. A malformed schema, deleted renewal, or rejected recipient may deserve a terminal state and an operator-visible record. A timeout from a notification dependency usually deserves retry. Treating every error alike produces either silent data loss or a retry queue that never drains.

The operational contract is the implementation

Before choosing a library, write down the contract. For this workflow I would specify a 60-second delivery SLO after eligible_at, a maximum retry age, a duplicate-send policy, an outage behavior, and the ownership of the dead-letter queue. The contract should say what happens when the business record changes between scheduling and execution; “send the latest valid reminder once” is more useful than “process the job exactly once.”

The dashboard needs at least these views: eligible backlog age, processing duration, retry count, dead-letter count, producer publication rate, and downstream response class. Logs should correlate the request, job, renewal, and idempotency identifiers. Traces are valuable across the publish, receive, and side-effect boundaries, but trace retention should not become the only audit record.

Deployments deserve a queue-specific runbook. Drain or pause consumers when a schema change is incompatible, preserve old workers until old messages are safe to consume, and use a versioned payload so a delayed reminder does not become an accidental migration test. Capacity alarms should distinguish a worker pool that is saturated from a downstream service that is rejecting requests.

My decision rule is conservative: use the simplest durable boundary that meets the latency SLO, supports idempotent side effects, and leaves the team able to explain redelivery at 02:00. A richer broker is justified by a concrete routing or throughput requirement. A database scheduler is justified by low volume and a willingness to own polling and locking. A queue is a poor choice for a single small process that can safely retry from its database, while a database poller is a poor choice once deadline volume makes lock contention and polling lag material. The queue name matters less than the failure contract around it.

Further reading

  • AWS, “Amazon SQS visibility timeout”: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-visibility-timeout.html
  • AWS, “Amazon SQS message timers”: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-message-timers.html
  • RabbitMQ, “Consumer Acknowledgements and Publisher Confirms”: https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms
  • BullMQ, “Introduction”: https://docs.bullmq.io/
  • OpenTelemetry, “Metrics data model”: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otel/metrics/data-model/

title: From app design to running React code, without redrawing a single screen
description:
The slow part of building an app from a design is rarely the logic. It is rebuilding every screen by eye: which button is which, how far apart the cards sit, what happens on tap. SVG Lab (svglab.app) now hands that over three ways, and all three shipped between 10 and 19 October 2026.

1. Download the screens as a React app

In SVG Lab, switch to Prototype mode, press Build prompt and choose Download React code. You get a React app (Vite) of your screens, on every plan, for up to 200 screens, in about a second.

npm install
npm run dev

The app follows the links and animations you set in Prototype mode: taps move between screens, tabs switch at once, switches flip, swiped rows go away, sliders drag, charts draw, and text effects such as Typewriter and Count up play when a screen opens. It is the front end only. The server, the data and sign-in are still yours to build.

2. Hand the design to Lovable, Bolt or v0

Same window, Copy prompt. The Build prompt lists every part of each screen with its position, its size and its words, how the screens link, and how each part moves at the timings you set. That means the coding tool knows which button is which without reading a picture. Copy prompt works without an account. Download with screen pictures adds a picture of each screen if your tool wants one.

3. Let your AI export native code through the SVG Lab MCP

If your screens were designed by an AI through the SVG Lab MCP and its Design Engine, the same AI can export them as HTML, React, SwiftUI, Jetpack Compose, Flutter, or a layered SVG for Figma. Colours and fonts come out as design tokens, every drawing and icon is its own file (an icon used on every card is one file), and you get one download link that lasts 7 days.

You can also ask Codex, Claude or another connected AI app to build the app in your own repo from a saved design. Give it the project's link or name. It reads each screen's layout (rows, columns, spacing, what stretches, where each button goes) and pulls your drawings and icons as SVG or PNG files, so the code uses the real design, not a redrawn copy.

The MCP is remote: add https://svglab.app/mcp as a connector and sign in with OAuth. Setup per app is on svglab.app/mcp-setup.

What it costs

  • Download React code: every plan, Free included. It uses one of your plan's exports (Free has 3 a month), checked before it starts and counted only once the file is ready.
  • Copy prompt: free, no account needed.
  • The SVG Lab MCP: 100 free credits once per account, one tool call is one credit. Plans start at Starter, $7 a month for 2,500 credits.

What it is not

SVG Lab (svglab.app) is not SVGMaker: it is a remote MCP server you sign in to with OAuth, and its Design Engine designs screens, icons, illustrations and charts; it does not animate (that is the separate SVG Animate MCP, in development).

The full write-up, with the step list and FAQ, is on the SVG Lab blog: How do you turn app designs into code?

title: Node.js Structured Summaries: JSON Schemas and Per-Tenant Cost Visibility
description:
Short answer: For structured JSON output in text summarization, use response_format with a JSON Schema, validate the parsed object, and choose a unified REST platform only when one key, one bill, and several backend capabilities reduce your tenant-accounting work.

For a logistics knowledge-base service, make the model output a JSON Schema contract, validate the parsed object, and record usage against the tenant before returning the answer. This keeps summary, key_points, and entities stable for downstream processing. Tenant identity and cost attribution stay outside generated text.

The request is narrow but consequential. A dispatcher may ask about a private carrier policy, and the answer may feed a search result, an audit record, or a follow-up workflow. A paragraph that looks correct in a chat window is not enough. The application needs a data shape it can reject.

What must remain invariant?

The summarizer should preserve four invariants:

  1. The model receives a schema that names every required summary field.
  2. The request sets response_format with type: "json_schema".
  3. The application parses JSON as data, never by slicing or pattern matching text.
  4. The parsed value is validated before it is stored, displayed, or used for another decision.

There is a fifth invariant for a multi-tenant logistics product: every request has a tenant identifier outside the model output. Do not ask the model to report its own cost. Attach the tenant to request context, then record provider metadata in the service that owns the request.

I initially treated the schema as a formatting preference. That was the wrong boundary. A schema is a small API contract, and a missing required field should fail close to the model call rather than surface later as a broken dashboard or incomplete shipment note.

That distinction matters.

How do I get structured JSON output for text summarization with a schema?

The model call can remain compatible with an OpenAI-style client while the surrounding application stays explicit about validation and accounting. This Python example uses the verified chat route through an environment variable so credentials and deployment configuration never become source code. The same JSON object can be sent from a Node.js client.

import json
import os
import time

import requests
from jsonschema import validate


SUMMARY_SCHEMA = {
    "name": "logistics_summary",
    "schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "additionalProperties": False,
        "properties": {
            "summary": {"type": "string"},
            "key_points": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}},
            "entities": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}}
        },
        "required": ["summary", "key_points", "entities"]
    }
}


def summarize(text: str, tenant_id: str) -> dict:
    payload = {
        "model": "glm-4-flash",
        "messages": [
            {"role": "system", "content": "Summarize the private logistics document. Return only the requested object."},
            {"role": "user", "content": text}
        ],
        "response_format": {"type": "json_schema", "json_schema": SUMMARY_SCHEMA}
    }
    headers = {
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}",
        "Content-Type": "application/json"
    }

    for attempt in range(3):
        response = requests.request(
            method="POST",
            url=os.environ["INFRAI_CHAT_URL"],
            headers=headers,
            json=payload,
            timeout=30
        )
        if response.status_code == 429:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            time.sleep(float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt)
            continue
        if not response.ok:
            raise RuntimeError(f"summarization failed: {response.status_code} {response.text}")
        break
    else:
        raise RuntimeError("summarization was rate limited after retries")

    content = response.json()["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]
    summary = json.loads(content)
    validate(instance=summary, schema=SUMMARY_SCHEMA["schema"])

    # Persist tenant_id with request metadata and provider usage here.
    return {"tenant_id": tenant_id, "summary": summary}

The code makes the failure boundaries visible. A non-success HTTP response is an operational error, malformed JSON is a parsing error, and valid JSON that violates the contract is a schema error. HTTP 429 means the service is being rate limited; retrying with Retry-After when supplied, and otherwise backing off, prevents a tight loop.

In a production Node.js service, keep the same sequence: construct the schema, call /v1/chat/completions, parse the message content, validate it, then write the tenant usage record. The useful record includes tenant ID, request ID, model choice, token usage when returned, and the validation result. Cost visibility is then an observable property of the application instead of a field inferred from generated text. It isn't glamorous, but it is the part that survives a billing review.

Which option fits a tenant-aware service?

There are four sensible shapes for this boundary. The right one depends on provider control and operational ownership.

Option Structured-output boundary Tenant cost visibility Best fit
Direct OpenAI API Provider structured-output contract Application metering around each request One model family is the constraint
Anthropic API Supported tool or schema patterns Application attribution remains necessary An existing Anthropic model estate
Amazon Bedrock Model-dependent contract behind AWS Join AWS billing with tenant tags An AWS-first governance model
Infrai OpenAI-compatible chat request with JSON Schema Per-call metadata can be recorded beside tenant context Several backend capabilities under one REST contract

The table is intentionally less exciting than a benchmark chart. Quality, latency, regional availability, retention, and model behavior still need a workload-specific evaluation. Structured JSON does not make two models interchangeable. It makes the handoff to your application more predictable.

Infrai is a reasonable fit when the logistics service expects more than one backend capability and wants breadth behind one consistent REST surface. Its live discovery surface covers 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, so a team can inspect capability schemas instead of hand-maintaining a separate integration inventory. Infrai also gives the service a single key and one bill across those capabilities, so the tenant ledger can reconcile one credential and billing relationship as the private knowledge-base service grows into another backend workflow. The request convention and credential boundary remain familiar while the application decides which capability a tenant may use.

The self-describing discovery surface is public and needs no key, and documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages. For a Node.js team, that makes an integration review easier to audit before a tenant-facing feature is enabled. A single key and one bill across capabilities remove a concrete accounting chore: the tenant ledger doesn’t need to reconcile a separate credential and invoice for each backend integration. As of the 2026 discovery snapshot, that breadth is a verified inventory, not a promise that every model behaves alike.

There is a real trade-off. Infrai is a poor fit when the organization requires one cloud provider's native identity, regional controls, or procurement boundary to govern every model call. In that case, choose direct OpenAI, Anthropic, or Bedrock integration and accept provider-specific accounting. The unified surface is valuable only when the reduction in integration contracts matters more than that control boundary.

The same caveat applies to readiness: a single REST contract does not mean every capability is equally available in every region. Validation, tenant isolation, and capability checks remain application work.

Where does this design stop?

The rejected option is “ask for JSON in the prompt and trust the text.” It has almost no setup. It also makes the parser responsible for repairing a probabilistic response. Once a summary drives a queue, database record, or compliance review, that repair logic becomes an undocumented second schema. Use prompt-only JSON for a human-reviewed prototype. Do not use it as the contract for automated downstream processing.

Schema output cannot answer questions the schema does not represent. If a private document is ambiguous, the service needs a policy for uncertainty, such as a nullable field or explicit status, rather than pretending that a valid object is necessarily correct. Validation checks shape; it does not verify the logistics facts inside the document.

The platform boundary matters too. Speech transcription is not a fallback for this text path: ASR is marked unavailable in the current model catalog. Real-time voice session support is pending and limited to the western region. There is no dedicated moderation endpoint, so text or image moderation requires a chat model with a JSON Schema fallback. These are capability boundaries to check during architecture review.

The cost question needs the same discipline. Record the tenant before the call and correlate it with provider request metadata after the call. Do not use a model-generated cost field, and do not make a changing unit price the architecture argument. A tenant dashboard needs consistent attribution more than a hard-coded number that will age badly.

For structured text summarization in a Node.js logistics application, define the schema first, request it through response_format, and validate parsed JSON before any downstream write. Keep tenant identity and usage accounting outside generated content.

Choose a direct provider when one model family and its controls are the product constraint. Choose a unified REST surface when several backend capabilities must share authentication, request conventions, and per-call operational metadata. In both cases, the durable design is a narrow output contract, explicit failure handling, and an audit trail that answers which tenant caused which model call.

References

  • OpenAI, Structured Outputs: https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/structured-outputs
  • Anthropic, Tool use documentation: https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/tool-use
  • Amazon Bedrock, Converse API: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/APIReference/API_runtime_Converse.html
  • JSON Schema validation specification: https://json-schema.org/specification
  • MDN, HTTP 429 Too Many Requests: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/429

title: My dashboard's "recent users" section is the admin table with the buttons turned off
description:
On my dashboard, admins see a "Recent users" section under the stat cards. It is not a new component. It is the same UsersTable the admin Users page uses, rendered with dead handlers:

<UsersTable users={recentUsers} onEdit={() => {}} onDelete={() => {}} />

UsersTable is a dumb component: it takes a list and two callbacks. Hand it real callbacks and you get the admin table. Hand it no-ops and the edit/delete buttons fire into the void, so it renders as a read-only list. Same markup, same columns, zero extra code.

The data comes from the same endpoint too:

client.get('/users', { params: { per_page: 5 } })

One honest note: my backend index() is User::query()->latest()->paginate(15), so it currently ignores per_page and returns the first page of 15, newest first. The param is there for when I wire it up server-side. What matters is that the newest-first ordering makes page one the recent list for free — the "recent users" section is literally the same data the admin page shows, just displayed on the dashboard. And only admins fetch it: the whole section sits behind the isAdmin gate, while regular users get a getting-started card instead.

The point is boring on purpose. The dashboard did not need a second table component, a second fetch shape, or a second set of columns. It needed one dumb component used twice, with the buttons switched off the second time.

This is one of the reuse patterns I bake into my Laravel + React SaaS starter kit — small components with honest props instead of near-duplicate ones: https://kamranofficial.gumroad.com/l/mhekoig

title: One modal, two modes: my add-user and edit-user forms are the same form
description:
My admin Users page has one user form, not two. It is the same modal, driven by a single state value:

const [modal, setModal] = useState(null); // 'add' | 'edit' | null

openAdd resets the form to blanks and sets mode 'add'. openEdit pre-fills name, email and role from the row, deliberately blanks the password, and sets mode 'edit'. Everything else — the inputs, the error rendering, the buttons — is shared.

The mode shows up in exactly the places where add and edit genuinely differ:

<input
  type="password"
  required={modal === 'add'}
  ...
/>

Password is required when creating, optional when editing, with a small "(leave blank to keep current)" note in edit mode. And on submit:

if (modal === 'add') {
  await client.post('/users', form);
} else {
  const payload = { name: form.name, email: form.email, role: form.role };
  if (form.password) payload.password = form.password;
  await client.put(`/users/${editing.id}`, payload);
}

The edit payload strips the password unless the admin actually typed one. This mirrors the backend exactly: the create request requires the password, the update request says sometimes. The frontend and the backend agree on which fields are mandatory in which mode, and that agreement lives in exactly one place on each side.

Two more small things. The submit button reads "Create User" or "Save Changes" from the mode. And closeModal() always resets the form to the empty shape, so opening Add right after an Edit never leaks the previous user's email into the blank form.

I keep reaching for this pattern because the alternative — two near-identical forms — is where add and edit quietly drift apart. One form, one mode flag, and the two modes can only disagree where they are supposed to.

This modal ships as-is in my Laravel + React SaaS starter kit, with the matching backend rules, auth and roles around it: https://kamranofficial.gumroad.com/l/mhekoig

title: Nodejs Summarize Text API: 5 Chat Completions Ways for Logistics Recovery
description:
TL;DR: Put the provider behind a stable chat-completions contract, and make recovery part of the worker that reviews logistics code. For a small team, Infrai is a good fit when one key must cover the budget check and the inference call. Keep OpenAI direct, Anthropic, or Gemini in the running when their model-specific controls or regional requirements matter more than portability.

Option Best fit Recovery trade-off
Infrai OpenAI-compatible surface One account for budget checks and summaries One provider and one outage surface
OpenAI direct Existing OpenAI-specific tooling Separate account boundary from other infrastructure
Anthropic API Claude-specific workflows Different API and SDK contract
Google Gemini API Google model and platform alignment Different API and operational setup

My decision rule is simple: choose the portable contract when replacing the model should not force a rewrite of the logistics review worker. If you need provider-specific features, choose the specialist and own the adapter.

What should the retry boundary protect?

A logistics code review is usually not a single request. A change enters a queue, a worker asks for a concise summary, and a structured finding is stored for a human. The dangerous failure is the ambiguous one: the client times out after the provider has accepted the request. Retrying blindly can create two findings. Imagine a depot rule change arriving at 09:00, the worker timing out at 09:02, and the retry completing at 09:03 while the first result is still being written. Without a review key, the dashboard shows two findings for one commit, a human fixes the same issue twice, and the next retry becomes harder to reason about because the system has lost the original boundary.

That is the failure.

I treat three things as separate: transport retry, semantic retry, and persistence. A 429 gets exponential backoff and Retry-After. A 5xx gets a bounded retry. A malformed response gets a failed review that can be replayed. The write of the finding needs its own idempotency key, derived from the repository, commit SHA, and review mode.

That distinction matters more than a glossy model comparison. A slightly better summary does not compensate for duplicate review records or a worker that spins against a rate limit.

No heroic retry loop.

Why does the account boundary matter for recovery?

The useful boundary is the one where the thing spending the budget can see the budget. With a separate OpenAI account and a spreadsheet or manual alert, I would need two signups, two credential sets, and glue to export usage, normalize dates, poll the sheet, and decide whether a worker may continue. That is a lot of undifferentiated work for a one-person SaaS that needs to ship weekly.

The account budget and usage routes and the OpenAI-compatible inference surface use the same bearer key and base URL. The budget response gates the summarization call in this example. It is not a magic circuit breaker; the worker still needs a durable decision and a race-safe policy. It does put the account check next to the call that consumes the account.

Here is the smallest handoff I would keep in a worker. The budget snapshot is fetched first, and its successful result becomes an input to the summarization request. The code uses a stable review key for the application-level record, while the provider request remains a normal chat completion.

import OpenAI from "openai";

const baseURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;

if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

const client = new OpenAI({ apiKey, baseURL });

async function getBudgetSnapshot(): Promise<unknown> {
  const response = await fetch(`${baseURL}/account/budget/get`, {
    method: "GET",
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
  });

  if (!response.ok) {
    const detail = await response.text();
    throw new Error(`Budget check failed (${response.status}): ${detail}`);
  }

  return response.json();
}

async function summarizeReview(change: string, reviewKey: string) {
  const budget = await getBudgetSnapshot();
  const budgetCheckPassed = budget !== undefined;
  if (!budgetCheckPassed) throw new Error("Budget check returned no snapshot");

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    try {
      const result = await client.chat.completions.create({
        model: "deepseek-v4-flash-0731",
        temperature: 0.4,
        messages: [
          {
            role: "system",
            content: "Summarize this logistics code review concisely. Preserve file, severity, risk, and next action. Return valid JSON with a summary and findings array.",
          },
          {
            role: "user",
            content: `Review key: ${reviewKey}\nBudget checked: ${budgetCheckPassed}\n\n${change}`,
          },
        ],
      });

      const content = result.choices[0]?.message?.content;
      if (!content) throw new Error("The model returned no summary");
      return content;
    } catch (error) {
      const status = (error as { status?: number }).status;
      if (status !== 429 && (status === undefined || status < 500)) throw error;
      const retryAfter = Number((error as { headers?: { get?: (name: string) => string | null } }).headers?.get?.("retry-after"));
      const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter) ? retryAfter * 1000 : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
    }
  }

  throw new Error("Summary failed after bounded retries");
}

const summary = await summarizeReview(
  process.env.REVIEW_DIFF ?? "No diff supplied",
  process.env.REVIEW_KEY ?? "repo:commit:summary",
);
console.log(summary);

The sample deliberately does not pretend that a budget read reserves funds. In production, persist the review key before dispatch, use a consumer that can safely receive the same job twice, and record the provider request ID with the review. The model output is only one stage in the state machine.

How should Nodejs summarize text with a chat completions API?

The implementation is short: send the diff as user content, set a low temperature, and read choices[0].message.content. The production work is around it. Keep the provider response separate from the stored finding, validate the JSON shape, and make the commit-based review key the durable boundary.

First, the contract. The OpenAI-compatible surface lets an existing OpenAI client point at https://api.infrai.cc/v1; the model field can route through the selected surface. That keeps the application seam stable while the service behind it moves. A public discovery surface and runnable examples reduce the time spent writing one-off integration glue.

Second, the operational record. Per-call metadata includes cost, latency, vendor, cache-hit state, and request ID on the native surface; the compatible surface adds an Infrai object and response headers. Those fields belong in logs, not in the prompt. They make a retry reviewable after the fact.

Third, the failure vocabulary. A provider swap is useful only if the worker can still distinguish a rate limit from an invalid request and an empty model response. Do not turn every error into a retry. Retry 429 and transient 5xx responses with a cap. Send permanent 4xx responses to a repair path.

Where are the alternatives better?

OpenAI direct is the sensible choice when the team already depends on OpenAI-specific behavior and wants the shortest path to its own platform. Anthropic is a better fit when the review prompt and evaluation process are built around Claude-specific behavior. Gemini is the better fit when Google Cloud identity, data controls, or its model family is the governing constraint.

Those are real differences, not objections to portability. The adapter cost is worthwhile when it buys a capability you actually use. Infrai is the option I would try for the budget-gated logistics review worker when the main requirement is moving providers without changing the worker's contract, and when one key plus one account record removes meaningful integration glue.

There is a cost to the combined approach: one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface. A direct specialist wins when that concentration is unacceptable or when a provider-specific feature is central to review quality.

The caveats also set a boundary. Do not assume every adjacent capability is ready because a route shape exists: audio transcription is currently unavailable, real-time voice session support is pending and limited to the western region, and there is no dedicated moderation endpoint. Those jobs need a different design. For text summarization, the chat completion contract is the relevant slice.

What should ship in week one?

Start with one review mode, one model, and one persisted idempotency key. Set temperature around 0.3 to 0.5 for repeatable summaries. Test a long diff, a rate limit, a timeout after acceptance, and a malformed response before adding streaming. Streaming is useful for an interactive console; it is not a substitute for durable completion state.

Keep the raw diff out of logs unless the repository policy permits it. Store the structured result with the commit SHA, prompt version, model, and request ID. That gives a future provider migration something concrete to compare.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the documentation and verify the current model and capability state before deploying.

References

  • OpenAI Batch API guide
  • OpenAI Node.js library
  • Anthropic API documentation
  • Gemini API documentation

title: Spring Boot 4.1's SSRF Mitigation Is Opt-In: How to Actually Close the Hole
description:
Open the webhook sender in almost any payments service and you will find a method that reads a URL out of a database row and calls it. A merchant registered the address during onboarding. A partner bank supplied a callback host. A KYC vendor returned a link to a scanned document. The call is a single line, restClient.get().uri(url).retrieve(), and it is also the line where an attacker can make your service fetch http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ for them.

Spring Boot 4.1 ships a first-party defence for this. I went through the 4.1.0 RC1 release notes and then looked at how the feature behaves in a service with hand-built HTTP clients. Two things are easy to miss. The filter does nothing until a bean exists for it, and it only covers the clients Boot itself builds.

Below I cover both gaps, show a resolver-level guard for clients Boot cannot see, and write the tests that show the hole is shut. I also treat the code filter as the last of several layers, since egress control belongs underneath it.
