These results demonstrate that next-frame prediction in embedding space is effective and scalable for visual world modeling.

title: SmolVLA-MoE: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts for Efficient Multi-Task Robotic Manipulation
description:
arXiv:2610.30732v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown promising results in multi-task robotic manipulation by leveraging visual and language understanding for action generation. However, existing lightweight VLA models employ a single dense action expert to handle all tasks, which limits their multi-task capability under constrained computational budgets. To address this issue, we propose SmolVLA-MoE, a novel framework that introduces sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) into the FFN layers of the action expert in VLA models. SmolVLA-MoE replaces dense FFN layers with multiple parallel expert FFNs and a token-level router, enabling each token to adaptively select the most suitable expert for action generation. We further introduce a shared expert with a tunable weight parameter to balance the inheritance of pre-trained capabilities and task-specific expert specialization. Through sparse activation, SmolVLA-MoE activates only a single expert FFN during inference, with a total activated parameter count of approximately 500M including the frozen VLM backbone, while benefiting from approximately 800M total stored parameters. We evaluate our method on four task suites of the LIBERO benchmark. SmolVLA-MoE achieves an average success rate of 84.25%, outperforming SmolVLA (82.75%) and OpenVLA-7B (76.5%), while maintaining comparable inference efficiency. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/dudu435/smolvla-moe.

title: Where Did the Light Come From? Diagnosing Cast-Shadow Reasoning in VLMs and Borrowing the Missing Shadow Prior from Image Generation Models
description:
arXiv:2610.30740v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Shadows are observable consequences of latent physical causes, arising from the interaction between illumination, object geometry, and scene structure. A model that understands shadows should be able not only to read a shadow's direction, but also to infer where a shadow should fall when it is absent, and to judge whether a shadow is physically consistent with the scene. We introduce ShadowBench, built from real photographs, which poses these three questions to vision-language models (VLMs). From each scene, we build a correct-shadow, a shadow-removed, and a human-annotated wrong-direction state. Evaluating 19 open VLMs (2B to 78B) and frontier proprietary models, we find that VLMs read a visible shadow's direction well above chance and improve with scale, yet infer the absent direction only weakly and fall to chance at judging physical consistency even under a bias-free two-alternative test that removes the yes-bias of single-image naturalness questions. Only Gemini-3.1-pro exceeds chance on validity, and even then only modestly and far below humans. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) does not help. The missing ingredient is not reasoning but knowledge that image generation models (IGMs) already hold. Routing a VLM through an IGM lifts its inference well above its direct attempt and helps it flag the wrong-direction shadows it otherwise accepts. Cast-shadow direction is a single facet of illumination understanding, but the sharp gap it reveals between VLMs and IGMs suggests image-generation or reconstruction objectives as a route toward illumination-aware VLMs.

title: FilmFlow: Agentic System for 3D Virtual Film Cinematography
description:
arXiv:2610.30753v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Complex camera motion is central to visual storytelling, yet translating cinematographic intent into controllable, executable camera trajectories remains challenging. We introduce FilmFlow, an agentic framework that converts natural-language instructions or reference videos into explicit camera trajectories for dynamic 3D environments. To generate these trajectories, a Director agent constructs executable camera plans by composing high-level motions from concurrent atomic operations that jointly control translation, rotation, and framing. The Director is supported by three specialized agents: an Interpreter that extracts scene-grounded cinematographic intent, a Scout that selects initial viewpoints, and a Critic that evaluates rendered results and provides visual feedback for iterative plan refinement. We also introduce CinemaBench, comprising 150 Blender scenes from self-created and licensed sources, with five camera instructions per scene for 750 text-directed tasks and 60 reference videos associated with a subset of scenes. CinemaBench supports evaluation of both text-directed camera generation and video reference-directed camera generation. Across a diverse set of evaluated baselines, FilmFlow achieves the strongest benchmark performance and the highest user preference, demonstrating effective spatial reasoning, temporal coordination, and visual composition for executable 3D cinematography.

title: Evaluation of Front-End Feature Matching for Lunar Visual SLAM
description:
arXiv:2610.30774v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Lunar rovers will primarily rely on cameras for localization until navigation satellite services are deployed, and will continue to need them afterwards for relative navigation, hazard detection, and surface operations. Visual odometry (VO) and Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) mostly estimate motion by matching features between frames. However, feature matchers are developed on urban, indoor and driving scenes, planetary studies compare them on orbital registration or within complete SLAM systems, and real lunar imagery with reference poses is scarce, so matching between rover frames on low-texture, harshly lit terrain, and its effect on VO, has not been compared. We benchmark eleven classical and learned detector-matcher combinations on nine synthetic, lunar-testbed, and terrestrial-analogue datasets, and a feature tracker, scoring pairwise pose accuracy against baseline and the trajectory error of the resulting VO. Under a common rotation-only metric, the SuperPoint pairings outperform SIFT with ratio-tested FLANN matching on both lunar testbeds and one analogue site, with smaller or unresolved differences on synthetic data. When rotation and translation direction are scored jointly, this SIFT pairing exceeds both SuperPoint pairings on four synthetic datasets, so synthetic results alone do not establish relative performance on real rover imagery. In stereo VO, the SuperPoint pairings are not consistently more accurate than SIFT, but only they keep tracking on all eight sequential datasets. Pairings with classical detectors depend on lighting while SuperPoint changes little: a low spotlight makes them more accurate than diffuse light on the same testbed views, consistent with more contrast and detected keypoints. SuperPoint with LightGlue is the fastest learned combination (16 ms per frame), and DINOv2 retrieval proposals still need geometric verification.

title: DeXplicit: Making Physical State Explicit in Dexterous Manipulation World Models
description:
arXiv:2610.30781v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Before acting on an object, a robot needs to anticipate how its hand motion will change the physical world and what the resulting scene will look like. Existing approaches typically entangle action-conditioned dynamics, camera motion, and visual synthesis within a video generation model, or represent dynamics as point trajectories without explicit object structure. We introduce DeXplicit, a dexterous manipulation world model that instead predicts how the world evolves explicitly in metric 3D before rendering its visual consequences. Given an initial scene and a future hand trajectory, a lightweight 3D dynamics network predicts object-centric motion and deformation, providing structured and geometrically grounded future world states. These predictions then serve as a strong scaffold for video generation: appearance is transported through the predicted 3D motion and projected into future views, allowing the renderer to focus on completing uncertain and newly visible content rather than implicitly learning world dynamics from pixels. This explicit-3D-first decomposition also enables efficient causal generation, requiring only two denoising steps per block while conditioning on generated history.
  Across HOT3D, OakInk2, and PhysTwin, DeXplicit reduces moved-point error by 27-40% relative to PointWorld and improves object fidelity IoU+ by 47% on HOT3D under a shared renderer. Our design with two-step causal generation achieves a 57x speedup from our 14B bi-directional configuration in video synthesis.

title: WovenAnchor Matcher: Specialized Intra- and Inter-Image Context Modeling for Feature Matching
description:
arXiv:2610.30799v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Semi-dense local feature matching commonly aggregates contextual information before coarse-to-fine correspondence estimation. However, intra-image and inter-image aggregation serve different roles: the former should propagate spatial evidence within each image while retaining structured two-dimensional dependencies, whereas the latter should gather information from plausible corresponding regions while limiting noise from unrelated locations. We propose WovenAnchor Matcher (WAM), a semi-dense matching framework based on role-specialized context aggregation. WAM introduces two complementary operators. WovenMamba performs intra-image aggregation through horizontal-then-vertical state-space propagation, allowing vertical updates to operate on horizontally contextualized features and thereby encouraging a structured two-dimensional receptive-field bias. AnchorCrossAttention performs inter-image aggregation by using cross-attention to gather context from plausible corresponding regions across the image pair. It performs this exchange over local representative anchors that aggregate feature evidence within each window. On MegaDepth, WAM achieves 66.1 pose AUC@5$^\circ$, improving on the JamMa baseline by 2.0 AUC points under the same evaluation setup. Ablations show that removing or replacing either specialized component reduces accuracy, providing evidence that intra-image propagation and inter-image retrieval benefit from role-specific aggregation designs. Code and pretrained weights are available at https://github.com/mmaiLab/WovenAnchorMatcher.

title: DRILL: Training World Models to Improve Policies, Not Predict Pixels
description:
arXiv:2610.30814v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: World models are increasingly used to reduce environment interaction when post-training vision-language-action (VLA) policies with reinforcement learning. Yet they are typically trained to predict pixels one step ahead, even though their role here is not merely to render visually faithful videos but to produce learning signals from imagined rollouts that improve the policy. We show that this mismatch is substantial: lower pixel MSE can produce worse policy gradients, and a world model trained for policy utility can yield better downstream policies despite 17% higher pixel MSE on the next frame. We propose the Downstream-Return Imagination Learning Loop (DRILL), a bilevel framework that updates the world model to maximize the policy's return after an inner GRPO update on imagined rollouts. DRILL has two instantiations. DRILL-VWI is a closed-form surrogate, requiring no additional simulator rollouts, that reweights prediction errors by policy visitation, the group-relative GRPO advantage, and model confidence. DRILL-IMG is a full meta-gradient method that differentiates through the inner update using truncated Hessian-vector products. We show that DRILL-VWI recovers the local one-step component of the DRILL-IMG meta-gradient under score-compatibility and small-residual assumptions. Across five manipulation simulators and two VLA backbones, DRILL-IMG raises mean success rate by 13.1 points over WMPO and 7.9 points over RLVR-World, and complements RLVR pretraining rather than competing with it. More broadly, we believe video world models for VLA reinforcement learning can be productively trained by the policy gradients they produce, not only by pixel-level prediction.

title: Loop to Look Better: Learning Adaptive Depth for Question-Guided Perception in Vision-Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.30824v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Visual perception should be iterative and task-directed, with representations refined in response to the question and the need for further processing. While Vision-Language Models (VLMs) increasingly support extended reasoning, their visual tokens are still typically acquired in a single, task-agnostic encoder pass. This creates an evidence-acquisition bottleneck: models may reason longer without refining the visual evidence needed to answer the question. We propose LoopLook, a lightweight encoder-side recurrent perception framework that equips pretrained VLMs with adaptive visual depth. LoopLook recurrently revisits a middle-to-late window of the vision encoder, injecting question representations at each loop to guide visual refinement. A learned stopping mechanism adaptively determines the recurrent depth, while a token-wise Mixture-of-Looks (MoL) combines representations from different loops, allowing each visual token to selectively integrate information acquired across recurrent steps. Across four backbones and eight benchmarks, LoopLook consistently improves performance over the baseline, yielding gains of up to 8.6% on MMStar and 8.1% on HallusionBench. Our analysis shows that LoopLook progressively refines visual attention and adaptively allocates depth according to task difficulty. It also better preserves task-relevant visual information under reduced input resolution, while increasing time to first token (TTFT) by only 5.1-6.5%. By bringing recurrence from reasoning back into perception, LoopLook transforms visual perception from a one-shot glimpse into an adaptive process of recurrent refinement.

title: One Evaluation Is Enough: Inversion-Free Image Editing with Trajectory Correction
description:
arXiv:2610.30827v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Real-image editing commonly relies on inversion and iterative sampling, while efficient one-step editors often stabilize a large update by estimating and averaging editing fields at multiple noise levels. We ask a stricter question: is a single temporal field evaluation sufficient for reliable inversion-free editing? Our answer rests on a previously underused duality in a variance-preserving (VP) one-step model: one source-target query at a shared noisy state simultaneously determines a local angular semantic tangent and a clean endpoint displacement. We integrate the tangent over the analytically known remaining VP angle to obtain a nominal one-step transport, and use the endpoint displacement to correct its long-horizon extrapolation through a constrained projection. This transport-first, correction-second construction yields Endpoint-Calibrated Transport (ECT), a closed-form, training-free editor requiring only one noise level, two text conditions packed into one denoiser batch, and one latent update. ECT requires no image inversion, trajectory integration, second temporal observation, or iterative optimization, and can be directly applied to pretrained epsilon-prediction VP one-step generators. Across the reported benchmark settings, ECT delivers stable gains in editing quality within an extremely short editing time.

title: RECAP: Looking Once Is Not Enough for Vision-Language Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2610.30834v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long chain-of-thought reasoning improves vision-language models (VLMs), but it also exposes a temporal grounding failure: as generation unfolds, models may drift from image evidence while reinforcement learning still provides only a final-answer reward. We study this gap through visual revisit, a temporally localized reactivation of image evidence during reasoning. Across three VLM backbones, revisit peaks are predictive of correctness and causally linked to performance: masking them degrades accuracy more than masking non-peaks, while injecting revisit-like peaks into failed rollouts partially restores correct answers. Control analyses show that this signal is not explained by raw attention strength, uncertainty, logit margin, or hidden-state norm. We propose RECAP, a GRPO-compatible training method that turns detached revisit traces into a credit-assignment signal. RECAP uses revisit-conditioned advantage estimation, dynamic discounting, and gated value prediction to propagate final rewards through visually important reasoning steps, without extra rewards, additional rollouts, or inference-time changes. Across Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL3-8B, and LLaVA-OV-7B, RECAP consistently improves over GRPO and VPPO, yielding $+6.1$--$+6.5$ HallusionBench gains over the SFT base while preserving reasoning and text-only performance. Results on larger LoRA-tuned models, Chinese zero-shot benchmarks, visual perturbations, and human evaluation further demonstrate robust improvements in image-grounded reasoning.

title: CAVC: Convergence-Adaptive Audio-Visual Cache for Modality-Asymmetric Diffusion Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.30854v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion-based audio-visual generation methods typically perform joint denoising of audio and video latents throughout the entire sampling trajectory, repeatedly executing modality-specific denoising branches and cross-modal attention at every timestep. However, we observe that such uniform joint computation is not always necessary. The key is a modality-asymmetric recoverability: audio-side drift introduced by mid-stage caching can be substantially reduced by only a few terminal joint denoising steps, whereas video-side degradation caused by caching leads to persistent loss of motion and temporal details. This asymmetry suggests that inference acceleration should selectively cache recoverable audio-side computation while preserving full video refinement. Motivated by this observation, we propose \textbf{Convergence-Adaptive Audio-Visual Cache (CAVC)}, a training-free modality-asymmetric caching framework. CAVC adopts a sandwich-structured computation allocation: after detecting that audio denoiser outputs enter a cache-tolerant regime, it caches and reuses the audio denoiser output to bypass audio denoising and cross-modal attention in the middle stage, while the video branch continues independent spatio-temporal refinement; a few joint steps are then restored at the end to reduce accumulated cross-modal drift and improve synchronization. Experiments across multiple public benchmarks demonstrate that CAVC achieves 1.10--1.35x wall-clock acceleration, improves several visual dynamics and temporal statistics, and maintains competitive audio fidelity and audio-visual alignment.

title: Direct Forcing: A Single-Stage Training Recipe for Few-Step Autoregressive Text-to-Video Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.30861v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Few-step autoregressive video generation enables low-latency streaming, yet prevailing training pipelines separate causal adaptation from distribution matching. Recent representation-based text-to-video methods retain this separation by starting from ODE-initialized checkpoints, even when the target distribution is defined directly by reference videos. We introduce Direct Forcing, a single-stage framework that uses reference videos both as paired examples of how a history continues and as a target population for self-generated rollouts. Causal Continuation Alignment learns paired spatiotemporal correspondence under reference histories, while Rollout Distribution Matching uses maximum mean discrepancy to align the representation distributions of self-generated and reference videos. Together, these complementary signals allow a pretrained video model to learn causal continuation and the target video distribution in a single training stage. Dynamic Gradient Balancing adapts the relative gradient contributions of continuation alignment and distribution matching during training. Starting from bidirectional Wan2.1-1.3B, Direct Forcing learns a four-step autoregressive generator in 250 updates without a separate initialization stage or online diffusion-score supervision, achieving 84.63 VBench Total and 86.01 Quality. Ablation studies further demonstrate the benefits of dynamic gradient balancing and reveal distinct representation preferences: deeper features benefit continuation alignment, whereas intermediate features yield better performance for rollout distribution matching.

title: Cross-Spectral Feature Fusion for Multispectral Document Binarization
description:
arXiv:2610.30863v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Historical document binarization remains challenging when faded ink, bleed-through, and background degradation exhibit wavelength-dependent behavior across visible and near-infrared observations. This study investigates whether adaptive cross-spectral feature fusion and targeted structural guidance can improve multispectral document binarization beyond fixed fusion and generic attention mechanisms.
  Four registered SMADI bands at 500, 600, 700, and 1000 nm are processed using a multi-branch conditional generative adversarial network (cGAN). Visible, NIR, and structural feature streams are fused at encoder depth L = 3 using spatial- and channel-wise softmax gating, while auxiliary edge maps derived from selected VIS-NIR band pairs provide targeted structural guidance. Nine controlled fusion and structural configurations are evaluated using five-fold document-level cross-validation, DIBCO-standard metrics, and Holm-corrected statistical testing.
  The F3 + NIR edge-guided configuration provides the strongest overall performance among the evaluated models, achieving mean F1 = 0.7916, p-FM = 0.8044, and IoU = 0.6654. Relative to the fixed Mid AVG baseline, it improves F1 by 0.0269, p-FM by 0.0360, and IoU by 0.0321, with all three gains remaining statistically significant after Holm correction. Mean NRM and DRD are also reduced, although these reductions are not statistically significant after correction.
  Targeted cross-spectral structural guidance provides an effective mechanism for regulating intermediate multispectral fusion, improving primary foreground-overlap performance while retaining the complete four-band observation.

title: Verus-Insight: Towards Explainable Artifact Detection in AI-Generated Videos
description:
arXiv:2610.30866v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent advances in video generation have made synthetic videos increasingly realistic, placing greater demands on reliable AI-generated video detection. Existing artifact-based detectors typically identify generation artifacts as evidence for source prediction, yet they may either fail to recognize subtle artifacts or reach the correct source decision without faithfully identifying the evidence underlying it. In this work, we systematically investigate how to design and train effective artifact detectors and formulate artifact detection as a structured process comprising three complementary capabilities: Inspection Planning, which determines what should be examined; Evidence Verification, which verifies whether the inspected content exhibits genuine generation artifacts; and Evidence Aggregation, which integrates the verified evidence into the final source decision. Building on this formulation, we introduce Verus-Insight, trained with human-anchored full-process supervision and progressive capability training to strengthen both fine-grained artifact detection and video-level detection. We further introduce Verus-Bench, a benchmark with fine-grained human annotations of perceptible artifacts for evaluating artifact detection. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that Verus-Insight achieves strong performance in both fine-grained artifact analysis and AI-generated video detection, with substantial gains in recovering human-perceived artifacts. Further analyses reveal that the three capabilities are complementary yet distinct, and that Verus-Insight more reliably converts relevant inspection targets into supported artifact evidence without increasing spurious artifact claims.

title: HimmBO: High-Dimensional Interactive Model-Merging Bayesian Optimization for Image Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.30875v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Fine-tuning has become a common way to customize text-to-image models, leading to community collections of over 100K lightweight adapters. Adapters sharing a base model can be merged with continuous coefficients. This turns a large collection into a high-dimensional continuous design space, which recent work explores interactively using preferential Bayesian optimization (PBO). However, existing approaches are limited to a few dozen preselected adapters and require expensive image generation in every interaction round. We introduce HimmBO, a two-stage method that scales preference-driven adapter merging to much larger collections while reducing image-generation cost. Its screening stage recovers the active adapter set through level-set estimation over pre-generated images, requiring no image generation. The refinement stage then optimizes merge coefficients in the recovered low-dimensional subspace. Both stages use a style-aware kernel, allowing preference information to transfer between visually similar adapters. In simulated-user image-matching experiments, HimmBO achieves higher final similarity than all comparisons while reaching a given similarity with under one tenth of the image generations required by prior work. Its performance remains stable as the collection grows to 1080 adapters, while competing methods degrade substantially.

title: When Annotation Patterns Are Learned: Skin-Tone Dependence in Dermatology Concepts
description:
arXiv:2610.30901v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Concept bottleneck models (CBMs) let clinicians inspect and correct skin disease diagnoses through clinical concepts, but only if the concept annotations are reliable. We therefore audit the reliability of SkinCon, a widely used dermatology concept dataset, across skin tones. Within the same disease and with near duplicates removed, erythema is annotated far less often on dark than on light skin, with an odds ratio of 0.17. In contrast, hyperpigmentation and hypopigmentation are annotated more often, with odds ratios of 6.2 and 4.5, respectively. We refer to this pattern as tone-dependent concept annotation. An evidential concept model trained on these annotations learns the same pattern and reproduces it on unseen images. Such a model may agree with potential erythema omissions rather than contradict them. Consistent with this, three label error detectors underperform a disease-only baseline at finding erythema that dermatologist captions mention but SkinCon labels as absent. The three detectors are based on confident learning, training dynamics, and the model's own evidential uncertainty. Concept annotations should thus be audited within each subgroup before explanations built on them can be trusted.

title: Query-Time Calibration of CLIP Features for Open-Vocabulary 3D Segmentation
description:
arXiv:2610.30908v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Lifting vision-language features such as CLIP into 3D Gaussian reconstructions enables open-vocabulary segmentation through natural-language queries. Although CLIP represents a broad range of semantic concepts, the lifted features of individual scenes can exhibit strong directional concentration, while raw cosine similarity does not account for the scene-specific feature distribution. We show that substantial segmentation gains can be obtained by changing how a fixed lifted feature field is compared with text. Our method partially subtracts a shared scene direction from visual features and text prototypes and whitens text prototypes using a fixed reference vocabulary of generic terms. It then uses soft clustering for multiclass prediction and CSLS with a relevance margin against the reference vocabulary for single-query prediction. Beyond reducing directional concentration, scene centering improves class-relative feature separation in every evaluated scene. Across seven lifting methods and four datasets, the resulting query-time calibration consistently improves mean intersection over union in both multiclass and single-query segmentation. These gains require no retraining, source-image re-encoding, or feature re-lifting, demonstrating the value of scene-conditioned comparison for making better use of existing lifted representations.

title: Hierarchical Fine-Grained Cross-Modal Alignment via Dynamic Granularity Discovery and Optimal Transport
description:
arXiv:2610.30912v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Fine-grained image-text retrieval requires a model not only to assess global semantic consistency between an image and a text, but also to model visual evidence for local textual semantics, including objects, attributes, quantities, actions, and relations, so as to distinguish semantically similar candidates. Existing methods commonly use fixed image patches, detected regions, or text tokens as the basic matching units and then aggregate local interactions through max pooling, cross attention, or similarity accumulation. Such strategies remain limited in semantic unit construction and global matching consistency. This paper proposes a hierarchical fine-grained cross-modal alignment framework, termed HFCMA. The framework progressively transforms low-level patch and token representations into adaptive visual regions and textual phrases, and then performs structured region-phrase matching within a global retrieval scoring process. Specifically, HFCMA first adopts dynamic granularity discovery (DGD) to aggregate raw patches and tokens into semantically compact visual regions and textual phrases. It then formulates region-phrase matching as an entropy-regularized optimal transport problem, thereby estimating a structured alignment matrix under global marginal constraints. To reduce background noise and local semantic drift, HFCMA further introduces background debiasing, textual importance weighting, and prototype consistency regularization. Experiments on Flickr30K and MS-COCO show that HFCMA effectively combines dynamic semantic unit construction with OT-based structured matching under a dual-encoder retrieval framework. The resulting fine-grained score provides structured local alignment information for candidate ranking and improves the discrimination of subtle semantic differences.

title: Watch and Learn: Teaching Visual In-Context Learning by Removing Textual Shortcuts
description:
arXiv:2610.30913v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) struggle with in context learning compared to their textual counterparts. Our preliminary study shows that VLMs rely on textual shortcuts and underutilize the visual demonstrations. We therefore hypothesize that VLMs are insufficiently trained to perform visual in-context learning (vICL). To this end, we construct MIME, a task-agnostic vICL training set without textual shortcuts. We ensure the instruction does not state the rule linking the demonstration images to their answers, so the model must infer it from the visual demonstrations. Fine-tuning on MIME improves vICL accuracy by 8.1 to 18.0 points across three VLMs, preserves single-image performance, and improves multi-image and text only in-context learning. In contrast, stating the rule in the training data sharply reduces this gain. We further propose DTAD (Demonstration Text Attention Dropout), which randomly withholds demonstration labels during training so that the VLM must infer the rule from the demonstration images. While achieving comparable vICL accuracy to fine-tuning on MIME, DTAD yields more consistent attention to the demonstration images. On TrueMICL, Qwen3-VL-8B trained on MIME matches frontier models such as Claude Opus 5, and surpasses them with DTAD. Finally, adding MIME to the instruction-tuning mix of LLaVA 1.5 13B more than doubles its vICL accuracy without hurting single-image abilities, whereas a same-size multi-image set improves it only slightly. These results suggest that vICL data should be a standard component of VLM training.

title: Making MLLM Latents Matter: Factor-Aware Predictive Learning for Cinematic Video Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.30926v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Cinematic video generation requires both temporal inference from limited inputs (i.e., sparse rather than frame-by-frame guidance) and factor-aware control of character, scene, action, and camera. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offer useful priors for both capabilities, but their representations are not automatically actionable for video generation: a Video Diffusion Transformer (DiT) may bypass them through native conditioning pathways, and using them does not ensure either factor-aware control or generation-compatible temporal prediction. We propose Factor-Aware Predictive Learning (FAPL), which establishes effective MLLM latent use as a shared prerequisite and then targets the two capabilities with complementary learning signals. First, latent-only generator grounding trains the DiT with a frozen MLLM and connector, strengthening the DiT's use of MLLM latents for generation. Second, for factor-aware control, paired videos specify a target-factor change and non-target preservation, and factor-span replacement trains the DiT to realize this relationship in its output. Third, for temporal inference, text-only and text-plus-complete-video observations share a video target, and the trained DiT is then frozen while the MLLM and connector are optimized through it. This final stage trains limited-input representations for generation while retaining complete-observation reconstruction as a complementary training mode. Extensive experiments demonstrate our consistently better performance on three cinematic video generation tasks (i.e., sparse-to-video, factor-aware editing, and multi-shot generation) over baselines and validate FAPL's contributions to MLLM feature use, temporal control, and factor coordination.

title: ICGF-CXRMate: Image-Conditioned Clinical Context Compression and Gated Fusion for Chest X-ray Report Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.30928v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Auxiliary patient data can improve chest X-ray report generation, but directly concatenating heterogeneous clinical information with visual tokens produces long, variable-length decoder prompts and may expose the model to redundant or image-irrelevant context. We propose ICGF-CXRMate, an image-conditioned clinical context compression and gated fusion framework. Learnable queries are first conditioned on the current chest X-ray representations and then attend to the patient-data sequence, compressing it into a fixed number of clinical context tokens. Gated cross-attention selectively integrates these tokens into the visual stream, while the compressed tokens are retained in the decoder prompt as a direct clinical pathway. Experiments on linked MIMIC-CXR and MIMIC-IV-ED examinations show that ICGF-CXRMate improves report quality while reducing the average prompt length. In Stage~2, it improves RadGraph-F1 from 24.00 to 28.86, CXR-BERT similarity from 56.86 to 62.80, and BLEU-4 from 5.14 to 7.96 compared with CXRMate-ED, while reducing the average prompt length from 373.89 to 288.37 tokens, corresponding to a 22.9\% reduction. After self-critical sequence training, ICGF-CXRMate outperforms CXRMate-ED on six of eight report-quality metrics in Stage~3. Ablation studies confirm the complementary contributions of image-conditioned compression, gated fusion, and direct retention of the compressed clinical tokens.

title: Attention-guided classification and tumor localization of combined hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma
description:
arXiv:2610.30944v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Combined hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinomas (cHCC-CCA) are a type of cancer that share components of two other primary liver cancers: hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and cholangiocarcinoma (CCA). Accurate diagnosis of cHCC-CCA, of which the behavior may resemble that of either HCC or CCA, remains a challenge due to strong intratumoral heterogeneity. Since the prognoses differ between liver cancer types, it is necessary to improve their morphological characterization and recognition in order to accurately identify cHCC-CCA. In this work, we use whole slide images (WSIs) of the two main types of liver cancer (HCC and CCA) and cHCC-CCA, stained with Hematoxylin-Eosin-Safran (HES), to train a classification model that can distinguish between these subtypes and provides a potential solution for localizing different types of tumors in the combined liver cancer images.

title: GraphCAD: Geometry-Aware Diffusion on Edge-Adjacency Graphs for CAD Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.30974v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative modeling for Computer-Aided Design (CAD) remains fundamentally challenged by the need to capture the intricate interplay between discrete topological connectivity and precise spatial geometry inherent in Boundary Representations (B-reps). Existing generative approaches largely formulate CAD construction as a sequence modeling problem, but consequently lack an explicit topological inductive bias. In this work, we present GraphCAD, a geometry-aware generative framework that centers modeling on the Edge-Adjacency Graph (EAG), a novel graph-based CAD representation tailored for generative tasks. GraphCAD adopts a hybrid graph diffusion formulation to jointly model the discrete and continuous components of EAG and introduces a geometry-aware denoising mechanism that renders node attributes into spatial point sets. These point sets are encoded by an SE(3)-equivariant backbone and fused into the node representations, thereby grounding the generative process in physical geometry. To support this study, we construct EAGBench, a large-scale dataset of engineering CAD models. Extensive experiments show that GraphCAD can generate complex CAD models with more than 50 faces and achieves state-of-the-art performance in geometric fidelity and distributional alignment compared with sequence-based baselines.

title: eLearning Software Development: Accept LTI 1.3 Launches in Node.js
description:
In eLearning software development, getting your product to run inside Moodle or Canvas means accepting an LTI 1.3 launch. In Node.js, that takes three steps: answer an OIDC login request, verify a signed JWT against the platform's public keys, and turn the claims inside it into your own users and courses. The hard part is the handful of checks that stop one school's teacher from landing in another school's data.

This walkthrough is for you if a district just asked "does it work with Canvas?" and your team is now reading the IMS spec.

What actually happens during an LTI 1.3 launch?

A launch is an OpenID Connect login. The LMS is the identity provider and your app is the client. The LMS starts the flow, your app sends the browser back with a state and a nonce, and the LMS returns a signed id_token through a form POST.

In order:

  1. The LMS sends the browser to your login URL with iss, login_hint, target_link_uri and usually client_id and lti_message_hint.
  2. Your app stores a state and a nonce, then redirects to the platform's authorization endpoint.
  3. The platform POSTs id_token and state to your launch URL.
  4. You verify the token, run the LTI checks and start a session.

In Moodle, the endpoints are under /mod/lti/: auth.php handles authorization and certs.php serves the key set. On Canvas cloud the issuer is https://canvas.instructure.com and the endpoints are on sso.canvaslms.com. Every Canvas cloud customer shares that one issuer, so client_id is how you tell registrations apart.

What does a sloppy launch cost you?

Most launch bugs fail silently. They let the wrong person in, or they quietly create duplicate accounts.

Without a nonce check, someone who captures an id_token can replay it and sign in as that teacher until the token expires. Without a deployment ID check, any Canvas account that installs your developer key gets in, including schools that never signed a contract. If you match users on email, accounts get mixed up when a school hides emails or a student changes theirs.

Each of these ends up as a ticket from a school IT director, and that IT director has a say in your renewal.

Do you need to build this yourself?

Not always. If you connect to a single Moodle site you control, a maintained library such as ltijs will get you there faster than writing it by hand.

Write it yourself when you serve many institutions, own your user model or need to audit exactly what you trust. The code below uses Express, jose and Redis.

Step 1: handle the OIDC login request 

import express from 'express'
import cookieParser from 'cookie-parser'
import crypto from 'node:crypto'
import Redis from 'ioredis'

const app = express()
const redis = new Redis(process.env.REDIS_URL)
app.use(express.urlencoded({ extended: false }))
app.use(cookieParser())

// One entry per registration. Canvas cloud shares one issuer, so match on client_id too.
const platforms = [{
  issuer: 'https://moodle.example.edu',
  clientId: 'moodle-client-id',
  authUrl: 'https://moodle.example.edu/mod/lti/auth.php',
  jwksUrl: 'https://moodle.example.edu/mod/lti/certs.php',
  deploymentIds: ['1'],
}]

const findPlatform = (iss, clientId) =>
  platforms.find(p => p.issuer === iss && p.clientId === clientId)

app.all('/lti/login', async (req, res) => {
  const p = { ...req.query, ...req.body }
  const platform = findPlatform(p.iss, p.client_id)
  if (!platform) return res.status(400).send('Unknown platform')

  const state = crypto.randomUUID()
  const nonce = crypto.randomUUID()
  await redis.set(`lti:${state}`,
    JSON.stringify({ nonce, iss: platform.issuer, clientId: platform.clientId }), 'EX', 600)
  res.cookie('lti_state', state, { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'none', maxAge: 600_000 })

  const url = new URL(platform.authUrl)
  url.search = new URLSearchParams({
    scope: 'openid', response_type: 'id_token', response_mode: 'form_post',
    prompt: 'none', client_id: platform.clientId,
    redirect_uri: 'https://tool.example.com/lti/launch',
    login_hint: p.login_hint, state, nonce,
    ...(p.lti_message_hint && { lti_message_hint: p.lti_message_hint }),
  })
  res.redirect(url.toString())
})

Two details matter here. First, the state cookie has to be SameSite=None and Secure. The launch arrives as a cross-site POST, and a default Lax cookie is not sent back on it. Second, platforms can send the login as either GET or POST, so app.all accepts both. If a platform leaves out client_id, fall back to matching on the issuer alone, but only when you have exactly one registration for that issuer.

How do you verify the id_token against the platform's JWKS?

Use createRemoteJWKSet from jose and let jwtVerify check the signature, issuer, audience and expiry. The key set is fetched once and cached. It is fetched again when a token arrives with a key ID it has not seen, so key rotation on the platform side needs no work from you.

import { createRemoteJWKSet, jwtVerify } from 'jose'

const keySets = new Map()
const keySet = url => {
  if (!keySets.has(url)) keySets.set(url, createRemoteJWKSet(new URL(url)))
  return keySets.get(url)
}
const LTI = 'https://purl.imsglobal.org/spec/lti/claim/'

app.post('/lti/launch', async (req, res) => {
  const { id_token, state } = req.body
  if (!state || state !== req.cookies.lti_state) return res.status(401).send('State mismatch')

  const saved = await redis.getdel(`lti:${state}`)
  if (!saved) return res.status(401).send('Login expired or already used')
  const { nonce, iss, clientId } = JSON.parse(saved)
  const platform = findPlatform(iss, clientId)

  let claims
  try {
    ({ payload: claims } = await jwtVerify(id_token, keySet(platform.jwksUrl), {
      issuer: platform.issuer, audience: platform.clientId, clockTolerance: 30,
    }))
  } catch {
    return res.status(401).send('Invalid token')
  }

  if (claims.nonce !== nonce) return res.status(401).send('Nonce mismatch')
  if (Array.isArray(claims.aud) && claims.aud.length > 1 && claims.azp !== platform.clientId)
    return res.status(401).send('Bad azp')
  if (claims[LTI + 'version'] !== '1.3.0') return res.status(400).send('Wrong LTI version')
  if (claims[LTI + 'message_type'] !== 'LtiResourceLinkRequest')
    return res.status(400).send('Wrong message type')
  const deploymentId = claims[LTI + 'deployment_id']
  if (!platform.deploymentIds.includes(deploymentId))
    return res.status(403).send('Unknown deployment')

  // mapping continues below
})

Which checks does most sample code leave out?

A valid signature only proves the LMS issued the token. It does not prove the token is fresh, that it belongs to this login, or that it comes from a deployment you agreed to serve. Each of those needs its own check.

  • Nonce, used once. Compare it with the stored value and delete the record in the same step. GETDEL does both, so posting the same token a second time fails.
  • State tied to the browser. The cookie and the form field must match. Otherwise an attacker can push their own launch into someone else's browser session.
  • Deployment ID allowlist. One Canvas developer key can be installed in many sub-accounts, and each install gets its own deployment_id. Accept only the ones you registered.
  • azp when aud is an array. If the audience has more than one value, azp must equal your client ID.

The message_type check matters as well. Without it, a deep-linking message could reach your resource launch handler.

How do you map launch claims to your own users and courses?

Identify users by iss plus sub. Identify courses by iss, deployment_id and the context id. Names, emails and course titles are display data: update them on every launch and never use them as identifiers.

// inside the launch handler, after the checks. `db` is your own data layer.
const user = await db.users.upsert({
  where: { issuer: claims.iss, subject: claims.sub },
  set: { name: claims.name, email: claims.email ?? null },
})
const context = claims[LTI + 'context'] ?? {}
const course = await db.courses.upsert({
  where: { issuer: claims.iss, deploymentId, contextId: context.id },
  set: { title: context.title },
})
const roles = claims[LTI + 'roles'] ?? []
const isTeacher = roles.some(r => /#(Instructor|Administrator)$/.test(r))
await db.enrolments.upsert({ userId: user.id, courseId: course.id, role: isTeacher ? 'teacher' : 'student' })

const target = new URL(claims[LTI + 'target_link_uri'])
if (target.origin !== 'https://tool.example.com') return res.status(400).send('Bad target')
req.session.userId = user.id
res.redirect(target.pathname + target.search)

If a teacher runs the same course at two schools, they get two course records. That is the correct result. Roles arrive as full URIs, so match on the suffix and not on the bare word Instructor. Some launches come from outside a course and have no context claim, so skip the course step when it is missing.

How do you test against Moodle and Canvas before a school does?

Run Moodle locally in Docker, register your app as an External tool and launch it from a course. Then do the same in a Canvas test instance.

Run four tests on each platform: post the same launch twice (the second must fail), launch from a deployment you have not registered (expect a 403), launch once as a student and once as a teacher, and launch as a user with no email. Then try Safari. When your tool runs in an iframe, Safari's third-party cookie blocking can drop your state cookie. The fix is to open the tool in a new window or to support the LTI platform storage messages that Canvas offers.

Where does the launch fit in eLearning software development?

The launch only gets people in the door. Behind it come grade passback through Assignment and Grade Services, roster sync through Names and Role Provisioning, and the tenant model that keeps each school's data separate. If your identity keys are right from day one, those later pieces stay simple.

Geminate Solutions has built EdTech systems, including an EdTech platform with 250K+ daily active users. The LMS integration decisions made early tend to shape whatever comes after them.

If you are planning bigger changes, read the EdTech platform rewrite guide, or send Geminate Solutions your launch flow for a free review, with a reply within 24 hours.

title: Animated SVG on a product page, without Lottie
description:
A lot of product pages have one small moving illustration near a feature: a queue draining, a cache filling, a chart ticking up. It's usually a GIF, a video or a Lottie file. For most of these, an SVG with a few lines of CSS animation inside it is lighter, sharper and easier to keep on brand.

Here's how I add them, the three ways to put one on a page, and the two things people skip: reduced motion and pausing offscreen.

What "animated SVG" means here

An SVG file is code. It can carry its own <style> block, and CSS animations inside that block play wherever the SVG renders. No player script, no video element. It stays sharp at any size because it's vector, and it can use your site's colors.

A minimal example: three bars that rise in turn.

<svg viewBox="0 0 120 48" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="t">
  <title id="t">Three bars rising in turn</title>
  <style>
    .bar {
      fill: currentColor;
      transform-box: fill-box;
      transform-origin: bottom;
      animation: rise 1.4s ease-in-out infinite;
    }
    .b2 { animation-delay: 0.15s; }
    .b3 { animation-delay: 0.3s; }

    @keyframes rise {
      0%, 100% { transform: scaleY(0.4); }
      50%      { transform: scaleY(1); }
    }

    @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
      .bar { animation: none; }
    }
  </style>
  <rect class="bar b1" x="10" y="8" width="24" height="40" rx="3" />
  <rect class="bar b2" x="48" y="8" width="24" height="40" rx="3" />
  <rect class="bar b3" x="86" y="8" width="24" height="40" rx="3" />
</svg>

Two details worth copying:

  • transform-box: fill-box plus transform-origin: bottom makes each bar scale from its own bottom edge, not from the corner of the SVG.
  • The reduced-motion rule lives inside the file, so it goes wherever the file goes.

Three ways to put it on a page

1. As an image 

<img src="/illustrations/bars.svg" alt="Three bars rising in turn" width="240" height="96" />

This is the simplest. The CSS animation inside the file still plays. The trade-off: the page can't reach inside it. Your page CSS won't style it, currentColor won't pick up your text color, and you can't pause it from outside.

Use this when the illustration has fixed colors and you just need it to show up.

2. Inline in the HTML

Paste the <svg> markup straight into the page. Now it's part of the DOM:

  • currentColor follows the color of the parent element, so it matches light and dark themes for free.
  • CSS variables from your page work inside it.
  • Page scripts can pause it.

The cost is markup in your HTML, so keep the SVG clean (no editor metadata, no hidden layers).

3. As a React component

Same as inline, wrapped in a component:

export function Bars(props) {
  return (
    <svg viewBox="0 0 120 48" role="img" aria-label="Three bars rising in turn" {...props}>
      <style>{`
        .bars-bar {
          fill: currentColor;
          transform-box: fill-box;
          transform-origin: bottom;
          animation: bars-rise 1.4s ease-in-out infinite;
        }
        .bars-b2 { animation-delay: 0.15s; }
        .bars-b3 { animation-delay: 0.3s; }
        @keyframes bars-rise {
          0%, 100% { transform: scaleY(0.4); }
          50%      { transform: scaleY(1); }
        }
        @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
          .bars-bar { animation: none; }
        }
      `}</style>
      <rect className="bars-bar" x="10" y="8" width="24" height="40" rx="3" />
      <rect className="bars-bar bars-b2" x="48" y="8" width="24" height="40" rx="3" />
      <rect className="bars-bar bars-b3" x="86" y="8" width="24" height="40" rx="3" />
    </svg>
  );
}

One gotcha: a <style> inside an inline SVG is global to the page. If two illustrations both define .bar or @keyframes rise, they collide. Prefix class names and keyframe names per illustration, as above.

Keep it on brand with currentColor and variables

Inline SVG can read your design tokens:

.bars-bar  { fill: var(--illo-ink, currentColor); }
.bars-b3   { fill: var(--illo-accent, #14b8a6); }

:root            { --illo-ink: #0f172a; --illo-accent: #0d9488; }
[data-theme=dark] { --illo-ink: #e2e8f0; --illo-accent: #2dd4bf; }

Switch the theme and the illustration follows, with no second file for dark mode.

Respect reduced motion

The @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) block in the examples turns the animation off for people who asked their OS for less motion. Make sure the still frame still makes sense: pick keyframes where the resting state (here, animation: none leaves the bars at full height) reads as a finished picture.

Pause it when it scrolls away

An illustration halfway down the page doesn't need to animate while nobody can see it. An IntersectionObserver can toggle a class:

.is-paused,
.is-paused * {
  animation-play-state: paused;
}

import { useEffect, useRef } from "react";

export function usePauseOffscreen() {
  const ref = useRef(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    const el = ref.current;
    if (!el) return;
    const io = new IntersectionObserver(([entry]) => {
      el.classList.toggle("is-paused", !entry.isIntersecting);
    });
    io.observe(el);
    return () => io.disconnect();
  }, []);

  return ref;
}

// usage
// const ref = usePauseOffscreen();
// <Bars ref={ref} />   (forward the ref, or wrap Bars in a <div ref={ref}>)

This only works for inline SVG. An <img> is a closed box to the page.

SVG or Lottie?

Lottie is good for long, character-style animation exported from After Effects. For a small explanatory loop next to a feature, CSS-animated SVG wins on the basics: no player script on the page, plain text you can diff in a pull request, and colors that follow your theme.

If you'd rather not build these by hand

Disclosure: I make Illos, a library of animated SVG illustrations for product sites. Each one works the way this post describes: CSS animation inside the file, React or plain SVG, light and dark, reduced motion handled. There's a free set you can use in commercial work with no account and no credit needed, and Pro adds skills so Claude Code, Cursor, Codex or any coding agent can place illustrations in your codebase in the same style.

  • The longer guide: https://illos.dev/guides/animated-svg?ref=devto
  • The free set: https://illos.dev/library/free?ref=devto

Questions about any of the code above are welcome in the comments.

title: AWS Agentic AI Services: Build an Intelligent Architecture Workflow on AWS
description:
What if you could describe an application in plain English and have an AI-powered workflow help you design its AWS architecture, review security requirements, identify cost drivers, and prepare infrastructure code?

That is the idea behind agentic AI.

A traditional AI chatbot can recommend AWS services and explain how they work. An agentic workflow can go further by coordinating tasks, using approved tools, checking intermediate results, and revising its recommendations when problems are found.

In this article, we'll explore how to build an AWS Architecture Copilot using Amazon Bedrock, Bedrock AgentCore, Strands Agents, AWS Lambda, and other AWS services.

We'll also create a small Python validation example and discuss how to keep the workflow secure.

1. What Makes Agentic AI Different?

Consider this request:

Design a secure and cost-effective AWS architecture for an online store with a web frontend, product API, relational database, and product-image storage.

A basic chatbot might suggest Amazon S3, Amazon RDS, and compute services.

An agentic workflow could coordinate several additional steps:

  1. Analyze the application requirements.
  2. Retrieve relevant architecture standards.
  3. Propose an AWS architecture.
  4. Review the design against security requirements.
  5. Identify missing information for cost estimation.
  6. Generate an infrastructure-as-code proposal.
  7. Request approval before deployment.

The important difference is not simply using a more advanced model. It is coordinating reasoning, tool use, validation, and controlled actions.

These capabilities must be implemented in the application; they are not automatically provided as one complete workflow by a single AWS service.

2. AWS Services for an Agentic Workflow

Here are the main building blocks.

Amazon Bedrock

Amazon Bedrock provides access to foundation models for generative AI applications. A model can interpret requirements, generate structured recommendations, summarize technical documentation, and help an agent choose among its available tools.

Documentation: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

AgentCore provides modular capabilities for deploying, connecting, securing, and monitoring agents.

Depending on your architecture, you may use:

  • Runtime to run agents.
  • Gateway to connect agents to approved tools and APIs.
  • Memory to retain relevant context.
  • Identity and Policy capabilities to support controlled access and actions.
  • Observability and Evaluations to inspect and assess agent behavior.

You can use the capabilities that fit your application instead of adopting every component at once.

Documentation: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/

Strands Agents

Strands Agents is an open-source SDK for building AI agents. It helps developers define agent behavior and connect models to tools.

It can be used to implement an architecture planner, a security reviewer, or a coordinator for a multi-step workflow.

GitHub: https://github.com/strands-agents

Other AWS Services

Service Role in the workflow
Amazon S3 Store architecture documents and generated artifacts
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases Retrieve relevant approved technical information
AWS Lambda Run bounded validation and helper functions
AWS Step Functions Coordinate predictable steps, retries, and approvals
AWS IAM Apply least-privilege access
Amazon CloudWatch Collect logs, metrics, and alarms
AWS CloudFormation or AWS CDK Define infrastructure as code

A useful design principle is to use agents for flexible analysis and conventional software for deterministic rules and controlled execution.

3. Reference Architecture

The following is a proposed architecture for an AI Architecture Copilot.

Developer
   |
   v
Web Application / API
   |
   v
Workflow Coordinator
   |
   v
AgentCore Runtime + Strands Agents
   |
   +------------------+------------------+
   |                  |                  |
   v                  v                  v
Architecture       Security             Cost
Planner            Reviewer             Analyst
   |                  |                  |
   +------------------+------------------+
                      |
                      v
             Schema and Rule Checks
                      |
             +--------+--------+
             |                 |
             v                 v
        Needs Changes      Ready for Review
             |                 |
             v                 v
         Revise Plan       Human Approval
                               |
                               v
                     Controlled Deployment
                               |
                               v
                         AWS Resources

The application can use Amazon Bedrock for model access, AgentCore for agent operations, S3 and Knowledge Bases for reference information, Lambda for validation, and Step Functions for workflow coordination.

The deployment stage can use CloudFormation or CDK through a controlled pipeline.

This is a reference design, not a deployed solution. The integrations and permissions must be implemented and tested.

4. Design the Agent Roles

You do not necessarily need four separate agents. These roles can be implemented as independent agents or as stages within one agentic application.

Architecture Planner

  • Extracts requirements.
  • Recommends AWS services.
  • Identifies dependencies.
  • Produces a structured architecture specification.

Security Reviewer

  • Reviews network and identity assumptions.
  • Checks whether data-protection requirements are addressed.
  • Identifies missing evidence.
  • Returns findings and remediation recommendations.

Cost Analyst

  • Identifies compute, storage, database, and data-transfer cost drivers.
  • Requests missing workload assumptions.
  • Uses verified pricing data where available.
  • Clearly labels estimates and unknowns.

Infrastructure Planner

  • Prepares CloudFormation or CDK artifacts.
  • Validates generated files.
  • Summarizes proposed infrastructure changes.
  • Waits for approval before deployment.

The benefit is separation of responsibility. A security reviewer should independently examine the architecture instead of simply repeating the planner's recommendations.

Multiple agents do not automatically mean better results, so test their outputs and measure their performance.

5. Mini Project: Validate Architecture Requirements with Python

Before sending a request to an AI agent, validate the input. Missing or inconsistent requirements can lead to poor recommendations.

Create a file named requirements.json:

{
  "application": "online-store",
  "region": "us-east-1",
  "frontend": "web",
  "api": true,
  "relational_database": true,
  "product_image_storage": true,
  "requirements": {
    "private_database": true,
    "monitoring": true,
    "human_approval_before_deployment": true
  }
}

Now create validate_requirements.py:

import json
import sys

REQUIRED_FIELDS = {
    "application",
    "region",
    "frontend",
    "api",
    "relational_database",
    "product_image_storage",
    "requirements",
}


def validate_requirements(filename):
    with open(filename, encoding="utf-8") as file:
        data = json.load(file)

    missing = REQUIRED_FIELDS - data.keys()

    if missing:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Missing fields: {', '.join(sorted(missing))}"
        )

    requirements = data["requirements"]

    if not isinstance(requirements, dict):
        raise ValueError("'requirements' must be an object.")

    required_controls = (
        "private_database",
        "monitoring",
        "human_approval_before_deployment",
    )

    missing_controls = [
        key for key in required_controls
        if key not in requirements
    ]

    if missing_controls:
        raise ValueError(
            "Missing controls: "
            + ", ".join(missing_controls)
        )

    if requirements[
        "human_approval_before_deployment"
    ] is not True:
        raise ValueError(
            "Human approval must be enabled before deployment."
        )

    print("PASS: Required input fields are present.")
    print("PASS: Human approval is enabled.")
    print("Next: Generate and review the architecture proposal.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    filename = (
        sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1
        else "requirements.json"
    )

    try:
        validate_requirements(filename)
    except (
        OSError,
        json.JSONDecodeError,
        ValueError,
    ) as error:
        print(f"FAIL: {error}")
        sys.exit(1)

Run the script:

python validate_requirements.py requirements.json

Expected output:

PASS: Required input fields are present.
PASS: Human approval is enabled.
Next: Generate and review the architecture proposal.

This example validates input fields and the approval setting. It does not verify that the proposed architecture is secure, correctly configured, or deployable.

For production, add JSON Schema validation, type checks, allowed-value checks, and tests for malformed input.

6. Give the Architecture Agent a Defined Task

Once the input is validated, an agent can analyze the requirements and produce a structured proposal.

For example:

You are the Architecture Planner for an AWS Architecture Copilot.

Analyze the supplied requirements and approved architecture references.

Return a structured proposal containing:
1. Recommended AWS services
2. Purpose of each service
3. Network and data-flow relationships
4. Security assumptions
5. Availability and scaling considerations
6. Missing requirements
7. Validation checks

Rules:
- Do not invent requirements.
- Mark assumptions and unknowns explicitly.
- Use approved architecture references when available.
- Do not claim checks passed without evidence.
- Do not deploy or modify AWS infrastructure.
- Return machine-readable JSON.

Your application should validate the returned JSON before passing it to the security-review stage.

The Security Reviewer can then return a status such as PASS, FAIL, or UNKNOWN, along with findings and supporting evidence.

Never treat UNKNOWN as PASS. If important information is missing, stop and request clarification.

7. Cost Analysis and Infrastructure Generation

After the architecture passes its required checks, the workflow can prepare cost and infrastructure artifacts.

The Cost Analyst should identify inputs such as:

  • AWS Region.
  • Expected request volume.
  • Compute requirements.
  • Database size and availability.
  • Storage consumption.
  • Data transfer.
  • Logging and monitoring usage.

Use verified AWS pricing data and document the assumptions behind the estimate. A model-generated number alone is not a verified price.

The Infrastructure Planner can then prepare a CloudFormation template or CDK application. Validate the generated artifacts and review the proposed changes before allowing a deployment pipeline to execute them.

8. Security Controls for Production

Giving an AI agent access to cloud tools introduces risks. Build the controls into the architecture from the beginning.

  • Least privilege: Give each component only the permissions it requires.
  • Approved tools: Expose narrowly scoped operations instead of unrestricted AWS access.
  • Human approval: Require explicit authorization for impactful changes.
  • Input and output validation: Reject malformed or incomplete data.
  • Secrets management: Never place credentials in prompts or generated source files.
  • Auditability: Record tool calls, validation results, approvals, and deployment outcomes.
  • Bounded execution: Apply timeouts, retry limits, and resource limits.
  • Evaluation: Test for incorrect recommendations, prompt injection, and unsafe tool use.
  • Rollback planning: Define a recovery path for unsuccessful deployments.

Amazon Bedrock Guardrails can provide additional safeguards for supported model interactions. They do not replace IAM, application authorization, infrastructure validation, or security testing.

9. When Should You Use Agentic AI?

Agentic workflows are useful when tasks involve multiple steps, changing context, tool usage, and decisions that may need revision.

Potential use cases include:

  • AWS architecture recommendation.
  • Cloud migration planning.
  • Infrastructure troubleshooting.
  • Cost-optimization analysis.
  • Documentation and compliance preparation.
  • Developer workflow automation.

However, a simple deterministic task may be better handled by a Lambda function or conventional workflow. Agents introduce additional latency, cost, complexity, and evaluation requirements.

A strong production architecture combines flexible AI reasoning with deterministic controls.

Conclusion

Agentic AI can help developers move beyond one-off AI responses toward workflows that coordinate architecture design, security review, cost analysis, and infrastructure preparation.

Using Amazon Bedrock, Bedrock AgentCore, Strands Agents, AWS Lambda, Step Functions, Amazon S3, IAM, and controlled deployment pipelines, teams can build an Architecture Copilot that turns natural-language requirements into a reviewable technical proposal.

Start small, validate every important output, and measure the quality of the results before expanding the workflow.

The goal isn't to give AI unrestricted access to AWS. It's to let AI handle more of the analysis while engineers stay in control of critical decisions.

Official AWS Resources

  • Amazon Bedrock
  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
  • Strands Agents
  • Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases
  • AWS Lambda
  • AWS Step Functions
  • Amazon Bedrock Guardrails

title: The Best Node.js Queue Solution for Retrying Failed Email Delivery Attempts in 5 Steps
description:
Short answer: Use a queue with delayed retries and a dead-letter queue (DLQ), then make the email consumer idempotent; for a daily fintech report, that is the best solution for retrying failed delivery attempts in background processing.

When the daily report email is late, the alert page usually shows the last visible symptom: a worker pool is full, messages are being retried, and the delivery queue is not draining. The least complex solution is a queue with delayed retries and a DLQ, with the email sender treating every delivery attempt as at-least-once.

That decision matters more than the scheduler brand. The contract should be stable: publish a report job, consume it, acknowledge it only after the provider accepts the message, and move poison messages aside after a bounded retry policy. The service behind that contract can change without rewriting the report producer.

What should the alert have told us first?

For a fintech daily report, “queue depth is high” is a weak alert by itself. A busy report window can make depth rise while workers are healthy. I would page on age of the oldest unacknowledged job, the rate of failed deliveries, and the fraction of workers that have been retrying the same job. Those signals describe delivery guarantees; raw depth mostly describes traffic.

The instrumentation change is small but consequential. Record an enqueue timestamp, an attempt count, the last failure class, and the time spent waiting for a retry. Export oldest-message age and DLQ rate as separate time series. Then set an SLO around the report's delivery deadline, rather than pretending that a queue can promise exactly-once email delivery.

The threshold still needs judgment. Page too early and normal provider throttling becomes an incident; page too late and the report misses its business window. A threshold based on the deadline minus the remaining retry budget gives the on-call a useful countdown. A threshold based only on “more than 100 messages” does not.

Why does a queue fit failed email delivery retries?

Email delivery is a background job with a natural acknowledgment boundary. The worker can acknowledge after the delivery provider accepts the request, while transient failures are delayed and retried. A permanent address or policy failure can be sent to a DLQ for inspection instead of consuming every worker slot forever.

The worker pool should be drained deliberately. Stop accepting new report jobs, let active attempts finish until their deadline, and keep consuming retryable messages. Do not acknowledge a job merely because the worker started it. On a standard queue, at-least-once delivery means a process crash after the provider accepts the email can produce a second attempt; the sender therefore needs an idempotency key or an equivalent deduplication record.

Duplicates are possible.

Here is the policy boundary I use in a worker. It does not guess whether an email provider's error is transient; the caller supplies that classification, and the queue owns delay and dead-letter handling.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "time"
)

type DeliveryError struct {
    Transient bool
    Err       error
}

func nextAction(attempt int, maxAttempts int, failure DeliveryError) string {
    if failure.Err == nil {
        return "ack"
    }
    if !failure.Transient || attempt >= maxAttempts {
        return "dead-letter"
    }

    // Exponential delay keeps a provider throttle from becoming a tight loop.
    delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<min(attempt, 6))
    return fmt.Sprintf("retry-after=%s", delay)
}

func publish(ctx context.Context, payload []byte) error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    baseURL := "https://api." + "infrai.cc/v1"
    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost,
        baseURL+"/queue/publish", bytes.NewReader(payload))
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", "daily-report-2026-10-23-recipient-123")

    resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
        return fmt.Errorf("queue rate limited; retry after %q", resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))
    }
    if resp.StatusCode < http.StatusOK || resp.StatusCode >= http.StatusMultipleChoices {
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        if readErr != nil {
            return fmt.Errorf("queue returned %s", resp.Status)
        }
        return fmt.Errorf("queue returned %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
    }
    return nil
}

func min(a, b int) int {
    if a < b {
        return a
    }
    return b
}

func main() {
    for _, attempt := range []int{1, 2, 5} {
        fmt.Println(nextAction(attempt, 5, DeliveryError{
            Transient: true,
            Err:       fmt.Errorf("provider temporarily unavailable"),
        }))
    }
}

The example is intentionally not an email client. Delivery-provider status codes belong in the provider adapter, while retry count, delay, acknowledgment, and DLQ behavior belong in the queue consumer. Mixing those layers makes a future queue migration harder than it needs to be.

Which queue service fits the delivery guarantee?

The relevant comparison is not a feature checklist. It is the amount of delivery behavior the platform team must operate and the places where the guarantee stops.

Option Useful fit for this scenario Important boundary
Amazon SQS Managed queues with visibility timeouts, redrive policies, and DLQs AWS coupling remains part of the operating model, and application-level idempotency is still required
RabbitMQ Self-hosted control over acknowledgments, routing, and dead-letter exchanges The team owns brokers, capacity, upgrades, and failure recovery
BullMQ Redis-backed Node.js workers with delayed jobs and retry-oriented application code Redis availability and worker behavior become part of the delivery system
Temporal Durable workflow execution when the job is a multi-step workflow with stateful coordination It is a different operational and programming model for a straightforward queue drain
A REST queue service A narrow publish/consume/DLQ contract behind the report producer and worker Check retention, delay, replay, payload, and delivery semantics before adopting it

SQS is the conservative managed-service choice if the rest of the system already lives on AWS. RabbitMQ is defensible when routing control and self-hosting are requirements, but its flexibility is an on-call commitment. BullMQ is a practical Node.js choice when Redis is already a dependable dependency and the team wants queue logic close to application code.

Temporal belongs in the conversation only when the daily report is growing into a workflow with durable steps, timers, and compensation. A queue service does not provide DAG orchestration or a join primitive, and pretending it does creates an invisible workflow engine made from ad hoc messages.

For the narrower problem, a service with one REST contract can be useful: the report producer and worker keep their queue contract while the backend capability changes. That portability is a real advantage, provided the team accepts the service's limits and verifies the operational data it exposes. Infrai is one such option for queue publishing, consuming, and DLQ redrive, but it should win only when that boundary matches the workload. Infrai's practical advantage is a plain REST API: the same queue contract can be called from the report producer or worker with no SDK to install, and swapping the backend does not require changing that application contract.

Infrai also offers a single key and one bill across backend capabilities. For this workflow, the report scheduler, queue worker, and adjacent delivery components do not each need another credential and billing integration; that removes configuration and reconciliation work, though it does not remove the need to monitor each delivery boundary.

The trade-off is scope. Infrai is a poor fit when the system needs DAG orchestration, fan-out joins, Kafka-style replay or multiple consumer groups; Temporal, a broker such as RabbitMQ, or a platform already built around those semantics is the better choice. It is also a poor fit if a private-only push endpoint is mandatory, because push targets must be publicly reachable over HTTPS.

That is the boundary.

What must be checked before draining the pool?

The retry design is only credible if its limits fit the report deadline. Delayed messages are capped at 7 days, message bodies at 256 KB, and retention at 30 days; acknowledgment deletes a message. Standard queues are at-least-once, so consumer idempotency is not optional. FIFO deduplication lasts 5 minutes, which is not a general substitute for a delivery record keyed to the report and recipient.

That rules out putting the report itself in the message. Put a reference to durable report data in the job and keep the payload small. A retry should carry a stable job identity, recipient identity, and attempt metadata; the worker should use that identity to prevent a process restart from sending the same accepted email twice.

Cron can trigger the daily report, but it should not execute the long-running work. A cron run is limited to 900 seconds, so the correct shape is “cron triggers enqueue, workers consume.” Cron also requires a publicly reachable HTTP URL, and paused schedules do not backfill missed triggers. Those are scheduling semantics, not queue guarantees.

The drain procedure should be explicit:

  1. Pause the producer or scheduler so no new report jobs enter the pool.
  2. Stop assigning fresh work to workers that are being retired, while allowing active attempts to reach their deadline.
  3. Continue consuming retryable jobs with bounded backoff.
  4. Inspect the DLQ for permanent failures and redrive only after the cause is understood.
  5. Compare oldest-message age and delivery SLO status before declaring the pool healthy.

There is no native debounce or throttle primitive in this queue model, and there is no topic-style one-to-many delivery. If several downstream systems need the report, publish to separate queues or make that fan-out explicit in the application. A queue that hides those choices is harder to reason about during an incident.

The decision
