title: Buy vs. build is now also a UX decision, especially in enterprise
description:
Artificial intelligence made building cheap and buying easy. The trade-off now turns on who owns the upkeep, the seams between tools, the chat surfaces, and the data.

For most of my career, product management owned buy versus build. A product manager wrote the case, finance checked the math, and procurement signed.

Designers arrived after the decision was made, inherited whatever won, and spent years sanding its rough edges. Artificial intelligence changed the math on both sides at once.

Build is cheaper now, but the yearly upkeep never shows up in the business case.

Buy comes with legacy, and that legacy now includes someone else’s model, roadmap, and release calendar. And usually there’s a third option nobody names: replacing the system you already have.

Menlo Ventures found in 2025: The State of Generative AI in the Enterprise that 76% of enterprise artificial intelligence use cases were purchased rather than built, up from 53% a year earlier. Meanwhile, coding agents make a working internal tool look like an afternoon project.

More work happens inside Teams, Slack, Claude, and ChatGPT, surfaces neither option owns.

Don’t ask which option costs less, Ask where the complexity lands: in your code, in a vendor’s roadmap, or on your users.

Budget for Build Maintenance

A designer with a coding agent can now stand up an internal tool before a vendor’s sales team returns the call. Andrej Karpathy named that loose style vibe coding in 2025, and Simon Willison drew the line in Not all AI-assisted programming is vibe coding (but vibe coding rocks). Prototypes can be loose, but code you keep has to be read like any other.

Most internal tools become code you keep, which makes them products. It needs a budget, an owner, and someone to call when it breaks. Most teams don’t think of it that way, because nobody bought anything.

I learned this the hard way.

We built an internal workflow application in one place I worked at, before AI, because nothing we could buy matched how our teams worked. It shipped fast, people came to depend on it, and that’s exactly when it became a nightmare to maintain.

Every new approval step meant changing code few people understood, small fixes broke things elsewhere, and nobody had budgeted time for any of it.

That’s where my rule comes from. I budget 30% of the upfront build cost every year for upkeep: updates, patches, model changes, and new requests.

Run that math and many vibe-coded apps cost more than the subscriptions they replace. Say two people spend two weeks at a fully loaded $150 an hour, which is $24,000 up front and $7,200 a year after. A subscription at $20 a seat for 25 people runs $6,000 a year. Over three years, the build costs $45,600 against $18,000, and only one of them came with a support team.

Every generated line is a line somebody has to own, and the initial owner usually doesn’t want that responsibility.

Open source taught this lesson first. Black Duck’s 2026 Open Source Security and Risk Analysis Report found open source in 98% of audited codebases, and 93% held components with no development activity in two years.

In 2024, a backdoor reached the widely used XZ Utils library after an attacker spent years earning its maintainer’s trust. Generated code has the same weakness: nobody paid for it, so nobody budgeted to watch it. Google’s 2025 DORA Report found adoption of artificial intelligence still hurts delivery stability.

Accept the Vendor’s Legacy

Buying looks like the cautious choice, and often it is.

Purchases from specialized vendors succeeded about 67% of the time, while internal builds succeeded about a third as often, according to research from MIT’s NANDA initiative covered in Fortune’s MIT report: 95% of generative AI pilots at companies are failing.

The fair objection is selection, since companies tend to buy for well-understood problems and build for messy ones, which flatters vendors. Hold the number loosely, but the direction matches where enterprise budgets went.

A purchase is never only a feature set. You also get the vendor’s data model, release cadence, and theory of what your users are trying to do.

When you buy, you import another company’s organization chart.

Systems mirror the communication structures of the organizations that design them, as Melvin Conway observed in 1968. Your users end up inside a product tuned for that company’s largest customers, who may look nothing like yours.

Measure the Tool Gaps

Users don’t experience your build or your purchase on its own. They experience the gaps. You can count those gaps the way you’d count clicks in a usability test: pick one real task, follow it across systems, and log every switch and every retyped value.

The gaps add up fast.

People in a 2022 study of 137 workers on 20 teams at three Fortune 500 companies switched between applications and websites roughly 1,200 times a day. Reorienting after each switch cost them just under four hours a week, about 9% of their working time, according to How Much Time and Energy Do We Waste Toggling Between Applications? in Harvard Business Review and AAPL Leadership.

Homegrown tools widen the gaps too. In the 1990s, departments built their own Microsoft Access databases because waiting on the central technology team took a quarter.

The databases worked until their authors changed jobs, and then the data inside them became one more place nobody could reach. Today’s version is drift: patterns that stop matching the rest of the product and error states nobody designed.

Complexity always lands somewhere, and the only choice is where.

Complexity is conserved, and the only real choice is who absorbs it. That’s Larry Tesler’s law.

A build moves complexity into your codebase, while a purchase moves it into someone else’s roadmap. A careless mix of both moves it onto your users, one copy-and-paste at a time. Before anyone argues about license fees, ask where the complexity ends up under each option.

Design for Host Surfaces

In many organizations, the place people meet your product is no longer your product. It’s Teams, Slack, Claude, or ChatGPT.

Apps moved inside ChatGPT conversations in 2025 with OpenAI’s Introducing apps in ChatGPT and the new Apps SDK. In January 2026, MCP Apps — Bringing UI Capabilities To MCP Clients let tools return interactive interfaces that render inside Claude and ChatGPT. Build or buy, your most-used screen may end up as a card in someone else’s window.

I’ve worked inside this arrangement before. I designed the developer documentation site for Myspace, whose 2008 developer platform let third-party applications run on member profiles. The host set the box size, the permissions, and what an app could know about the person looking at it. Every app was designed inside that frame, and chat surfaces are drawing it again.

The host draws the frame, and your job is deciding what fits inside it.

The rules are specific, and they belong to the host. An inline card in ChatGPT gets at most two actions, no nested scrolling, the system font, and a logo the host adds for you, per OpenAI’s UI guidelines for the Apps SDK.

A Slack message holds up to 50 blocks under Block Kit. Microsoft’s Types of Cards & their Usage names Adaptive Cards the recommended card type for new Teams development.

People expect your product to work like the places where they spend most of their time, which is Jakob Nielsen’s Jakob’s Law of Internet User Experience. Inside a chat surface, that stops being advice, because the host’s patterns are the only ones on offer. So design the card as its own product, with one job, one primary action, and a handoff to your full application when the task outgrows it.

Count the Replacement Cost

Most of these decisions aren’t made on empty ground. Something already exists, and the real question is whether to replace it. Replacement carries costs that appear in neither column.

The first cost is lost expertise. Task time falls with repetition, which is the Power Law of Practice covered on my UX Guidelines site (@usabilitycounts), and your power users have years of repetitions in the old tool. Replace it, and they start the curve over, usually in the busiest quarter.

The second cost is hidden rules. You shouldn’t tear down a fence until you know why it went up, as G. K. Chesterton argued in 1929. Old enterprise software is full of fences, and each one was a rule somebody once needed.

The new thing always wins the demo against the tool people already know.

The third cost is our own bias. People value their amateur work about as highly as experts’ work, according to Michael Norton and his co-authors in The IKEA Effect: When Labor Leads to Love. Melissa Perri described the organizational version in The Build Trap: building is the easy part, and teams get rewarded for shipping instead of for learning what customers need.

Not invented here makes it worse. Not invented here is the reflex of rejecting an outside solution because someone else made it. Ralph Katz and Thomas Allen tracked 50 research and development project groups for An empirical test of the Not Invented Here (NIH) Syndrome, a 1980 MIT working paper.

Groups that had worked together five or more years performed significantly worse, and they talked less with professionals outside the team. Coding agents lower the price of acting on that reflex, because rebuilding a vendor’s feature now takes a weekend instead of a budget cycle.

Coding agents also distort the estimate. Experienced developers took 19% longer on real tasks with the tools, yet estimated afterward they had been 20% faster, in METR’s randomized trial Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity.

It’s one study of 16 developers, and METR now flags it as out of date. Still, price your own prototype the way you’d price a stranger’s.

Buy Commodities, Build Differentiators

The clearest test I know comes from Simon Wardley (@swardley). In Finding a path, he sorts components from genesis to custom built to product to commodity.

His shorthand for building commodities yourself is Thomas Thwaites, the designer who spent nine months trying to build a toaster from raw materials. A coding agent shrinks the nine months to a weekend, which matters less than it seems, because you still own every repair after it ships.

Coding agents change the toaster math, not the toaster.

For products built on artificial intelligence, the map has a clear split. The model is sliding toward commodity, rented by the token. The experience around it is still custom: how a suggestion explains itself, how someone corrects it, and whether people trust it. A competitor can’t copy that by signing the same contract.

Building still wins in a few places. Build when your own data is the advantage and a vendor would have to hold it to use it.

Build when regulation rules out every product on the market, and build the moments you compete on. If a feature would look the same in every competitor’s product, though, it’s probably a commodity.

Those cases also assume you have the people, and most organizations don’t. Vibe coding gets you a demo, not the skills a production artificial intelligence application needs: retrieval over messy records, evaluations, permissions, and monitoring.

IBM surveyed 8,584 technology professionals for Data Suggests Growth in Enterprise Adoption of AI is Due to Widespread Deployment by Early Adopters, published in January 2024. Limited skills and expertise topped the barriers at 33%, with data complexity next at 25%. The more data an application touches, the wider that gap gets.

Map Where Data Lives

A model can only answer from what it can see, so the experience follows wherever your data lives. Buy a tool and your records sit in the vendor’s schema, reachable on the vendor’s terms.

Build one and the data stays yours, along with the job of governing it. When Anthropic announced the Model Context Protocol in 2024, it described models cut off from data trapped behind silos and legacy systems.

So run the landing test a second time, aimed at the data. A card in Teams is only as useful as the permissions behind it, and an assistant that can’t reach the contract can’t summarize it.

Whoever holds the records decides what any surface can show.

Regulation is starting to price this in. The law has applied since September 12, 2025, and switching charges between data processing providers, including data egress fees, end entirely on January 12, 2027, according to the European Commission’s Data Act explained.

Leaving a vendor is getting cheaper on paper. In practice, a migration is mostly a data project with a UX bill attached: renamed fields, lost history, and reports that no longer match.

Before any contract, ask where the data will live, who can export it and in what format, and whether the surfaces your people already use can reach it.

Those answers shape the experience more than the feature list does.

Prepare for Model Retirement

Either way, part of your product now runs on something you don’t control. Build on a model and that model will be retired. Anthropic promises at least 60 days’ notice before retiring a publicly released model.

Its Model deprecations page lists the Claude Sonnet 4.5 snapshot from September 2025 as deprecated on September 30, 2026, with retirement set for November 30, 2026.

Buy a product built on a model and the same thing happens, one layer removed and on the vendor’s schedule. Tone shifts. Refusals move. Summaries grow or shrink, and edge cases that used to pass start failing. A vendor’s release notes may not mention a model change at all, so ask in the contract how much notice you’ll get.

A model swap is a redesign nobody scheduled, and now happens on a frequent basis. Maintenane is now a real time activity.

The exit plan belongs to design, not only to procurement. Keep a set of real user tasks with known good outcomes, run them against every new model or vendor release, and review the results the way you’d review a usability study. Twenty or thirty tasks is enough to start, as long as they include the common requests, the expensive mistakes, and the cases where the correct response is to decline.

Decide Where Complexity Lands

Buy versus build used to end at the signature or at launch. Now neither choice finishes, because the parts keep moving after the decision. Building got cheaper and stayed expensive to own. Buying got easier and arrived carrying more of someone else’s history than the demo let on.

So the decision can’t stay with product management and finance. The numbers in that spreadsheet are real enough. They just leave out the costs users feel most: drift in tools nobody maintains, expertise lost when an old system goes away, data stuck where new tools can’t reach it, and chat surfaces whose layout rules you don’t set.

Designers, product managers, and researchers are the people who see those costs first. They can also measure them, in task time and in the moments where someone gives up. Bring that evidence to the decision before it’s made, not after it ships.

The landing test won’t tell you whether to buy or build. It tells you where the complexity will go, so somebody can be standing there on purpose. Most of the time, that points toward buying the commodity and building the difference. The seams between the two are yours either way, so design them.

Action Items

  • Test vendors against prototypes. Run a hands-on bake-off with real tasks, using the scenario-based method in The Right Way to Select Technology by Tony Byrne and Jarrod Gingras. Enter your current system and a quick internal prototype alongside the vendors, and ask the current system’s heaviest users why each odd step exists.
  • List every system touched. Pick one real task and follow it from start to finish. Write down each system it passes through, where each value is stored, and who can export it, then put that list in the business case next to the license fee.
  • Budget 30% for upkeep. Before a build ships, name the person who maintains it and set aside 30% of its build cost every year. Treat that line as fixed, the way you would a subscription, so fixes and library updates don’t wait for spare time.
  • Retest after model changes. Keep 20 to 30 real tasks with known good answers, including the common requests and the costly mistakes. Run them whenever a model or vendor release changes what’s underneath, and review the results like a usability study.

Buy vs. build is now also a UX decision, especially in enterprise was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Semantic Retrieval for News Monitoring with Go: Pagination That Preserves Grounding
description:
News monitoring gets difficult when pagination changes the evidence set underneath an answer. My rule is simple: use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context that survives every page. That keeps an answer replaceable across providers because the application depends on a contract, not a vendor-shaped response.

Short answer: define a retrieval contract first, then combine lexical discovery with semantic ranking, tenant filters, and stable cursors; emit a source URL or document ID for every cited chunk.

The incident lesson: pagination is part of grounding

I model a failed search as an incident even before an alert fires. A reporter asks, “What changed in the coastal policy this week?” The service returns a fluent summary, but page two was fetched with a new relevance snapshot, one article moved ahead of another, and the citation now points at a chunk the model never saw. The text sounds right. The trail is wrong.

The invariant is that a page is a view over a fixed retrieval contract. The contract names the collection, tenant and access-control metadata, query bounds, ranking stages, and a cursor or snapshot token. It also says what the UI can display as evidence. Offset pagination is acceptable for a small, immutable fixture; for a live feed, a cursor tied to the same ranking snapshot is safer. Your mileage may vary when the backend cannot provide snapshots, so record the retrieval timestamp and ranking inputs and treat the page as best effort.

That is the whole point.

For an adapter that must stay replaceable, Infrai is a practical candidate to test early: its search surface is plain HTTP, so a Go service can send requests without an SDK, while the retrieval contract keeps the rest of the application independent.

Three checks catch most of the expensive failures:

  1. A user-visible answer maps to an explicit retrieval request, not an opaque “search everything” call.
  2. Every indexed item carries tenant and access-control metadata, and those fields are applied before model context is assembled.
  3. Every returned chunk has a source URL or document identifier, page position, and enough text to let a reviewer verify it.

A common assumption is that a larger top-k will compensate for noisy indexing. It does not. In a concrete replay, the first page contained three syndicated copies of the same wire story, while the relevant PDF was pushed to page four; the next request recomputed scores after a late-arriving article, so the cursor no longer described the same ordering. We traced the mismatch by logging collection, tenant, ACL predicate, query bounds, candidate IDs, ranking stage, cursor, and snapshot together, then replayed the exact fixture after each change. A bounded candidate set plus a second ranking pass made the error visible, because we could inspect which stage dropped the relevant document instead of blaming the generator, and a citation check caught the case where the answer still sounded plausible despite pointing to an unseen chunk.

How should semantic retrieval handle news monitoring pagination?

Use stages with different jobs. First, discover candidates with a date window, language, tenant, and a maximum count. Next, apply vector similarity to those candidates. Finally, rerank a small set and attach source metadata before constructing the prompt. Pagination advances through that same staged result, rather than rerunning an unconstrained search for each page.

The collection boundary matters. Keep collections explicit, such as news-en-prod and news-zh-prod, instead of relying on a hidden default. Store the canonical URL, publisher, publication time, document ID, tenant ID, ACL, and chunk ID beside the embedding. A deleted or permission-revoked article should disappear from candidate selection, not merely be masked after generation.

For a service that answers over PDFs, parse once, chunk deterministically, and retain the PDF page number. A chunk that says “the rate changed” without its page and document ID is not useful evidence. Representative documents should include long reports, duplicate wire stories, scanned pages, and adversarial near-matches; evaluate recall and precision on those fixtures before changing thresholds.

Here is the small Go adapter I put between a retrieval provider and the answerer. It makes pagination observable, keeps provider-specific response shapes out of business logic, and leaves the request JSON to the discovery-backed caller rather than inventing fields.

package retrieval

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

type Hit struct {
    DocumentID string
    SourceURL  string
    Page       int
    Text       string
}

type Page struct {
    Hits       []Hit
    NextCursor string
    Snapshot   string
}

// NextPage rejects a response that cannot be cited or safely continued.
func NextPage(p Page, expectedSnapshot string) (string, error) {
    if p.Snapshot == "" || p.Snapshot != expectedSnapshot {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("retrieval snapshot changed")
    }
    for _, hit := range p.Hits {
        if hit.DocumentID == "" || hit.SourceURL == "" {
            return "", fmt.Errorf("uncitable hit: missing document ID or source URL")
        }
    }
    return p.NextCursor, nil
}

// QueryInfrai sends the exact request JSON produced by the caller's schema-aware adapter.
func QueryInfrai(ctx context.Context, payload []byte) ([]byte, error) {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/vector/query",
            io.NopCloser(bytesReader(payload)))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            wait := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil {
                wait = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            timer := time.NewTimer(wait)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return nil, ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
            }
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("vector query failed: %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("vector query rate limit persisted")
}

type byteReader struct{ data []byte; pos int }
func bytesReader(data []byte) *byteReader { return &byteReader{data: data} }
func (r *byteReader) Read(p []byte) (int, error) {
    if r.pos == len(r.data) { return 0, io.EOF }
    n := copy(p, r.data[r.pos:]); r.pos += n; return n, nil
}

This is deliberately boring. A provider adapter can call its search endpoint, including Infrai’s POST /v1/vector/query or POST /v1/web/search, then translate the response into Page. The answerer never learns a provider’s field names. Infrai’s plain REST surface is useful here because a Go net/http client can call it without installing an SDK; the same adapter boundary lets you swap in another backend later.

Buy, build, or keep the boundary portable

The right comparison is operational, not a leaderboard. A news desk cares about evidence review, ACL correctness, and what happens when a provider changes ranking behavior.

Option Good fit Trade-off for this workflow
Elasticsearch Teams already operating inverted indexes and vector search together Powerful controls, but cluster tuning and upgrades become part of the on-call budget
OpenSearch Organizations wanting an open-source-compatible search stack Migration flexibility is attractive; plugin and version compatibility still need testing
Pinecone A managed vector-first service with a small platform team Low cluster operations, but you must design lexical filtering, metadata rules, and export paths carefully
Infrai A thin adapter behind an explicit retrieval contract One REST API and one key reduce client integration work; verify collection, filtering, and cursor semantics against your own fixtures

The supporting Infrai advantage is consistency across capabilities: one key and a common HTTP convention can keep search code aligned with other backend calls. That is useful when the news service already has several providers, but it is not a reason to discard a specialist that offers a feature you require.

The catch is important. Infrai is not the best choice when you need deep, provider-specific control over shard layout, custom analyzers, or a mature offline export and replay toolchain. Stick with Elasticsearch or OpenSearch when those controls are central to your SLO. Choose Pinecone when managed vector operations outweigh the need to own a broader search stack. A reversible interface makes each decision less permanent.

A runbook for failed searches

Start from the answer and walk backward. Capture the request contract, collection, tenant, ACL predicate, query text, embedding model identifier, candidate count, rerank count, cursor, and snapshot. Then compare a failing query with a known-good fixture.

If recall is low, inspect ingestion and chunking before raising top-k. Missing PDF pages, language mismatches, and stale ACL metadata are common causes. If precision is low, check lexical filters and duplicate documents, then test a reranker on a bounded candidate set. A 429 is a capacity signal: apply exponential backoff and honor Retry-After; do not turn a rate limit into a tight retry loop.

Measure the stages separately. Set an SLO for retrieval completion and another for citation validity, because a fast answer with unverifiable sources is still a failed user request. Keep a sample of query, selected IDs, scores, and final citations with tenant-safe redaction. This lets you replay a regression after a provider migration without retaining unnecessary article text.

Pagination deserves its own test matrix: insert a document between page requests, revoke a tenant permission, duplicate an article, and repeat a cursor. The expected result is deterministic behavior under the declared snapshot policy, plus a visible signal when the policy cannot be honored.

When this design does not apply

Do not force semantic retrieval onto a workload that is fundamentally an exact lookup, such as a legal document ID or a strict publication-date export. A relational query or a specialist inverted index is clearer there. Likewise, if the editorial requirement is a continuously changing “latest” feed with no stable review trail, cursor snapshots may be the wrong product decision; state that limitation instead of promising archival citations.

The design is also a poor fit when the team cannot maintain representative evaluation documents. Without recall and precision checks, changing chunk size or ranking thresholds is guesswork. I’m not sure any vendor can remove that uncertainty; the missing ingredient is a test corpus and a reviewable contract.

For the common case, however, the boundary pays off: explicit collections, bounded staged retrieval, preserved ACL metadata, and citations that survive pagination. If that contract fits your system, the Infrai documentation is one place to inspect the available REST capabilities before wiring an adapter.

References

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/knn-search.html
  • https://opensearch.org/docs/latest/vector-search/
  • https://docs.pinecone.io/guides/indexes/understanding-indexes

title: Now Open Source: TorchTPU and the TPU Agent Suite for Native PyTorch on Google Cloud TPUs
description:
We’re excited to share that TorchTPU—our native PyTorch stack for Google Cloud TPUs—is now open source on GitHub, alongside the early preview of the TPU Agent Suite!

Co-developed with the PyTorch team at Meta, TorchTPU brings Cloud TPUs (v5e, v5p, v6e, and v7 / Ironwood) alongside GPUs and CPUs as a native backend option for PyTorch. You can now train, fine-tune, and serve PyTorch models on TPUs with minimal code changes using the standard APIs and open-source tools you already rely on.

⚡ Quickstart: Installing TorchTPU

You can install the latest torch_tpu release directly via pip (Python 3.11+):

python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

pip install torch_tpu --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu

🛠️ What’s Included in TorchTPU?

⚬ Native PyTorch Experience: Debug models effortlessly in eager mode (.to("tpu")) and transition to production-grade performance with torch.compile(), backed by custom ATen kernels and an XLA compilation cache.
⚬ Out-of-the-Box Ecosystem Integrations:
⚬ Hugging Face: Deploy popular open-weight models natively in Transformers v5 simply by passing device_map="tpu", plus native Diffusers support.
⚬ High-Throughput Serving: Native PyTorch backends for vLLM and SGLang, paired with llm-d for prefix-cache-aware Kubernetes fleet routing across GKE.
⚬ Distributed Training & RL at Scale: Production-grade integrations with TorchTitan (SimpleFSDP, custom Pallas kernels), VeRL for post-training/RL alignment, and Ray for heterogeneous compute orchestration.

🤖 Introducing the TPU Agent Suite (Early Preview)

To make onboarding and performance tuning even faster, we’ve also open-sourced the TPU Agent Suite in preview. It provides declarative bundles of multi-agent skills, routing protocols, and tools that compile and install natively across coding agent harnesses (including Claude Code and Antigravity, with Codex and Cursor support coming soon).

With the tpu-agent skill enabled, you can use natural language prompts directly in your coding environment to automate:

⚬ Model Onboarding & Benchmarking: Spin up vLLM inference servers on torch_tpu, run test completions, and benchmark TTFT, ITL, and throughput.
⚬ Profiling & Diagnostics: Analyze XProf profiles to pinpoint memory bottlenecks and TPU compute utilization.
⚬ Kernel Optimization: Optimize custom Pallas kernels and run automated self-refinement benchmark loops.

🔗 Resources & Links

⚬ TorchTPU GitHub Repository: https://github.com/google-pytorch/torch_tpu
⚬ TPU Agent Suite GitHub Repository: https://github.com/google-pytorch/tpu-agent-suite
⚬ Official Google Cloud Documentation: https://docs.cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/pytorch-on-tpu
⚬ Launch Blog Post: https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/ai-infrastructure/torchtpu-is-now-open-source-run-native-pytorch-on-tpus

We’d love for you to try out both projects! If you have questions about migrating a workload, feedback on the agent skills, or run into any issues, drop a reply below or open an issue directly on the GitHub trackers. What PyTorch workloads are you most excited to test on TPUs?

title: Gostman: Unified Cross-Platform API Client Supporting REST, GraphQL, gRPC, WebSocket Across Go Versions and Environments
description:
Introduction to Gostman: A Unified API Client Solution

In the fragmented landscape of API development, where REST, GraphQL, gRPC, and WebSocket protocols coexist, developers often grapple with toolchain fragmentation. Each protocol demands specialized clients, and cross-platform compatibility becomes a nightmare. Gostman emerges as a unified solution, addressing this core problem by consolidating all request logic into a single Go engine. This engine, residing in the engine/ directory, handles everything from variable substitution to OAuth 2 authentication using the Go standard library and x/net/publicsuffix. The result? A consistent request pipeline shared across desktop, CLI, and web versions, eliminating environment-specific quirks.

Consider the CLI implementation: gostman run executes collections, generates JUnit reports, and enforces CI compatibility with non-zero exit codes on failures. Pre/post scripts run in a sandboxed JavaScript environment via goja, pinned to a Go 1.24-compatible commit. This decision, while pragmatic, introduces a security trade-off: delayed access to goja patches. However, the alternative—upgrading to Go 1.25—would break Wails CLI compatibility, a dependency deadlock resolved by prioritizing backward compatibility over cutting-edge features.

The MCP server exemplifies another constraint-driven design. Instead of relying on the official Go SDK (which requires Go 1.25), Gostman uses a handwritten stdio implementation. This workaround avoids Wails CLI limitations but sacrifices robustness. Secrets are redacted before reaching coding agents, a security mechanism that prevents accidental exposure. Yet, this custom solution lacks the SDK’s error handling maturity, a failure mode under edge cases like concurrent agent requests.

Gostman’s gRPC handling further illustrates its modularity. Services are loaded via server reflection or protocompile, bypassing protoc dependencies. While reflection avoids configuration overhead, it assumes service discoverability—a risk in environments with disabled reflection. YAML collections, stored as plain files, prioritize version control simplicity over advanced features like schema validation. This trade-off is deliberate: complexity in collection management would undermine Gostman’s open-source ethos.

In summary, Gostman’s architecture is a causal response to the API client ecosystem’s fragmentation. Its unified engine, cross-platform consistency, and constraint-aware implementations (e.g., Go version pinning, custom MCP server) deliver a practical solution for modern developers. However, these choices also embed failure points: security delays from pinned dependencies, robustness gaps in custom implementations, and protocol-specific limitations. Gostman’s value lies not in perfection, but in its ability to balance constraints while delivering a functional, unified API client.

Architectural Deep Dive: Design and Cross-Platform Compatibility

Gostman’s architecture is a masterclass in balancing technical constraints with functional requirements. At its core lies a single Go engine that consolidates all request logic—variable substitution, authentication, body encoding, redirects, cookie management, OAuth 2, proxy handling, and certificate management. This engine, housed in the engine/ directory, leverages the Go standard library and x/net/publicsuffix to ensure consistency across REST, GraphQL, gRPC, and WebSocket protocols. The engine’s modularity is its superpower: it’s invoked by the Wails v2 desktop app, the CLI, and the Vercel-hosted web proxy, ensuring that every request is built and sent identically, regardless of the environment. This unification directly addresses the fragmentation in API development, where specialized clients often lead to toolchain incompatibility and cross-platform inconsistencies.

CLI and CI Integration: The Devil in the Details

The CLI, powered by gostman run, is a workhorse for developers. It executes collections from folders or exports, generates JUnit-compatible output, and exits with a non-zero code on test failures—a critical feature for CI/CD pipelines. However, the CLI’s scripting capability, which relies on goja for pre-request and post-response scripts, introduces a trade-off. Goja is pinned to a specific commit compatible with Go 1.24 to ensure Wails CLI compatibility. This decision, while pragmatic, delays access to security patches and new features. The risk here is clear: if a critical vulnerability is discovered in goja, Gostman users are exposed until the pinned commit is updated. The causal chain is straightforward: pinning → delayed updates → prolonged exposure to vulnerabilities.

MCP Server: A Pragmatic Workaround with Hidden Risks

The MCP server, designed to enable coding agents to send saved requests, is a custom implementation over stdio. This approach was necessitated by the Wails CLI’s inability to load packages built for Go 1.25, which the official SDK requires. While this workaround avoids dependency conflicts, it sacrifices robustness. The server redacts secrets before output reaches the agent, but the lack of mature error handling means it’s susceptible to failures under edge cases, such as concurrent requests overwhelming the stdio pipeline. The trade-off is stark: custom implementation → reduced robustness → potential failures under load. A more robust solution would involve waiting for Wails CLI to support Go 1.25, but this delays immediate functionality—a classic time-to-market vs. long-term stability dilemma.

gRPC Handling: Reflection vs. Protocompile

Gostman’s gRPC support is a study in modularity. It loads services via server reflection or .proto files using protocompile, eliminating the need for protoc. Reflection avoids configuration overhead but assumes service discoverability, which may fail in environments where services are not properly exposed. Protocompile, on the other hand, provides a more deterministic approach but requires access to .proto files. The choice here depends on the environment: if service discoverability is guaranteed → use reflection; otherwise, rely on protocompile. The risk with reflection is undiscoverable services → failed gRPC requests → pipeline breakage.

YAML Collections: Simplicity with a Cost

Collections in Gostman are stored as plain YAML files, a decision driven by the open-source ethos of simplicity and version control compatibility. However, this simplicity comes at a cost: YAML lacks schema validation and advanced features like inheritance. While this keeps the barrier to entry low, it opens the door to human errors in collection configuration. The causal chain is clear: lack of validation → misconfigured collections → runtime failures. A potential mitigation would be to introduce optional schema validation, but this would complicate the user experience—a trade-off between simplicity and robustness.

Cross-Platform Compatibility: The Unifying Thread

Gostman’s ability to function across desktop, CLI, and web environments is its defining feature. This compatibility is achieved through the unified engine architecture, which abstracts away platform-specific details. However, this abstraction introduces a failure mode: engine-environment mismatches. For example, a feature that works seamlessly in the desktop app might fail in the web proxy due to differences in resource availability or runtime constraints. The rule here is simple: if a feature relies on platform-specific capabilities → it will fail in other environments. Mitigating this requires rigorous cross-platform testing, but even then, edge cases will slip through.

Conclusion: A Balanced Solution with Known Trade-Offs

Gostman’s architecture is a testament to constraint-aware design. By unifying request logic, prioritizing cross-platform consistency, and making pragmatic trade-offs, it delivers a functional solution to the fragmentation in API development. However, these trade-offs—pinning dependencies, custom implementations, and protocol-specific limitations—introduce failure points that must be managed. The optimal solution depends on the context: if cross-platform consistency is paramount → use Gostman; if robustness under edge cases is critical → consider specialized clients. Gostman’s value lies in its ability to balance these constraints, making it a powerful tool for modern developers—but one that requires awareness of its limitations.

Practical Applications and Use Cases

Gostman’s unified architecture and cross-protocol support make it a versatile tool for diverse API-driven scenarios. Below are six real-world use cases, analyzed through the lens of its system mechanisms, environment constraints, and typical failures.

1. Cross-Platform API Testing in CI/CD Pipelines

Gostman’s CLI (gostman run) is designed for CI/CD integration, executing collections from YAML files and generating JUnit-compatible output. The non-zero exit code on test failures ensures pipeline integrity. However, this relies on the Go 1.24-pinned goja for scripting, which introduces a security trade-off: delayed patches due to version pinning. For example, a pre-request script with a vulnerability remains unpatched until the pinned commit is updated. Rule: Use Gostman for CI/CD if Go 1.24 compatibility is non-negotiable; otherwise, consider specialized tools with up-to-date dependencies.

2. Secure API Interaction in Coding Agents

The MCP server enables coding agents to send saved requests via a custom stdio implementation, redacting secrets before output. This workaround avoids Go 1.25 dependency conflicts with Wails CLI but lacks robust error handling. For instance, concurrent requests may overwhelm stdio, causing data corruption or pipeline failure. Rule: Use MCP server for lightweight agent integration; avoid for high-concurrency scenarios.

3. gRPC Service Testing Without Protoc

Gostman loads gRPC services via server reflection or protocompile, eliminating protoc dependencies. However, reflection assumes service discoverability, which fails if the service does not expose reflection APIs. For example, a private gRPC service without reflection enabled breaks the pipeline. Rule: Use reflection for discoverable services; fallback to protocompile with .proto files for private services.

4. Version-Controlled API Collections

Collections stored as plain YAML files enable seamless version control integration. However, the lack of schema validation increases the risk of misconfigurations. For instance, a typo in a YAML key (e.g., methdo: GET instead of method: GET) causes runtime failures. Rule: Use YAML for simplicity; enforce manual reviews or external validation tools for critical collections.

5. OAuth 2.0 Authentication Across Protocols

Gostman’s unified engine handles OAuth 2.0 authentication for REST, GraphQL, and WebSocket APIs. However, the shared cookie jar may cause conflicts in multi-tenant environments. For example, concurrent requests to different tenants overwrite cookies, leading to authentication failures. Rule: Use Gostman for single-tenant OAuth 2.0; isolate tenants with separate instances or custom cookie handling.

6. Desktop App API Debugging

The Wails v2 desktop app invokes the same engine as the CLI and web proxy, ensuring consistent request behavior. However, platform-specific resource limitations (e.g., memory constraints on low-end devices) may cause crashes during complex requests. For example, a large GraphQL query with deep nesting exhausts memory, terminating the app. Rule: Use the desktop app for lightweight debugging; offload complex requests to the CLI or web proxy.

In each case, Gostman’s strengths—unified logic, cross-protocol support, and modularity—are balanced against trade-offs like pinned dependencies, custom workarounds, and protocol limitations. Understanding these mechanisms enables informed decisions tailored to specific constraints and failure modes.

title: Building My Cloud Resume Challenge on AWS (Almost for Free)
description:
I recently finished the Cloud Resume Challenge: host a resume as a static site on a cloud provider, add a serverless visitor counter, define everything as code, and deploy it all through CI/CD. You can see the result at charliewinslow.com.

One goal drove most of my decisions: keep the bill as close to zero as possible. This post covers the architecture, how I kept costs down, and the things that broke along the way, which taught me more than the parts that worked on the first try.

The architecture

A visitor's browser resolves my domain through Route 53, which points at a CloudFront distribution. CloudFront serves the site over HTTPS using a free ACM certificate, and it pulls files from a private S3 bucket using Origin Access Control, so the bucket itself is never public.

When the page loads, a small script calls an API Gateway HTTP API. That triggers a Python Lambda function, which increments a counter in DynamoDB and returns the new count. The backend is defined in AWS SAM and lives in its own repository, separate from the frontend.

Keeping costs close to zero

  • HTTP API instead of REST API. It's cheaper and simpler, and it was all I needed.
  • On-demand DynamoDB. No provisioned capacity, so an idle table costs nothing.
  • CloudFront's Free flat-rate plan. AWS recently introduced flat-rate plans. The Free tier covers far more traffic than a resume will ever see, so there's no usage-based billing to think about.
  • A cheaper registrar. I compared domain prices and bought mine at Porkbun instead of Route 53, then delegated DNS to Route 53 so CloudFront aliases work cleanly.

The one recurring AWS charge is the Route 53 hosted zone, about fifty cents a month, plus the yearly domain renewal. Everything else runs in free-tier or no-cost territory at this traffic level.

Infrastructure as code

The backend (DynamoDB table, Lambda function, API, and IAM role) is one SAM template. The Lambda uses a DynamoDB update_item with ADD, which increments atomically, so two simultaneous visitors can't overwrite each other. Its IAM role allows exactly one action on exactly one table. I also marked the table DeletionPolicy: Retain so the count survives if the stack is ever deleted.

Unit tests run with pytest, with DynamoDB mocked by moto.

CI/CD without stored credentials

Both repos deploy with GitHub Actions. Instead of pasting AWS access keys into repository secrets, I used GitHub's OIDC provider. Each workflow requests a short-lived token that AWS exchanges for temporary credentials. Each repo has its own IAM role, and each role can only be assumed by runs on main of that specific repository.

The backend pipeline runs the tests and then deploys with sam build and sam deploy. The frontend pipeline syncs files to S3 and invalidates the CloudFront cache so changes appear within a couple of minutes.

What broke (and what I learned)

My CORS change never deployed

I tightened the API's CORS settings to allow only my own domains, deployed, and the API still returned a wildcard header. Checking the live Lambda's environment variables showed the old variable name. The cause was simple: I had edited the generated copy of the template inside .aws-sam/build instead of the real one at the project root, so every deploy rebuilt the old code. Lesson: when a deploy "succeeds" but behavior doesn't change, check what's actually running before assuming the new code is live.

That debugging also showed me that API Gateway's built-in CORS handling takes priority over headers set in the Lambda. For an origin that isn't allowed, it simply omits the header.

GitHub changed the OIDC subject claim

The first pipeline run failed with a "not authorized to assume role" error, even though my trust policy looked correct. I added a temporary step to the workflow that printed the token's claims. The subject now includes numeric IDs for my account and repository, not just their names, so my policy's expected string never matched. Updating the trust policy to the new format fixed it. Lesson: when an authentication error makes no sense, look at what's actually being sent, not what you assume is being sent.

CloudFormation used a different role than I expected

The next deploy failed, and the stack ended up in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED. The error named a CloudFormation service role attached to the stack. That role, not my GitHub role, does the actual resource changes, and it couldn't read the code package from the SAM bucket. I added the missing S3 permission, resumed the rollback with continue-update-rollback, and re-ran the pipeline. Lesson: know which identity is actually being denied. The error message names it.

A dry run caught a leak

Before the first frontend deploy, I ran aws s3 sync with --dryrun. It showed it was about to publish my IAM policy files, which I'd accidentally created inside the repo, along with editor config. They contained no secrets, but they would have exposed my account ID and permission layout. I moved them out and added exclusions. Lesson: preview anything that syncs or deletes.

What I'd do next

  • Add a smoke test that calls the live API after each backend deploy.
  • Add a billing alarm so a cost surprise gets caught early.
  • Trim the GitHub deploy role further now that I understand which role does the work.

Final thoughts

The challenge is a great way to touch a lot of AWS at once: networking, security, serverless, infrastructure as code, and pipelines. The most useful parts weren't the working architecture but the debugging, because each failure forced me to understand how the pieces really fit together.

The code is on GitHub: frontend and backend.

title: Amazon Connect Customer now supports customizing the Customer Profiles app on the agent workspace
description:
Amazon Connect Customer Profiles now allows administrators to customize which customer data that agents see in the agent workspace, and how it is displayed, using layouts they build in Profile Explorer. Customer Profiles provides agents with a real-time, unified view of each customer during interactions, combining contact history with customer data from multiple sources. Agents who handle different kinds of requests need different customer data in front of them.

Within Profile Explorer, administrators can create and save each layout of Customer Profiles widgets, such as contact history, contact information, and lifetime value calculated attributes, and assign it to agents in place of the legacy Customer Profiles view. To learn more about Profile Explorer, see Profile Explorer in the Amazon Connect Customer administrator guide.

title: Creating a Custom A4 Page Layout for TipTap 3 Editor to Replace Paid and Buggy Alternatives
description:
Introduction

Achieving a Word-style A4 page layout in TipTap 3 is deceptively complex. The problem isn’t just about dividing content into pages—it’s about preserving document integrity, handling edge cases like split tables and floated images, and ensuring the output remains clean and CSS-friendly. The official Pages extension, while functional, comes at a cost. Community alternatives, though free, often fail by directly modifying the document structure or breaking existing CSS rules. This creates a critical gap: developers are forced to choose between paying for a solution or accepting technical compromises that hinder productivity.

The Core Problem: Why Existing Solutions Fail

The root issue lies in how pagination is implemented. Most extensions modify the document’s DOM directly to enforce page breaks. This approach has two fatal flaws:

  • CSS Incompatibility: Direct DOM manipulation often conflicts with existing styles, causing margins, floats, and table layouts to break. For example, a floated image might overlap with text or a table header might disappear when split across pages.
  • Dirty HTML Output: Modifying the document structure means getHTML() returns altered markup, which disrupts workflows that rely on clean, unmodified content.

The Mechanism Behind tiptap-a4-pagination

To address these issues, tiptap-a4-pagination takes a fundamentally different approach. Instead of altering the document, it inserts spacer decorations at page boundaries. These spacers act as invisible markers that trigger page breaks without modifying the underlying structure. Here’s the causal chain:

  1. Impact: The editor content remains untouched, ensuring getHTML() returns clean, unmodified HTML.
  2. Internal Process: Spacer decorations are calculated dynamically based on the document’s height and the A4 page size. When the content exceeds the page height, a spacer is inserted to force a break.
  3. Observable Effect: The document appears paginated in the editor, but the underlying structure remains intact, preserving CSS compatibility.

Edge-Case Handling: Tables and Floated Images

Tables and floated images are where most pagination solutions fail. tiptap-a4-pagination handles these cases through specific mechanisms:

  • Tables: Tables are split between rows, never within a rowspan. The header row is automatically repeated on the next page. This is achieved by detecting table boundaries and inserting spacers only after complete rows, ensuring no data is truncated.
  • Floated Images: Floated elements are handled by adjusting the spacer height to account for the image’s position. This prevents overlaps and ensures the layout remains consistent across pages.

Why This Solution Dominates

Compared to alternatives, tiptap-a4-pagination is optimal because it:

  • Maintains clean HTML output, critical for workflows that rely on unmodified content.
  • Preserves CSS compatibility, avoiding the need to rewrite styles or fix broken layouts.
  • Handles complex elements like tables and floated images without compromising functionality.

The solution stops working if the document contains elements that dynamically change size (e.g., SVGs with responsive heights) or if the CSS uses non-standard box models. In such cases, the spacer calculations may become inaccurate, leading to misaligned page breaks.

Rule for Choosing a Solution

If you need A4 pagination in TipTap 3 and require clean HTML output with full CSS compatibility, use tiptap-a4-pagination. If your document contains dynamic or non-standard elements, consider pre-processing the content to ensure consistent sizing.

Try the demo with a long document or large table. Feedback, especially on edge cases, is welcome to further refine the solution.

Challenges with Existing Solutions

When I set out to achieve Word-style A4 pagination in TipTap 3, I quickly hit a wall with the available options. The official Pages extension was a non-starter due to its paid nature, leaving me to explore community alternatives. However, these alternatives introduced a cascade of issues, primarily CSS incompatibilities that disrupted my document’s layout. Let’s break down the core problems and why they forced me to build tiptap-a4-pagination.

CSS Breakage: The Root of the Problem

Community extensions often rely on direct DOM manipulation to enforce page breaks. While this approach seems straightforward, it ignores the delicate balance of CSS rules. For instance, inserting a `

with page-break-before: always` can collapse margins, misalign floated images, or truncate tables mid-row. The mechanism here is clear: injecting elements into the document structure triggers unintended side effects in CSS rendering, as browsers recalculate layout without preserving contextual rules.

In my case, floated images would overlap text, and tables would split mid-cell, rendering the document unusable. The observable effect was a visually broken layout, while the internal process involved CSS’s inability to reconcile forced breaks with existing styles.

Dirty HTML Output: A Hidden Cost

Another critical issue was the modification of the document structure. Community extensions often wrap content in additional containers or add inline styles to enforce pagination. This approach pollutes the HTML output, making it harder to process or export. For example, a clean `

element might end up nested inside a

` with arbitrary classes or styles. The causal chain here is: DOM manipulation → added markup → loss of semantic integrity → downstream processing issues.

This was unacceptable for my use case, as I needed to maintain a clean getHTML() output for further processing. Any solution that altered the document structure was a non-starter.

Why Existing Solutions Fail: A Comparative Analysis

  • Official Pages Extension: Effective but paid, making it inaccessible for budget-constrained projects. Its closed-source nature also limits customization.
  • Community Alternatives: Free but flawed. Their reliance on DOM manipulation breaks CSS and produces dirty HTML. For example, splitting a table mid-row instead of between rows leads to truncated data, as the browser’s table rendering engine cannot recover from incomplete rows.

The optimal solution needed to avoid both the cost barrier of the official extension and the technical flaws of community alternatives. This led to the development of tiptap-a4-pagination, which uses a spacer decoration mechanism to trigger page breaks without modifying the document structure.

Edge Cases and Limitations: Where It Breaks

While tiptap-a4-pagination solves the core problems, it’s not without limitations. The spacer decoration approach fails with dynamically sized elements, such as responsive SVGs or elements using non-standard CSS box models. The mechanism of failure is straightforward: dynamic sizing → unpredictable height calculations → misaligned spacers → incorrect page breaks.

For example, if an SVG expands beyond its initial height due to responsive styling, the spacer calculation will be off, causing the page break to occur prematurely or too late. The rule for adoption is clear: If your content includes dynamic or non-standard elements, pre-process them to ensure fixed dimensions before applying pagination.

Professional Judgment: When to Use tiptap-a4-pagination

Use tiptap-a4-pagination if you need a free, CSS-friendly A4 pagination solution that preserves clean HTML output. It’s particularly effective for documents with complex elements like tables and floated images. However, avoid it for content with dynamic sizing or non-standard CSS, as these will trigger misaligned page breaks. For such cases, either pre-process the content or consider alternative solutions—though none currently address all these issues without compromise.

Designing the Custom Solution: A Deep Dive into tiptap-a4-pagination

When I set out to create a Word-style A4 page layout for TipTap 3, the goal was clear: deliver a free, CSS-friendly solution that handles complex elements like tables and floated images without breaking the document’s integrity. The journey began with a frustration—paid extensions and buggy community alternatives left me with no choice but to build my own. Here’s the thought process and technical approach behind tiptap-a4-pagination.

The Core Problem: Preserving Document Integrity While Paginating

The primary challenge was to achieve pagination without modifying the document structure. Existing solutions either polluted the HTML with arbitrary markup or broke CSS rendering through direct DOM manipulation. For example, injecting page-break-before: always caused margin collapse and misaligned floated images. The causal chain was clear: DOM manipulation → browser layout recalculation → unintended CSS side effects.

To avoid this, I opted for a spacer decoration mechanism. Instead of altering the document, the extension inserts invisible spacers at page boundaries. These spacers trigger page breaks without touching the underlying HTML. The result? getHTML() stays clean, and CSS rendering remains intact. The mechanism works because spacers are calculated dynamically based on document height and A4 page size, ensuring breaks occur only when content exceeds page height.

Handling Edge Cases: Tables and Floated Images

Tables and floated images are where most pagination solutions fail. Here’s how tiptap-a4-pagination handles them:

  • Tables: Tables are split between rows, never inside a rowspan. The header row repeats on the next page to maintain context. Spacers are inserted after complete rows to prevent truncation. The risk here is splitting a table mid-row, which would break semantic integrity. By enforcing row-level splits, the solution avoids this.
  • Floated Images: Floated images require precise spacer height adjustments to prevent overlaps. The mechanism calculates the height of floated elements and adjusts spacers accordingly. Failure occurs if the image’s height is dynamic (e.g., responsive SVGs), causing misaligned breaks. The rule for adoption is clear: Pre-process dynamic elements to ensure fixed dimensions before applying pagination.

Why This Solution Dominates Alternatives

Compared to existing options, tiptap-a4-pagination is optimal for three reasons:

  • Clean HTML Output: By avoiding DOM manipulation, the solution preserves semantic integrity, ensuring downstream processing remains unaffected.
  • CSS Compatibility: Spacers don’t interfere with CSS rendering, preventing issues like margin collapse or misaligned floats.
  • Edge-Case Handling: Tables and floated images are managed without functionality loss, a common failure point in community alternatives.

However, the solution has limitations. It fails with dynamically sized elements or non-standard CSS box models, as these disrupt height calculations and cause misaligned spacers. The rule for adoption is categorical: If your content includes dynamic or non-standard elements, pre-process them to ensure fixed dimensions before using this extension.

Practical Insights and Professional Judgment

The spacer decoration mechanism is the linchpin of this solution. It’s lightweight (about 5 KB gzipped) and TipTap 3-specific, ensuring efficiency. For developers, the takeaway is clear: Avoid direct DOM manipulation for pagination. Instead, use decorations to trigger breaks without altering the document structure. This approach maintains both clean HTML and CSS compatibility, making it ideal for professional, paginated documents.

Test the solution with complex documents via the demo. Feedback, especially on edge cases, is welcome. The goal is to refine this tool further, ensuring it remains the go-to free alternative for TipTap 3 pagination.

Implementation and Testing of tiptap-a4-pagination

Step-by-Step Implementation

The core mechanism of tiptap-a4-pagination revolves around spacer decorations, which act as invisible markers inserted at page boundaries. These spacers trigger page breaks without modifying the document's HTML structure, ensuring clean output and CSS compatibility. Here’s how it’s implemented:

1. Spacer Decoration Mechanism

The system calculates the document’s height dynamically and inserts spacers when content exceeds the A4 page size. This is achieved by:

  • Measuring Content Height: The editor’s content is continuously measured using JavaScript’s getBoundingClientRect() to determine when it surpasses the A4 height (297mm or ~11.69 inches at 96 DPI).
  • Inserting Spacers: When the threshold is reached, a spacer decoration is inserted. This decoration is a zero-width, non-breaking element that forces a page break without altering the DOM structure.

2. Handling Tables

Tables are split between rows, never inside a rowspan, to maintain semantic integrity. The header row is repeated on the next page. This is implemented by:

  • Row-Level Splitting: The algorithm identifies complete rows and inserts spacers after them, ensuring no row is truncated.
  • Header Repetition: When a table spans multiple pages, the header row is cloned and inserted at the start of the next page.

3. Managing Floated Images

Floated images are handled by adjusting the spacer height to prevent overlaps. This involves:

  • Height Calculation: The height of floated elements is measured, and the spacer height is adjusted to accommodate them, ensuring layout consistency.
  • Edge-Case Handling: If a floated image spans multiple pages, the spacer ensures it doesn’t overlap with subsequent content.

Testing Process

Testing focused on ensuring functionality, compatibility, and edge-case handling. Key tests included:

1. Document Integrity

Verified that getHTML() remains clean and unmodified. This was confirmed by:

  • Before-and-After Comparison: Comparing the HTML output before and after pagination to ensure no additional markup was introduced.
  • Semantic Validation: Running the output through HTML validators to confirm semantic integrity.

2. CSS Compatibility

Tested with complex CSS layouts to ensure no breakage. This involved:

  • Margin Collapsing: Verifying that margins around floated elements and tables remained consistent.
  • Float Handling: Ensuring floated images didn’t overlap with text or other elements across page breaks.

3. Edge-Case Scenarios

Tested with documents containing large tables, multiple floated images, and dynamic elements. Key findings:

  • Table Splitting: Confirmed that tables split correctly between rows and headers repeated accurately.
  • Dynamic Element Failure: Identified that responsive SVGs and non-standard CSS box models caused misaligned page breaks due to unpredictable height calculations.

Practical Insights and Rules for Adoption

Based on testing, the following rules were formulated:

1. Optimal Use Cases

Use tiptap-a4-pagination if:

  • You need clean HTML output and CSS compatibility.
  • Your document contains complex elements like tables and floated images.

2. Limitations and Workarounds

Avoid using it if:

  • Your content includes dynamically sized elements (e.g., responsive SVGs) or non-standard CSS box models.
  • Workaround: Pre-process dynamic elements to ensure fixed dimensions before applying pagination.

3. Key Takeaway

Avoid direct DOM manipulation for pagination. Use decorations to trigger breaks while preserving document structure and CSS compatibility. This approach ensures reliability and maintains professional document integrity.

For hands-on testing, visit the demo and experiment with long documents or large tables. Feedback on edge cases is highly encouraged to further refine the solution.

Results and Benefits: A Custom A4 Layout That Works

After battling paid extensions and buggy community hacks, tiptap-a4-pagination delivers a free, CSS-friendly A4 layout for TipTap 3. Here’s how it outperforms alternatives and what it means for your documents.

Core Mechanism: Spacer Decorations, Not DOM Surgery

The solution avoids the cardinal sin of pagination tools: direct DOM manipulation. Instead, it inserts invisible spacer decorations at page boundaries. These spacers act as triggers for page breaks without altering the document structure. Why this matters:

  • Clean HTML Output: getHTML() remains untouched, preserving semantic integrity for downstream processing.
  • CSS Compatibility: No injected elements mean browsers don’t recalculate layouts, preventing margin collapse, float misalignment, or table truncation.

Handling Complex Elements: Tables and Floated Images

Tables: Split Rows, Repeat Headers

Tables are split between rows, never inside a rowspan. The header row is cloned and repeated on the next page. Mechanism: Spacers are inserted after complete rows, ensuring no truncation. This enforces row-level splits, maintaining semantic integrity.

Edge Case: Tables with dynamic row heights (e.g., responsive SVGs) fail because spacer height calculations become unpredictable. Rule: Pre-process tables to ensure fixed row dimensions before pagination.

Floated Images: Adjusted Spacers Prevent Overlaps

Floated images are handled by adjusting spacer height based on the image’s dimensions. Mechanism: The spacer “pushes” the content down, preventing overlaps with subsequent text or images. Limitation: Dynamically sized images (e.g., responsive SVGs) disrupt this calculation, causing misalignment. Rule: Fix image dimensions before applying pagination.

Advantages Over Alternatives: Why This Solution Dominates

Compared to paid extensions (e.g., TipTap’s official Pages) and community hacks, tiptap-a4-pagination excels in:

  • Cost: Free, eliminating budget constraints.
  • Document Integrity: Preserves clean HTML, unlike hacks that wrap content in arbitrary <div>s.
  • CSS Reliability: Avoids layout recalculations, ensuring floated images and margins behave as expected.

Typical Choice Error: Opting for community hacks due to cost, only to face CSS breakage and dirty HTML. Rule: If clean HTML and CSS compatibility are non-negotiable, use tiptap-a4-pagination.

Limitations: Where It Breaks and Why

The solution fails with dynamically sized elements (e.g., responsive SVGs, non-standard CSS box models). Mechanism: Dynamic heights disrupt spacer calculations, leading to misaligned page breaks. Rule: Pre-process content to ensure fixed dimensions before pagination.

Practical Insights: When to Use It

Optimal Use Cases:

  • Complex documents with tables and floated images.
  • Projects requiring clean HTML output for downstream processing.
  • CSS-heavy layouts where margin collapsing or float behavior must be preserved.

Avoid For: Content with dynamic sizing or non-standard CSS unless pre-processed. Key Takeaway: Decorations, not DOM manipulation, are the reliable path to pagination in TipTap 3.

Demo and Feedback: Test the Limits

Try the demo (link) with long documents or large tables. Challenge it: Submit edge cases (e.g., responsive SVGs, non-standard CSS) to help refine the solution. Feedback drives improvement.

Conclusion and Future Improvements

The development of tiptap-a4-pagination addresses a critical gap in TipTap 3's functionality by providing a free, CSS-friendly A4 page layout solution. By avoiding direct DOM manipulation and instead using spacer decorations, this extension preserves document integrity and maintains clean HTML output—a stark contrast to paid and community alternatives that often disrupt CSS or pollute the document structure.

Key Takeaways

  • Mechanism Matters: The spacer decoration mechanism triggers page breaks without altering the document, ensuring CSS compatibility and semantic integrity. This is achieved by inserting invisible, zero-width elements at calculated page boundaries, which prevents layout recalculations that cause margin collapse or float misalignment.
  • Edge-Case Handling: Tables split between rows (never inside rowspan), with headers repeating on subsequent pages. Floated images are accommodated by adjusting spacer heights, though dynamically sized elements (e.g., responsive SVGs) remain a limitation due to unpredictable height calculations.
  • Practical Insights: At ~5 KB gzipped, the solution is lightweight and TipTap 3-specific, making it ideal for professional paginated documents. However, pre-processing dynamic or non-standard elements is essential to ensure fixed dimensions and accurate pagination.

Encouraging Adoption

For developers and users seeking a reliable, free A4 pagination solution, tiptap-a4-pagination is the optimal choice when:

  • Clean HTML output is non-negotiable.
  • CSS compatibility must be preserved, especially in layouts with tables and floated images.
  • Dynamic or non-standard elements are pre-processed to ensure fixed dimensions.

Avoid this solution if your content relies heavily on dynamically sized elements without pre-processing, as it will lead to misaligned page breaks due to disrupted height calculations.

Future Improvements

While tiptap-a4-pagination is a robust solution, there’s room for enhancement:

  • Dynamic Element Support: Implementing a mechanism to detect and adjust spacers for dynamically sized elements could eliminate the need for pre-processing. This might involve real-time height recalculations or integration with responsive design frameworks.
  • Non-Standard CSS Handling: Extending support for non-standard CSS box models (e.g., box-sizing: border-box) would broaden compatibility, though this requires careful handling of element dimensions.
  • Performance Optimization: While already lightweight, further reducing the computational overhead of spacer calculations could improve performance for very large documents.

Final Judgment

tiptap-a4-pagination is the most effective solution for TipTap 3 users needing A4 pagination with clean HTML and CSS compatibility. Its spacer decoration mechanism outshines alternatives by preserving document integrity and handling complex elements like tables and floated images. However, its limitations with dynamic elements underscore the need for pre-processing or future enhancements. If you prioritize document consistency and avoid dynamic sizing pitfalls, this extension is a must-adopt.

Test the solution with edge cases via the demo and contribute feedback to refine its capabilities. The future of TipTap 3 pagination depends on such collaborative efforts.
